## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.
## Introductory Verses

The noble practice of the perfections, accumulated by the Great Seer (the Buddha) who constantly seeks virtues such as morality, is for the welfare of all beings in the entire world. I pay homage to that Leader of the world, of inconceivable power.

The Buddhas, endowed with the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen conducts, are able to lead beings out of the suffering of the cycle of existence through the practice of the four paths, the four fruits, Nibbāna, and the scriptures (Pariyatti). I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, which is superior to all in the world.

The assembly of Noble Ones (Ariya Saṅgha) is always established in the paths and fruits and is endowed with virtues such as morality. I pay homage to that assembly of the Ariya Saṅgha, which is like an unsurpassed field for planting merit.

There is merit generated by thus paying homage to the Triple Gem. By the power of that merit, may I be free from obstacles in all places.

The perfections such as giving (dāna), which were well-accumulated in this Bhadda-kappa and are difficult for others to perform, have reached the state of supreme perfections.

To manifest the power and influence of those practices for enlightenment (sambodhicariyā), the Buddha, the refuge of the world, while residing at the Nigrodhārāma monastery in the Sakyan country, taught the teaching named Cariyāpiṭaka to the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), who is like a pinnacle among all disciples.

The great elders such as Mahākassapa, who performed the rehearsal of the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya, recited the Cariyāpiṭaka in the Khuddaka Nikāya, which illustrates the fulfillment of the causes of the Teacher's perfections.
2:
Although it is difficult for me to provide an explanation of the meaning of this Cariyāpiṭaka teaching in accordance with the method of analyzing the requisites of omniscience (pāramīs), I shall do so because the ancient teachers have preserved the Teacher's Dispensation along with the commentaries, and because the established decisions (vinicchaya) still exist. Therefore, by relying on and thoroughly immersing myself in the ancient commentary (Porāṇaṭṭhakathā) of the residents of the Mahāvihāra—which is based on the Jātakas, follows the path of the traditional recitations, is extremely pure and undisturbed, and contains subtle decisions on meaning—and by illuminating the perfections through the distinctions of explicit meaning (nītattha) and implicit meaning (neyyattha), I shall compose this explanation of the meaning of the Cariyāpiṭaka.

May the virtuous ones listen and record from me as I analyze the meaning of this Cariyāpiṭaka, desiring the long-lasting endurance of the True Dhamma.

In this context of the Cariyāpiṭaka, for what reason is it called 'Cariyāpiṭaka'? It is called Cariyāpiṭaka because it is the scripture (pariyatti) that manifests the power of the Teacher's conduct in past lives. Here, the word 'piṭaka' has the meaning of 'scripture' (pariyatti), as in the phrase 'mā piṭakasampadānena' (do not go by the authority of the scriptures). Alternatively, it is called Cariyāpiṭaka because that scripture serves as a vessel (bhājana) for manifesting the power of the Teacher's conduct in previous lives. The word 'piṭaka' is also shown to have the meaning of 'vessel' (receptacle), as in the phrase 'then a man might come, taking a hoe and a basket (piṭaka).'

This Cariyāpiṭaka is included within the Suttanta Piṭaka among the three baskets: Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among the five Nikāyas—Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya—it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine limbs of the Teacher's Dispensation (sāsananga)—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—it is classified as Gāthā (Verses).

(As Venerable Ānanda stated:) "I learned eighty-two thousand teachings from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks (such as Sāriputta); thus, the teachings present in me are eighty-four thousand."
3:
Thus, it is a collection of some of the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates (dhammakkhandhas) acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda. In terms of groups (vaggas), it is a collection of three groups: Akitti Vagga, Hatthināga Vagga, and Yudhañjaya Vagga. In terms of practices (cariyās), it is a collection of thirty-five practices: ten in the Akitti Vagga, ten in the Hatthināga Vagga, and fifteen in the Yudhañjaya Vagga. Among these three groups, the Akitti Vagga is the first; among the practices, the Akitti Cariyā is the first. In that Akitti Cariyā, this verse is the beginning:

"Whatever practice was performed within
Four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons,
All of that was for the purpose of maturing enlightenment."

From this verse onwards, the explanation of the meaning will proceed in order.

## The Introductory Verse Section is Finished.

## Discussion on the Origins (Nidānakathā)

When this explanation of the meaning is spoken by showing these three origins—the Distant Origin (Dūrenidāna), the Not-so-distant Origin (Avidūrenidāna), and the Proximate Origin (Santikenidāna)—it is well understood by the listeners from the beginning of the fulfillment of the perfections. Therefore, the classification of these origins should be known as follows:

The sequence of the story from the time the Great Bodhisatta made his resolution at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until his rebirth in the Tusita heaven is called the Distant Origin. The sequence of the story from the time he left the Tusita heaven until his attainment of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa) is called the Not-so-distant Origin. The sequence of the story from the time at the Great Bodhimaṇḍa until the events of the present is called the Proximate Origin. Among these three origins, since the Distant Origin and the Not-so-distant Origin are common to all (Buddhas), they should be understood in detail according to the method extensively explained in the Jātaka Commentary. However, since there are specific details in the Proximate Origin, this is a summary starting from the beginning of all three origins.
4:
The Blessed One, who had made the aspiration at the feet of the Blessed Dīpaṅkara, being a Bodhisatta and the refuge of the three worlds, fulfilled the thirty perfections (pāramīs) in accordance with his aspiration. Having brought the requisites for omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) to completion, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Waiting for the appropriate time to become a Buddha, he stayed there for the full lifespan. Passing away from there, he took conception in the Sakyan royal family. Growing up with great retinue and noble glory, he eventually reached youth. At the age of twenty-nine, he made the Great Renunciation. After practicing the great striving (dukkharacariyā) for six years, while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the full-moon day of Vesākha, he defeated the host of Māra even before the sun had set. In the first watch of the night, he recollected the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa); in the middle watch, he purified the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu); and in the last watch, he exhausted the fifteen hundred defilements and realized the peerless supreme enlightenment (sammā-sambodhi).

After becoming a Buddha, he spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) in that very place. On the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, he went to the Deer Park in Isipatana near Vārāṇasī. There, he offered the nectar of Dhamma to eighteen crores of Brahmas, led by Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). Having established Yasa and other veneyyas in the fruit of Arahantship, he dispatched those sixty Arahants to benefit the people of the world. While traveling to the Uruvelā forest, he established the thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so on in the Kappāsika grove. Proceeding to Uruvelā, he displayed three thousand five hundred miracles and disciplined the three matted-hair ascetic brothers, led by Uruvelā Kassapa, along with their thousand followers. Surrounded by those thousand ascetics, he stayed at the Laṭṭhivana Garden near the city of Rājagaha. There, he led one hundred and twenty thousand brahmins and householders, headed by King Bimbisāra, to enter the Dispensation (Sāsana) and resided at the Veဠုဝန (Veḷuvana) Monastery built and donated by the King of Magadha.

While the Blessed One was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, after Sāriputta and Moggallāna had been appointed to the position of Chief Disciples and the assembly of disciples had taken place, King Suddhodana, the father, heard: "My son, after practicing austerities (dukkharacariyā) for six years, has attained supreme enlightenment, set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, and is now residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery near the city of Rājagaha." He then sent ten ministers in succession, each accompanied by ten thousand men, saying, "Bring my son here and show him to me." Those ministers went to Rājagaha and, through the Buddha's teaching of the Dhamma, were established in the fruit of Arahantship. Subsequently, when Elder Kāludāyī informed the Buddha of the King's wish, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, departed from Rājagaha and reached the city of Kapilavatthu, sixty yojanas away, after a journey of two months. The Sakyan princes assembled, thinking, "We shall see the noblest of our kin." They prepared the Nigrodhārāma Garden for the Blessed One and the community of monks to reside in, and holding perfumes and flowers, they went out to welcome him and escorted the Blessed One to the Nigrodhārāma Garden. At that time, the Blessed One sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared for him, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants. The Sakyan princes, being stiff with pride, did not pay homage to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, observing their inclination, in order to break their pride and to analyze and preach the Dhamma to them, entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā), and from that fourth jhāna...
5:
(The Blessed One) reached the city of Kapilavatthu, sixty yojanas away, after two months. The Sakyan princes consulted and assembled together, thinking, "We shall see the noblest of our kin." They had the Nigrodhārāma Monastery built, which was suitable for the Blessed One and the community of monks (Saṅgha) to reside in, and holding perfumes, flowers, and so on in their hands, they went out to welcome him. They escorted the Blessed One to the Nigrodhārāma Monastery. At that time, the Blessed One sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared for him, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants. The Sakyan princes, being stiff with pride, did not pay homage to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, observing their inclination, in order to break their pride and to make them fit to listen to the Dhamma, entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā). Rising from it, he ascended into the sky and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) of water and fire, similar to the miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree, as if sprinkling dust from his soles upon the heads of those Sakyans. King Suddhodana, the father, seeing that wonder, paid homage, saying, "This son of mine is the supreme person in the world." When the King paid homage, the Sakyans could no longer remain without doing so, and all the Sakyans paid homage.

At that time, while performing the Twin Miracle, the Blessed One also performed the miracle of the Opening of the Worlds (Loka-vivaraṇa). While that miracle was taking place, people, remaining just as they were standing or sitting in the human world, saw with their own fleshly eyes (maṃsa-cakkhu), by the power of the Buddha, all the devas and brahmas from the Cātumahārājika heaven up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, playing in their respective mansions with divine power, shining brightly, enjoying great divine splendor, experiencing the bliss of peaceful attainments (samāpatti), and discussing the Dhamma with one another. Likewise, they saw the beings suffering great misery in the eight great hells in the earth below, the sixteen Ussada hells, and the Lokantara hell. Devas in the ten thousand world-systems also approached the Tathāgata with great divine power, and with hearts full of wonder and amazement, they worshipped and attended upon him with joined palms. They praised him by reciting verses related to the Buddha's qualities, clapped their hands, laughed joyfully, and expressed their rapture and happiness. With reference to such joy and delight, it is said:

"The earth-dwelling devas, those of Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa,
the Yāma devas, the Tusita, and the Nimmānarati,
the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, and those of the Brahma-kayika host,
being full of joy, made a great and extensive shout."
6:
At that time, the Blessed One, who is endowed with the ten powers, motivated by Great Compassion and thinking, "I shall display my incomparable Buddha-power," created a walkway in the sky as long as the gathering of ten thousand world-systems and twelve leagues wide, made of all kinds of jewels. Standing on that walkway, he displayed a miracle that was a focal point for the eyes of devas and humans like a flock of birds, a wondrous marvel not shared by others, demonstrating the power of the concentration and knowledge of the Buddhas. Then, walking upon that walkway, he taught the Dhamma with an inconceivable power and incomparable Buddha-grace, according to the inclinations of those ready to be tamed. Thus it was said:

"These devas and humans do not know what kind of person this Buddha is, the Supreme Man. They do not know what the power of his psychic abilities, the power of his wisdom, and the Buddha-power of the one who brings welfare to the world are like.

These devas and humans do not know that this Buddha is such a person, the Supreme Man. They do not know that the power of his psychic abilities, the power of his wisdom, and the Buddha-power of the one who brings welfare to the world are like this.

Now, I shall display the incomparable Buddha-power. I shall create a walkway in the sky, adorned with jewels."

While the Tathāgata was thus teaching the Dhamma after displaying the miracle that demonstrates his Buddha-power, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, staying on Gijjhakūṭa Hill in Rājagaha, saw this with his divine eye. Having a mind filled with wonder and amazement due to that demonstration of Buddha-power, the thought arose in him, "Now, I shall make the Buddha's power even more manifest to the world." He informed his retinue of five hundred monks of this matter and immediately came through the air by psychic power. Approaching the Blessed One with his retinue, he prostrated with the fivefold touch, and raising his joined palms like a blossoming lotus to his head, he asked about the Tathāgata's Great Aspiration (Mahābhinīhāra) and the fulfillment of the perfections (Pāramī). The Blessed One, making the Venerable Sāriputta a personal witness, and wishing to demonstrate his Buddha-power to the assembly of people gathered there as well as to the devas and Brahmās of the ten thousand world-systems, taught the Buddhavaṃsa discourse. Thus it was said:

Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna, having reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom, asks the Leader of the World: "O Great Hero, O Supreme Man, what was your Great Aspiration (Abhinīhāra) like? O Wise One, at what time did you aspire for the supreme Enlightenment (Bodhi)..."
7:
Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna, having reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom, asks the Leader of the World:

"O Great Hero, O Supreme Man, what was your Buddha-aspiration (Abhinīhāra) like? O Wise One, at what time did you aspire for the supreme Enlightenment (Sabbaññutañāṇa)?

What were your generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), renunciation (nekkhamma), wisdom (paññā), and energy (viriya) like? What were your patience (khanti), truthfulness (sacca), determination (adhiṭṭhāna), loving-kindness (mettā), and equanimity (upekkhā) like?

O Leader of the World, O Wise One, in what manner did you fulfill the ten perfections? How did you complete the secondary perfections (upapāramī)? And how did you complete the ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī)?

When thus questioned, the Buddha, whose voice is as sweet as that of the Karavīka bird, replied, bringing peace to the hearts of devas and humans and causing them to rejoice."

When the Blessed One had thus taught the Buddhavaṃsa discourse, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, directed his knowledge toward the attributes of the Buddha, thinking: "Oh, how wonderful is the attainment of the causes of the Buddhas! Oh, how wonderful is the success of their achievement! Oh, how wonderful is the fulfillment of the Great Aspiration! Indeed, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task by fulfilling the perfections for such a long time. This fruit—namely, mastery over omniscience and the powers, and such great psychic power and majesty—is truly worthy of the accumulation of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra)."

That Venerable Sāriputta contemplated the Buddha's virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation, shame, fear of wrongdoing, faith, energy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, purification of virtue, purification of view, tranquility, insight, the 3 roots of wholesome action, the 3 types of good conduct, the 3 types of right thought, the 3 types of blameless perception, the 3 elements, the 4 foundations of mindfulness, the 4 right efforts, the 4 bases of psychic power, the 4 noble paths, the 4 noble fruits, the 4 analytical insights, the knowledges that distinguish the 4 modes of birth, the 4 noble lineages, the 4 kinds of intrepidity, the 5 factors of striving, the fivefold right concentration, the 5 faculties, the 5 powers, the 5 elements of escape, the 5 knowledges of the bases of liberation, the 5 things that mature liberation, the 6 things to be remembered, the 6 bases of mindfulness, the 6 kinds of respect, the 6 elements of escape, the 6 constant abidings, the 6 unsurpassed things, the 6 perceptions leading to penetration, the six...
8:

seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the seven qualities of a good man (sappurisa-dhamma), the seven grounds for mastery (niddasa-vatthu), the seven perceptions (saññā), the seven teachings on (tathāgata-bala), the eleven benefits of loving-kindness (mettā-ānisaṃsa), the twelve modes of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka-ākāra), the thirteen qualities of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-guṇa), the fourteen Buddha-knowledges (buddha-ñāṇa), the fifteen qualities that mature liberation (vimutti-paripācanīya-dhamma), the sixteen kinds of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), the sixteen independent qualities (aparampariya-dhamma), the eighteen Buddha-qualities (buddha-dhamma), the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), the forty-four grounds of knowledge (ñāṇa-vatthu), the fifty kinds of knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), the fifty-six kinds of wholesome qualities (kusala-dhamma), the seventy-seven grounds of knowledge (ñāṇa-vatthu), the Great Diamond Knowledge (mahāvajira-ñāṇa) that ranges over twenty-four trillion meditative attainments, the teachings of reviewing knowledge that investigates the Universal Conditional Relations (Samantapaṭṭhāna) with its infinite methods, as well as the knowledges that analyze and clarify the inclinations and so forth of infinite beings in infinite world systems—reflecting and contemplating upon such Buddha-qualities of inconceivable power according to the nature of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta could see neither their end nor their limit.

Indeed, if the Elder, even when contemplating his own virtues, could see neither their end nor their limit, how could he see the limit of the Blessed One's qualities? Whosoever's wisdom is great and whose knowledge is clear, that person believes in the greatness of the Buddha's qualities. Thus, the Elder, unable to see the limit or the extent of the Blessed One's qualities, reached this conclusion: "If even one like me, established in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa), is unable to delimit the Buddha's qualities with knowledge, what need is there to mention others? How wonderful! The qualities of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) are inconceivable and of immeasurable variety, possessing great power. In truth, these qualities are entirely the domain of a single Buddha's knowledge alone, and not the domain of others. Even the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas themselves would not be able to describe them in detail."

It has been said:
9:
"If a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha, and were to speak of nothing else for an entire aeon, the aeon would come to an end in that long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted."

Based on the greatness of the Buddhas' qualities in this way, with powerful joy and gladness (pīti-somanassa) arisen, Venerable Sāriputta again reflected: "How great is the power of the perfections (pāramī), the Buddha-making qualities that are the cause of such Buddha-qualities! In how many births were the perfections cultivated and matured? And how did they reach maturity? By asking about this matter, I shall make the Buddha's power even more manifest to this world with its devas, starting from the very beginning of his attainment." Having thus reflected, he asked the Blessed One this question: "Venerable Sir, in how many births were these Buddha-making qualities cultivated and matured? And how did they reach maturity?"

Then the Blessed One, sitting in the triple-jointed cross-legged posture on that jeweled walkway, shining like the young sun atop Mount Yugandhara, spoke the Dhamma discourse of the Cariyāpiṭaka—also known by its second name, the Buddhāpadāniya—starting with the verse "Kappe ca satasahasse" (In an aeon and a hundred thousand...), showing: "Sāriputta, my Buddha-making qualities, from the time of their undertaking, have been maturing from existence to existence and from birth to birth throughout all aeons, through constant and respectful practice supported by energy. In this Auspicious Aeon (bhadda-kappa), however, they reached maturity in these specific births."

Other teachers, however, say: "The Buddha, the God over gods, while walking on the jeweled walkway and receiving the worship of devas and Brahmas, descended to the Nigrodhārāma monastery. There, seated on the noble Buddha-seat surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, the Blessed One, being questioned by the Venerable Sāriputta in the manner already mentioned, taught the Cariyāpiṭaka." By this sequence of words, the Distant Epoch (dūre-nidāna) and the Intermediate Epoch (avidūre-nidāna) are shown in brief, and it should be understood that the Proximate Epoch (santike-nidāna) of the Cariyāpiṭaka is explained in detail. The Distant Epoch will be made clear in the Asaṅkhyeyya-vibhāvanā.

Now follows the commentary on the meaning of the Cariyāpiṭaka Pali text, which proceeds in the manner beginning with "Kappe ca satasahasse". In that Pali text, the word "kappa" occurs both with and without a prefix (upasarga). This word "kappa" is found in various meanings such as: thought (saṅkappa), arrangement (vidhāna), designation (paññatti), time (kāla), life-span (āyu-parippāṇa), terminology of recluses (samaṇa-vohāra), being manifest all around (paridīpana), faith (saddhā), cutting (chedana), joining (yoga), Vinaya conduct (vinaya-ācāra), a hint (lesa), an intermediate aeon (antara-kappa), craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi), an incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa), and a great aeon (mahā-kappa). Among these meanings, the word "kappa" appears in the sense of "thought" in such terms as "nekkhamma-saṅkappa" (thought of renunciation) and "abyāpāda-saṅkappa" (thought of non-ill will). It appears in the sense of "arrangement" in such phrases as "cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjeyya" (should he enter into an arrangement regarding a robe). It reaches the sense of excessive arrangement.
10:
The word 'kappa', when not associated with a prefix, is evident in the senses of thought, arrangement, similarity, designation, time, lifespan, monastic usage, entirety, conviction, cutting, application, disciplinary action, hint, intermediate aeon, craving and views, incalculable aeon, and great aeon, among others.

Accordingly, in such passages as 'nekkhamma-saṅkappa, abyāpāda-saṅkappa', it occurs in the sense of thought. In passages such as 'should he perform a vikappana (assignment) of a robe', it occurs in the sense of arrangement; specifically, it means reaching an exceeding arrangement. In passages such as 'Friends, indeed, we did not know while we were consulting with a disciple who is like the Teacher', it occurs in the sense of similarity. Here, 'like the Teacher' is the meaning. In passages such as 'Here, venerable Kappa...', it occurs in the sense of designation. In passages such as 'Wherein I dwell for a constant time', it occurs in the sense of time. In passages such as 'Ānanda, if the Tathāgata so desires, he could remain for an aeon or for the remainder of an aeon', it occurs in the sense of lifespan. Here, 'kappa' is intended as the lifespan-aeon (āyu-kappa). In passages such as 'Monks, I allow you to enjoy fruit by means of the five monastic usages (samaṇa-kappa)', it occurs in the sense of monastic usage. In passages such as 'having illuminated the entire Jetavana with radiance', it occurs in the sense of entirety. In passages such as 'faith, believing, conviction, supreme clarity', it occurs in the sense of conviction; it means the act of believing. In passages such as 'adorned, with hair and beard cut (kappita)', it occurs in the sense of cutting. In passages such as 'Even so, may the gift given from here reach (upakappati) the departed', it occurs in the sense of application. In passages such as 'that which is not made according to the rule is sewn together with that which is made according to the rule (kappakata)', it occurs in the sense of disciplinary action. In passages such as 'There is a pretext (kappa) for lying down; come, I shall lie down', it occurs in the sense of a hint.

In passages such as 'One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is destined for a state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon... he is boiled in hell for an aeon', it occurs in the sense of an intermediate aeon.

'They do not conceptualize, they do not prefer,
Nor are the teachings accepted by them;
A Brahmin is not to be led by virtue and vows,
Having gone to the far shore, such a one does not return.'

In such passages, it occurs in the sense of craving and views. Accordingly, it is stated in the Mahāniddesa: 'Aeons (kappā): briefly, there are two aeons—the aeon of craving and the aeon of views.' In passages such as 'even during many aeons of dissolution, even during many aeons of evolution', it occurs in the sense of an incalculable aeon. In passages such as 'Monks, these are the four incalculables of a great aeon', the word 'kappa' occurs in the sense of a great aeon. In this term 'kappa-sata-sahassa' (a hundred thousand aeons) as well, only the great aeon should be understood. The grammatical derivation of the word 'kappa' is as follows: it is thought of as a division of time, therefore it is called 'kappa'.
11:
In passages such as 'vivaṭṭakappe', it refers to the incalculable aeon. In passages such as 'Monks, these are the four incalculables of an aeon', it refers to the great aeon. In this context (the term 'kappa-sata-sahassa') as well, only the great aeon should be understood.

The grammatical definition (viggaha) of the word 'kappa' is as follows: it is called 'kappa' because it is conceptualized and determined as a period of time. Because it is impossible to count by the number of years as 'this many years', 'this many hundreds of years', 'this many thousands of years', or 'this many hundreds of thousands of years', its magnitude is something that must be conceptualized and determined only through similes such as a heap of mustard seeds. Regarding this matter, it was said:

'Venerable Sir, how long is an aeon?' When asked thus, the Buddha replied: 'Monk, an aeon is long. It is not easy to count it as "this many years", "this many hundreds of years", "this many thousands of years", or "this many hundreds of thousands of years".' 'Venerable Sir, is it possible to give a simile?' When asked thus, the Blessed One said: 'It is possible, monk. Monk, suppose there were a great heap of mustard seeds, one yojana in length, one yojana in width, and one yojana in height. From that heap, a man might take out a single mustard seed once every hundred years. Monk, by this effort, that great heap of mustard seeds would be exhausted and come to an end more quickly than the aeon. Monk, so long is an aeon.'

That great aeon is comprised of four incalculable aeons by way of dissolution and so forth. Regarding this matter, it was also said: 'Monks, these are the four incalculables of an aeon. Which four? The aeon of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa), the continuation of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī), the aeon of evolution (vivaṭṭa), and the continuation of evolution (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī).'

Among those four incalculable aeons, the aeons of dissolution are of three types: dissolution by fire (tejo-saṃvaṭṭa), dissolution by water (āpo-saṃvaṭṭa), and dissolution by air (vāyo-saṃvaṭṭa). The boundaries of dissolution (the upper limits of world destruction) are three: the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm. Indeed, when the aeon is destroyed by fire, the world below the Ābhassara realm is burnt by fire. When it is destroyed by water, the world below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water. When it is destroyed by air, the world below the Vehapphala realm is demolished by air. In terms of extent, a hundred thousand crores of world systems (cakkavāḷa) are destroyed, which...
12: The realm of authority (āṇākhetta) of the Buddhas is spoken of. Among those three types of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa), the period from the falling of the great rain that destroys the world-cycle until the cessation of the destruction by flames, water, or wind is called one incalculable period of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa-asaṅkhyeyya). The period from the cessation of the world-destroying flames and so forth until the arising of the great rain of completion (sampatti-mahāmegha) that fills a hundred thousand crores of world-systems is called the second incalculable period of the duration of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-asaṅkhyeyya). The period from the falling of the great rain of completion until the appearance of the moon and sun is called the third incalculable period of evolution (vivaṭṭa-asaṅkhyeyya). The period from the appearance of the moon and sun until the falling of the great rain that destroys the world-cycle again is called the fourth incalculable period of the duration of evolution (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-asaṅkhyeyya). This duration of evolution is counted as sixty-four intermediate aeons (antarakappa). The periods of evolution and others, which have a duration equal to that duration of evolution, should also be understood. Some teachers say, "It is counted as twenty intermediate aeons." Thus, these four incalculable periods constitute one great aeon (mahākappa). Therefore, it is said, "That great aeon is a collection of four incalculable aeons by way of dissolution and so forth." In the word "kappe," the accusative plural case is used by way of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga). In the word "satasahasse" as well, it is shown in the masculine gender due to its connection with the word "kappa"; here too, the plural case is used by way of continuous connection. Indeed, these two words are in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa). In the phrase "caturo ca asaṅkhiye," the same method should be understood. If it is asked with which word "asaṅkhiye" is connected, since no other word is mentioned and only the word "kappa" is mentioned, the meaning "of the great aeons" is understood according to the context. Indeed, it is not proper to take something unmentioned while excluding what has been mentioned. The word "ca" has the meaning of conjunction. Therefore, the meaning here is "for four incalculables of great aeons and a hundred thousand great aeons." In the word "asaṅkhiye," it means "incalculable" because it is impossible to count; it means it transcends numerical calculation. Some teachers, however, say, "The incalculable is a specific numerical value." They say that after passing through fifty-nine places starting from one and ending with akkhobhiṇī, the sixtieth place is called "asaṅkhyeyya." That statement is not proper. A numerical place (saṅkhyāṭhānantara) is merely a specific calculation. Since that sixtieth number is not incalculable (not uncountable), the statement "it is both a specific place and incalculable" is contradictory. If it is objected, "Even if it is incalculable because it cannot be counted, it is not proper for that incalculable to have four divisions," it is not improper; it is proper. This is because the state of being incalculable is desired in four instances. In this matter, the explanation from the beginning is as follows: In a certain past aeon, four Fully Enlightened Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara appeared in the world in succession. Among those four Buddhas, in the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, there was a city named Amaravatī.
13: In that city of Amaravatī, there lived a Brahmin named Sumedha. He was well-born on both sides, from the mother's side and the father's side, of pure lineage for seven generations, unassailable and irreproachable in terms of birth. He was handsome, pleasant to look at, inspiring confidence, and endowed with the highest beauty of complexion. He did no other work but learned only the Vedas, the art of the Brahmins. While he was still young, his parents passed away. Then, the minister in charge of the wealth brought the record books and opened the treasuries filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth, saying, "O young man, this much is your mother's property, this much is your father's property, and this much is your grandparents' property." After showing the wealth accumulated for seven generations, he said, "Take possession of and manage this wealth." The wise Sumedha thought: "My parents and grandparents accumulated so much wealth, yet when they went to the next world, they could not take even a single copper coin (kahāpaṇa) with them. As for me, it is proper to act in a way that I can take it with me." He informed the King, had the drum beaten throughout the city, and after giving great gifts to the multitude, he went to the Himālaya region and went forth as an ascetic. Within only seven days of going forth, he attained the eight meditative attainments and the five supernormal powers, and lived in the bliss of the attainments. At that time, the Dīpaṅkara Buddha, having attained supreme enlightenment and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, was wandering in stages surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahants. He reached the city named Rammavatī and stayed at the Sudassana Mahāvihāra monastery not far from that city. The citizens of Rammavatī, hearing that "The Teacher has reached our city and is staying at the Sudassana Mahāvihāra," approached the Teacher with flowers, perfumes, and so forth in their hands. Having paid homage and honored him with flowers and perfumes, they sat at one side, listened to the Dhamma teaching, invited him for the next day's meal, rose from their seats, and departed. On the following day, they prepared a great offering, decorated the city, and with great joy and delight, they cleared and prepared the path for the arrival of the Buddha. At that time, the ascetic Sumedha, while flying through the air, saw those people who were joyful and delighted and asked, "Friends, for whom are you clearing this path?" When they replied, "We are clearing the path for the arrival of the Fully Enlightened Buddha," because of the meritorious resolution (adhikāra) he had made in the presence of past Buddhas, upon merely hearing the word "Buddha," a sense of rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa) arose in him. At that very moment, he descended from the sky and said, "Friends, give me a space as well, I too..."
14:
"I will also clear the path," he said, and at the place shown by them, he thought: "Even though I am able to decorate this place beautifully with the seven kinds of jewels by means of psychic power, today it is proper for me to perform physical service; I shall acquire merit through bodily exertion." Thinking thus, he removed grass, rubbish, and the like, brought earth, and leveled the ground to clear it.

Before the task of clearing that prepared spot was finished, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, surrounded by four hundred thousand monks who possessed great power, the six superknowledges, and were Arahants, proceeded onto that prepared path. The wise Sumedha, thinking, "May the Blessed One and the disciples of the Buddha not tread upon the mud," spread out his bark garment, his deer skin, and his matted hair, and he himself lay face down with his head towards the Blessed One. He also thought: "If I so desired, I could destroy all defilements this very day and become a disciple of this Blessed One. But what is the use of crossing over the great flood of Saṃsāra alone? It would be better if I, having become a Sammāsambuddha like this, were to save the world including the devas from the ocean of Saṃsāra." Thus, the hermit Sumedha made a resolution of mind by virtue of the Great Resolve (Mahābhinīhāra) endowed with the eight factors. Then the Blessed One came and stood at the head of the hermit Sumedha, and knowing that the hermit's intention would be fulfilled, he prophesied all the future events of the Blessed One, saying: "Four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons from now, this hermit will become a Sammāsambuddha named Gotama," and then he departed.

After that time, the Buddhas who appeared in succession, beginning with the Blessed One Koṇḍañña and ending with the Blessed One Kassapa, also prophesied to the Great Being, saying, "He will become a Buddha." Thus, while our Bodhisatta was fulfilling the perfections, twenty-four Sammāsambuddhas appeared. In the very aeon in which the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara appeared, three other Buddhas had also appeared. Since the Bodhisatta did not receive a prophecy in the presence of those three Buddhas, they are not included here. However, in the ancient commentaries, in order to show all the Buddhas starting from that aeon, it is said:

Taṇhaṅkara Buddha, Medhaṅkara Buddha, and also Saraṇaṅkara Buddha,
Dīpaṅkara the Blessed One, and Koṇḍañña Buddha, the supreme among men.

Maṅgala Buddha, Sumana Buddha, Revata Buddha, and the sage named Sobhita,
Anomadassī Buddha, Paduma Buddha, Nārada Buddha, and Padumuttara Buddha.
15:
Sumedha Buddha, Sujāta Buddha, and the famous Piyadassī Buddha, Atthadassī Buddha, Dhammadassī Buddha, and Siddhattha Buddha, the leader of the world.

Tissa Buddha, Phussa Buddha, Vipassī Buddha, Sikhī Buddha, Vessabhū Buddha, Kakusandha Buddha, Koṇāgamana Buddha, and the leader Kassapa Buddha.

Those Buddhas were free from passion and had concentrated minds. They appeared like the sun with a thousand rays, dispelling the great darkness. Having shone like great masses of fire, those Buddhas, along with their disciples, have attained Parinibbāna.

Among those Buddhas, in the interval between the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara and the Blessed One Koṇḍañña, the world was empty of Buddhas for one incalculable period of great aeons. Similarly, in the interval between the Blessed One Koṇḍañña and the Blessed One Maṅgala; similarly, between the Blessed One Sobhita and the Blessed One Anomadassī; and similarly, between the Blessed One Nārada and the Blessed One Padumuttara (the world was empty of Buddhas for one incalculable period each). This was indeed stated in the Buddhavaṃsa:

"Between the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara and the Teacher Koṇḍañña,
The aeons in between are incalculable by counting.

After Koṇḍañña, there was a leader named Maṅgala;
Between them also, the aeons are incalculable by counting.

After Sobhita, there was the famous Anomadassī;
Between them also, the aeons are incalculable by counting.

Between the Blessed One Nārada and the Teacher Padumuttara,
The aeons in between are incalculable by counting."

Thus, although they are incalculable because they exceed counting, it is said "four incalculables" because the number of great aeons was exceeded in four places; it should be understood that this is not due to a specific numerical distinction. Because between the Blessed One Padumuttara and the Blessed One Sumedha, there were thirty thousand aeons; between the Blessed One Sujāta and the Blessed One Piyadassī, there were sixty-nine thousand eight hundred and eighty-two aeons; between the Blessed One Dhammadassī and the Blessed One Siddhattha, there were twenty aeons; and between the Blessed One Siddhattha and the Blessed One Tissa, there was one aeon...
16:
Between the Blessed One Vipassī and the Blessed One Sikhī, there were sixty aeons; between the Blessed One Vessabhū and the Blessed One Kakusandha, there were thirty aeons. Thus, starting from the aeon in which the Blessed One Padumuttara appeared, including the aeons in which those respective Buddhas appeared below that and this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), there are one hundred thousand great aeons. Referring to those one hundred thousand great aeons, it was said: "Kappe ca satasahasse" (In a hundred thousand aeons).

If this meaning were to be expanded, the entire Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi would have to be brought in and explained; therefore, out of consideration for the minds of the many people who might fear excessive detail, we shall not expand it. Those who desire it should take it from the Buddhavaṃsa text. The sequence of the discourse to be mentioned here should also be understood according to the method stated in the commentary to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī named Atthasālinī and in the Jātaka Commentary.

In the word "Etthantare," the term 'antara' appears in the sense of cause (kāraṇa) in such passages as:
"On the riverbanks, in assemblies, in theaters, and on the main roads, people gather and consult, saying: 'What is the reason (antara) between me and you?'" and so forth.

It appears in the sense of a moment (khaṇa) in such passages as: "Venerable Sir, I saw a certain woman washing a vessel in the moment (antara) of a lightning flash," meaning the moment of the discharge of lightning.

It appears in the sense of the mind (citta) in such passages as: "In whose mind (antara) there are no angers."

It appears in the sense of an open space (vivara) in such passages as: "Between (antara) Gayā and the Bodhi tree."

It appears in the sense of the middle (vemajjha) in such passages as: "One should not interrupt with speech in the middle (antara) of the preceptor's recitation."

Here also, it should be understood in the sense of the middle (vemajjha); therefore, it means "in this interval, in the middle."

This is what is meant: When our Blessed One was the wise Sumedha, at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, he made the Great Aspiration (abhinīhāra) endowed with the eight factors stated thus:

Being human, being a male,
Having the cause (potential for Arahatship), meeting the Teacher (the Buddha),
Going forth (renunciation), possession of virtues (attainment of jhāna and abhiññā),
Great dedication (offering one's life), and having a strong desire (to become a Buddha).

Having made this aspiration, he selected and undertook the thirty perfections (pāramīs), and to fulfill all the qualities that make one a Buddha...
17:
Our Blessed One, as the wise Sumedha, at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, being endowed with the eight factors such as being human, being male, and being a monk, made the Great Aspiration (abhinīhāra). Thereafter, he selected and undertook the thirty perfections and strove to fulfill the qualities that make one a Buddha. Now, in this Bhadda-kappa, having fulfilled all the perfections, he realized the peerless Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). Thus, the specific period of time defined as being between these two great aeons—the beginning aeon and the final aeon—is specified by the term 'Etthantare'.

How can this period be known? It can be known by the statement: 'A hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables (asaṅkheyya).' This statement shows the number of great aeons by way of both limitation and non-limitation. Such a counting is not possible without taking the beginning and the end. Therefore, it should be understood that the point where the accumulation of the requisites for Enlightenment began in the life of Sumedha, and the point where those perfections reached their conclusion in the final life—both of these are shown by the meaning of 'in this interval' as the limit (avadhi).

This limit should be understood by way of inclusion (abhividhi), not by way of exclusion (mariyādā). This is because a portion of the beginning and ending aeons is included within it. If one objects: 'Since those aeons cannot be encompassed without remainder, is it not true that abhividhi is not possible here?'—it is not so, because the term abhividhi can be used even for a portion of those aeons. The beginning and ending aeons, which are portions, are indeed encompassed without remainder [in terms of the relevant events].

In the phrase 'Yaṃ caritaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ bodhipācanaṃ,' the word 'caritaṃ' means conduct (cariyā). It refers to the practices of giving (dāna), virtue (sīla), and so forth, which are comprised within the thirty perfections. Conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), and conduct for the sake of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā) are also included within those perfections. Furthermore, there are eight other types of conduct:

1. Conduct in the postures (iriyāpatha-cariyā) for Bodhisattas endowed with the aspiration during the four postures.
2. Conduct in the sense bases (āyatana-cariyā) for those with guarded sense doors regarding the internal bases.
3. Conduct in mindfulness (sati-cariyā) for those who dwell in heedfulness regarding the four foundations of mindfulness.
4. Conduct in concentration (samādhi-cariyā) for those devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta) regarding the four jhānas.
5. Conduct in knowledge (ñāṇa-cariyā) for those endowed with wisdom regarding the four Noble Truths.
6. Conduct in the path (magga-cariyā) for those practicing rightly regarding the four Noble Paths.
7. Conduct in attainment (patti-cariyā) for those who have attained the fruits regarding the four fruits of recluseship.
8. Conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā) for the three types of Buddhas regarding all sentient beings.

Among these eight, the lokattha-cariyā of the two types of Bodhisattas (for Paccekabuddhahood and Sāvakabodhi), of Paccekabuddhas, and of disciples is taken partially (padesa). However, the lokattha-cariyā of Mahābodhisattas and Sammāsambuddhas is taken without remainder (nippadesa). This matter is explained in detail in the Niddesa: 'Conduct means the eight conducts: conduct in the postures, conduct in the sense bases,' and so forth. There are also another eight types of conduct stated: 'One conducts oneself with faith while being resolved; one conducts oneself with energy while exerting; one conducts oneself with mindfulness while establishing it; one conducts oneself with concentration while being undistracted; one conducts oneself with wisdom while discerning; one conducts oneself with consciousness while cognizing. For one who practices thus, wholesome states arise (āyatanti), thus one conducts oneself with conduct in the sense bases (āyatana-cariyā); one who practices thus attains distinction, thus one conducts oneself with conduct of distinction (visesa-cariyā).'
18:
The inclusion of all the other eight types of conduct (cariyā) that have been taught should be understood as being within the thirty perfections (pāramīs). Therefore, it is said: "Caritaṃ refers to the conduct consisting of practices such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla), which are encompassed by the thirty perfections." In this context, although only the conduct that serves as the root cause is intended, it should be understood that the conduct of the path (maggacariyā) and the conduct of the fruit (phalacariyā) are not contradictory. Therefore, it is said: "All that matures the knowledge of enlightenment (bodhi-ñāṇa)."

In the phrase "sabbaṃ taṃ bodhipācanaṃ," the word "sabba" (all) is found in four senses: the absolute all (sabbasabba), the all of the bases (āyatanasabba), the all of the individual group (sakkāyasabba), and the partial all (padesasabba). This is seen in passages such as "All phenomena (sabba) in every aspect come into the range of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddha," where it is used in the sense of the absolute all. In the passage, "Monks, I will teach you the all; what is the all? It is the eye and forms... the mind and mental objects," it is used in the sense of the all of the bases. In passages such as "He perceives the all as the all," it is used in the sense of the all of the individual group. In passages such as "Sāriputta, the words of all of you are well-spoken in their own way," it is used in the sense of the partial all. Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of the partial all, because the conduct that constitutes the requisites of enlightenment is what is intended.

Bodhi refers to the tree, the Noble Path (ariya-magga), Nibbāna, and the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). In passages such as "At the foot of the Bodhi tree, he first attained full enlightenment" and "Between Gayā and the Bodhi tree," the tree is called Bodhi because he attained enlightenment there. In the context where it is said, "Knowledge of the four paths is called Bodhi," the Noble Path is called Bodhi because the four Noble Truths are realized through it. In the context where it is said, "Having reached the deathless, unconditioned Bodhi," Nibbāna is called Bodhi because it is realized as the object of that knowledge. In the context where it is said, "The Great Sage of noble wisdom reaches Bodhi," the knowledge of omniscience is called Bodhi because all phenomena are realized in every aspect through it. Here too, the knowledge of omniscience is intended. Alternatively, the knowledge of the path of Arahatship and the knowledge of omniscience should be understood as Bodhi here, because the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi) of the Blessed One is intended. Indeed, the knowledge of omniscience which has the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the destruction of taints which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause, are both called "Mahābodhi."

The summary of the meaning here is: "Whatever conduct, consisting of practices such as giving and virtue, was performed by me during the aforementioned period of time—all of that, without exception, matures, accomplishes, and brings about the Great Enlightenment." By this, he shows the continuous development of the requisites of enlightenment. Next...
19:
Alternatively, in this word "sabbaṃ," whatever conduct was practiced within the aforementioned period of time, all of that conduct, in its entirety and without exception, is indeed a requisite of enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra). By this word "sabbaṃ," he shows the development of all requisites (sabbasambharabhāvanā).

Indeed, there are four types of development (bhāvanā) regarding the requisites of enlightenment: the development of all requisites (sabbasambharabhāvanā), continuous development (nirantarabhāvanā), development over a long time (cirakālabhāvanā), and respectful development (sakkaccabhāvanā). Among these four, by the words "For a hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables," he states the development over a long time (cirakālabhāvanā). By the continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) expressed there, and by the inclusion of the word "sabba" in the first interpretation, he states the continuous development (nirantarabhāvanā). In the second interpretation, by the words "all conduct" (sabbaṃ caritaṃ), he states the development of all requisites (sabbasambharabhāvanā), and by the words "maturing enlightenment" (bodhipācanaṃ), he states the respectful development (sakkaccabhāvanā). This is because it illustrates the nature of that conduct in the manner that it matures perfect enlightenment (sammā-sambodhi). Therefore, that conduct deserves to be called "bodhipācana" (maturing enlightenment), and not otherwise.

How should the continuity (nirantara-bhāva) of the Bodhisatta's conduct (bodhicariyā) be understood here? If it is said to be the continuity of mind (citta-nirantaratā), that is not appropriate. This is because it cannot be said that for the Great Bodhisattas, after the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra), no other mind arises except the mind that accumulates the requisites of enlightenment. If it is said with reference to the occurrence of functional mind (kiriyamaya-citta), that too is not appropriate. This is because not all functional minds of those Bodhisattas occur solely by way of accumulating the requisites of enlightenment. For this very reason, the continuity of effort (payoga-nirantaratā) is also to be rejected.

Continuous development (nirantarabhāvanā) should be understood only through the continuity of births (jāti-nirantaratā). This is because from the birth in which the Great Bodhisatta made the Great Aspiration (mahāpaṇidhāna) until his final existence, there is no birth to be found in which he did not accumulate the requisites of enlightenment in their entirety, starting at the very least with the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī). This is the natural law (dhammatā) of Bodhisattas who have a fixed destiny. As long as they have not attained mastery (vasībhāva) over kamma and so forth, they apply effort in the requisites even partially. But when they have attained mastery over kamma and so forth in every way, from then on, their exertion and constant practice in the requisites of enlightenment become complete in an absolute (non-partial) manner. Respectful performance (sakkaccakāritā), however, occurs at all times. Thus, in whatever manner, the Bodhisattas' fulfillment according to their intention is accomplished in various births. Thus, it should be understood that by this verse, the four types of development—development of all requisites, development over a long time, continuous development, and respectful development—are revealed.

In that discussion, the terms Bodhisatta-carita, Bodhi-sambhāra, Bodhi-cariyā, Aggayāna, and Pāramī are identical in meaning and differ only in phrasing. Because the word "caritaṃ" is a general term for the perfections such as giving (dāna-pāramī) which will be discussed later in detail, the perfections are explained in this text for the sake of achieving proficiency in all the requisites of enlightenment. We shall explain them in every aspect later in the Miscellaneous Discussion (Pakiṇṇakakathā).

2. Thus, from the time the Blessed One began practicing the conduct in his life as a Bodhisatta until the end...
20:
The word "conduct" (carita) regarding the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī) and others, which will be explained in detail later, is a general term without distinction. Therefore, in this work, the perfections (pāramīs) should be explained for the sake of generating skill in all the requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra). I shall explain those perfections in all their aspects later in the Miscellaneous Discourse (Pakiṇṇakakathā).

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown generally that from the beginning of his efforts in the stage of a Bodhisatta until the final Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi) it was solely the maturing of omniscience, now, in order to show the extraordinary maturing of enlightenment through reaching the highest excellence of that conduct, spoke the words beginning with "Atītakappe," illustrating in detail some former conducts in this Auspicious Aeon (Bhaddakappa).

In that passage, "Atītakappe" means in a past or even earlier great aeon (mahākappa) of a defined period, during the four incalculables (asankheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons. "Caritaṃ" refers to the practiced conduct such as giving (dāna) and so on. "Ṭhapayitvā" means leaving aside or not taking, i.e., not mentioning. "Bhavābhave" means in various existences, both large and small. In the phrase "iti bhavābhava-kathaṃ," growth and decline are called "bhavābhava." In the phrase "iti bhavābhavatañca vītivatto," success, failure, growth, decline, the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi), the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi), merit, and demerit are intended by "bhavābhava." However, in the phrase "iti bhavābhava-hetu vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati," medicines such as ghee and fresh butter, which are better than the good, are intended by "bhavābhava." They also say that in successful existences, the more excellent and most excellent existences are "bhavābhava"; therefore, here too, that same meaning should be understood. It means in small and large existences. "Imamhi kappe" means in this Auspicious Aeon. "Pavakkhissaṃ" means I shall tell. With the word "Suṇohi," he urges the General of the Dhamma (Dhamma-senāpati) to listen. "Me" means in my presence, or "listen to what I am speaking from me."

## The Introduction is finished.
21:
## 1. Akittivagga
## 1. Akitticariyāvaṇṇanā
Thus, the Blessed One, having inspired the Venerable Sāriputta and the assembly including devas and humans to listen to his former conduct, and now wishing to make manifest that former conduct—which was hidden by intervening births—like an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand, spoke the verse beginning with "Yadā ahaṃ brahāraññe."

In that verse, "Yadā" means at which time. "Brahāraññe" means in a great forest, in a secluded woodland, in a vast forest. "Suññe" means secluded from people. "Vipinakanane" means in a dense and special woodland. By these two words, he shows only the dense and thick nature of that forest. All this was said in reference to Kāra Island (Kāradīpa). "Ajjhogāhetvā" means having entered in due order. "Viharāmi" means I lived, having dispelled bodily suffering through the dwelling in postures (iriyāpatha-vihāra) which possesses a special happiness produced by the divine, brahma, noble, and imperturbable dwellings (vihāras), and thus maintained the individual existence. "Akitti nāma tāpaso" means having become an ascetic of such name, at which time I lived in that forest. At that time, the Teacher told the General of the Dhamma about his state as the ascetic Akitti. In that regard, this is the sequential narrative (anupubbikathā):

In the past, in this very Auspicious Aeon, while King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the family of a wealthy Brahmin (brahmaṇa-mahāsāla) with a fortune of eighty crores. They named him "Akitti." When the boy Akitti was able to walk, a sister was also born. They named her "Yasavatī." At the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and returned. Later, his parents passed away. After performing their funeral rites and a few days had passed, he had the treasurers look over the treasure houses. Hearing, "This much wealth belonged to the mother, this much to the father, this much to the grandfather," he became stirred in mind (saṃvigga-mānasa) and thought, "Only this wealth remains manifest; those who accumulated the wealth are no longer manifest. All have gone, leaving this wealth behind. I, however, shall take this wealth and go." Having asked permission from the King, he had the drum beaten, announcing, "Let those who desire wealth come to the house of the wise Akitti."
22: The Bodhisatta Akitti, after providing a great alms-giving for seven days, thought, "What is the use of delighting in such wealth? Let those who desire it take it." Even though his wealth was not yet exhausted, he opened the doors of his house and ordered the treasuries filled with gold, silver, and other riches to be opened, saying, "Take what has already been given," and abandoned his home. While his relatives were weeping, he took his sister and departed from the city of Bārāṇasī. After crossing a river and traveling a distance of about two or three yojanas, he became an ascetic. He built a leaf-hut in a pleasant area and dwelt there. The gate through which he left the city at that time became known as the Akitti Gate, and the landing place where he descended to the river became known as the Akitti Landing. Hearing that the Bodhisatta had become an ascetic, many people living in villages, market towns, and the royal capital, their hearts drawn by his virtues, followed him into the homeless life. A great following gathered, and abundant gains and offerings arose, just as in the time of a Buddha's appearance. Then the Great Being thought, "These gains and offerings are vast, and the following is large. I cannot find even physical seclusion here. It is proper for me to live alone." Due to his fewness of wishes and his inclination toward seclusion, he departed alone without letting anyone know. In due course, he reached the Damila country and, dwelling in a park near the city of Kāvirapaṭṭana, he attained the meditative absorptions (jhānas) and higher powers (abhiññās). There too, great gains and offerings arose for him. Loathing those gains, he abandoned them and, traveling through the air, descended to Kāradīpa island. At that time, Kāradīpa was called Ahidīpa. There, he built a leaf-hut near a large Kāra tree and made his dwelling. Because of his fewness of wishes, he went nowhere else; during the fruiting season of that tree, he ate its fruits, and when there were no fruits, he ate its leaves sprinkled with water, spending his time in meditative attainments. Due to the power of his virtue, the Sakka's Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting, "Who wishes to displace me from this position?" saw the Wise One and thought, "For what purpose is this ascetic practicing such difficult austerities? Does he desire the status of Sakka, or something else? I will test him." He further thought, "This ascetic has very pure conduct of body, speech, and mind, and having no regard for life, he eats Kāra leaves sprinkled with water. If he desires the status of Sakka, he will give me his water-sprinkled Kāra leaves; if not, he will not give them." Disguised as a Brahmin, he went to him. The Bodhisatta, having boiled the Kāra leaves, sat at the door of his leaf-hut, thinking, "I will eat them when they have cooled." While he was sitting there, Sakka, in the guise of a Brahmin seeking alms, stood before him. Seeing the Brahmin, the Bodhisatta rejoiced, thinking, "I have gained! I have gained well!"
23:
Sakka, in the guise of a Brahmin, stood there as one desiring alms. When the Great Being (Mahāsatta) saw him, he felt joyful, thinking, "What a gain for me! What a wonderful gain for me! After a long time, I have seen a seeker of alms." Thinking, "Today I will fulfill my heart's desire and give alms," he took the pot of cooked food and, reflecting on the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī), poured it into the seeker's bowl without leaving any for himself. Sakka took the alms, walked a short distance, and disappeared. The Great Being, after giving to him, did not seek food again but spent the time in that very joy and happiness.

On the second day, he boiled Kāra leaves and sat at the door of the hut, thinking, "Yesterday I found a worthy recipient; how will it be today?" Sakka came again in the same manner. The Great Being gave as before and spent the time [in joy]. On the third day, he gave in the same way and thought, "What a gain for me! I am accumulating much merit! If I find a worthy recipient, I would like to give alms like this for a month or even two months." On all three days, he directed his mind according to his aspiration: "By this gift, I do not desire gains, offerings, fame, the prosperity of a Universal Monarch, the prosperity of Sakka, the prosperity of Brahma, the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvaka-bodhi), or the enlightenment of a Private Buddha (pacceka-bodhi). Instead, may this gift of mine be a condition for the attainment of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)." Thus it was said:

"Then, by the power of my austerity, Sakka, the lord of the Triple Heaven, became distressed and, assuming the guise of a Brahmin, approached me for alms.

Seeing him standing at my door, I poured into his bowl the boiled Kāra leaves, brought from the forest, without oil or salt, along with the pot.

After giving him the Kāra leaves, I turned the pot over, abandoned the search for more food, and entered my leaf-hut.

On the second and third days, he approached me again; unshaken and unattached, I gave in the same way.

Because of that giving, there was no loss of complexion in my body; I spent those days delighting in joy and happiness.

If I were to find a noble recipient for a month or even two months, I would give the supreme gift, unshaken and without shrinking back."
24:
"While giving the gift to that Brahmin, I did not desire fame or gain. Desiring only Omniscience, I practiced those meritorious deeds."

In that verse, 'tadā' refers to the time when I was the ascetic named Akitti, living in the Kāra forest on that island. 'Maṃ' means 'mine'. 'Tapatejena' means by the power of the Perfection of Virtue. Indeed, virtue is called 'tapa' (ascetic practice) because it burns away the defilements of misconduct. Alternatively, it could be by the power of the Perfections of Renunciation and Energy. These too are called 'tapa' because they burn away the defilements of craving and laziness. In this existence, those practices of the Bodhisatta reached their peak. Since the restraint of patience also reached the highest excellence, it is also appropriate to say 'by the power of the Perfection of Patience.' Was it not taught: 'Patience is the highest ascetic practice (tapa)'? 'Santatto' means that the Paṇḍukambala stone throne was heated by the heat of the natural phenomenon arising from the power of the aforementioned virtues. 'Tidivābhibhū' is Sakka, the lord of the celestial realm. Even though the kāra leaves were gathered near the leaf-hut, because the leaf-hut was in the middle of the forest, it is said 'brought by the wind.'

The phrase 'without oil and without salt' is said to show the great power and glory of the act of giving due to the fulfillment of intention and disposition, even though the gift itself was not grand. 'Mama dvāre' means at the door of my leaf-hut. By the words 'poured with a bowl,' he shows the state of giving without leaving even a little for himself.

'Giving up further search' means thinking that searching for food twice in a single day is not the practice of effacement (sallekha), and being as if satisfied by the joy of giving, he did not search for food again on that day.

'One who is unshaken' means not being shaken by stinginess because stinginess has been discarded far away, and not moving even slightly from the disposition to give. 'One who is unattached' means not being attached even slightly by the power of greed. In the phrase 'for the third time also,' the word 'pi' (also) includes the second time. 'In this way I gave' means that just as on the first day, I gave on the second and third days as well.

With the verse 'Na me tappaccayā,' he clarifies the meaning already stated. In that context, 'tappaccayā' means that the physical deterioration (exhaustion) that should occur in the body due to the lack of food for three days because of giving, did not exist in my body precisely because of the gift.
25:
I gave on the second day and the third day just as I did on the first day.

With the phrase "Na me tappaccayā," he clarifies the meaning stated in the verse. In that context, "tappaccayā" means that the physical deterioration that should occur in the body due to fasting for three days did not exist in me because of the gift. Why? Because of the blissful joy having the gift as its object, and because of the delight in giving (that state did not occur). "Vītināmemi taṃ divaṃ" means I passed all those days, which were three in number. To show that he could give in this way not just for three days, but for a month or two, he said "Yadi māsampi," and so on. "Anolīno" means having a mind that does not shrink back in giving.

"Tassa" refers to Sakka who came in the form of a Brahmin. "Yasaṃ" means fame or the fulfillment of a retinue. "Lābhaṃ" means I did not desire gains such as becoming a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) among gods and humans. Instead, desiring only Omniscient Enlightenment (Sabbaññuta-sammāsambodhi), I practiced the meritorious deeds consisting of giving that arose many times during those three days, and the meritorious deeds such as good bodily conduct which are the attendants of giving.

In this way, the Blessed One revealed only his own difficult meritorious practice in that existence to the Great Elder (Venerable Sāriputta) in this present life. In the Jātaka teaching, however, it is described that on the fourth day, Sakka approached and, knowing the Bodhisatta's disposition, invited him with boons; the Bodhisatta, while accepting the boons, gave a Dhamma discourse about the objects of giving and those worthy of receiving gifts; and his desire for Sakka not to come again. This was taught as follows—

Seeing the ascetic Akitti dwelling in peace, Sakka, the lord of beings, said—
"O Great Holy One, desiring what benefit do you dwell alone in peace in this heat?"

"O Sakka, to be reborn again in a new existence is suffering. The breaking up of the body is suffering. Death in delusion is suffering. Therefore, Vāsava, I dwell in peace," (the ascetic replied).

"Kassapa, because of those well-spoken and suitable words of yours, I shall give you a boon, whatever you desire in your mind," (Sakka said).

"O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you wish to give me a boon—though people obtain sons, wives, wealth, grain, and other dear things, they are not satisfied. May that greed not dwell in me," (the ascetic said).

"Kassapa, because of those well-spoken and suitable words of yours, I shall give you a boon, whatever you desire in your mind," (Sakka said).

"O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you wish to give me boons such as lands, gold, silver, cattle, horses, male and female slaves—in whatever existence those possessions arise, they are subject to aging and destruction. May that fault not stay or reach me," (the ascetic said).

"Kassapa, because of those well-spoken and suitable words of yours, I shall give you a boon, whatever you desire in your mind," (Sakka said).

"O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you wish to give me a boon—I do not wish to see a fool, I do not wish to hear a fool, I do not wish to live with a fool, I do not wish to speak with a fool, I do not wish to take pleasure in a fool," (the ascetic said).

"Kassapa, what has a fool done to you? Please tell the reason. Why do you not wish to see a fool?" (Sakka asked).

"Sakka, a fool who lacks wisdom brings harm. He applies himself to things that are not beneficial. One who lacks wisdom is lazy. Even when well-advised, he gets angry. That fool..."
26:
“O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you would grant me a boon: May that fault (of greed) for fields, houses, gold, cattle, horses, slaves, and workers—possessions which, when they arise, cause beings to grow old and decay—never dwell within me.”

“O hermit of the Kassapa clan, because of those well-spoken and appropriate words of yours, whatever boon you desire in your heart, I shall grant it to you.”

“O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you would grant me a boon: May I not see a fool, may I not hear a fool, may I not live with a fool, may I not engage in deceptive or evasive conversation with a fool, and may I not take delight in a fool.”

“Kassapa, what has a fool done to you? Tell me the reason. Why, Kassapa, do you not wish to see a fool?”

“O Sakka, an unwise fool leads one toward ruin and loss; he engages in that which is not beneficial; he is of a lazy nature; even when well-advised, he becomes angry; such a fool does not know discipline. It is truly best not to see such a fool.”

“O hermit of the Kassapa clan, because of those well-spoken and appropriate words of yours, whatever boon you desire in your heart, I shall grant it to you.”

“O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you would grant me a boon: May I see the wise, may I hear the words of the wise, may I live with the wise, may I engage in consultation and conversation with the wise, and may I take delight in the words of those wise ones.”

“Kassapa, what has a wise person ever done for you? Tell me the reason. Why, Kassapa, do you wish to see a wise person?”

“O Sakka, a wise person leads one toward good methods and principles; he does not engage in that which is not beneficial; he possesses noble ways; when well-advised, he does not become angry; such a wise person knows discipline. Association with such a virtuous person is truly excellent.”

“O hermit of the Kassapa clan, because of those well-spoken and appropriate words of yours, whatever boon you desire in your heart, I shall grant it to you.”

“O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you would grant me a boon: When the night has passed and the sun rises, may celestial food appear, and may virtuous recipients also appear.

May the objects of donation not be exhausted for me as I give; may I not feel regret after having given; and while in the act of giving, may I gladden my heart. O Sakka, I ask for this boon.”

“O hermit of the Kassapa clan, because of those well-spoken and appropriate words of yours, whatever boon you desire in your heart, I shall grant it to you.”
27:
“O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you would grant me a boon: May you never come to me again. This is the boon I choose, O Sakka.”

“O hermit, because of many practices of virtue, men and women desire to see me. Why do you see danger in seeing me?”

“Upon seeing such a divine form, endowed with all desired sensual pleasures, I might become negligent in my practice. Therefore, seeing you is a danger to my practice,” he said. (Jā. 1.13.83-103).

Then Sakka said, “Very well, Bhante, from this day forward I shall not come into your presence,” and after paying homage, he departed. The Mahāsatta (Great Being), living in that very forest for the rest of his life, was reborn in the Brahma realm at the end of his lifespan.

At that time, Sakka was the Elder Anuruddha, and Akitti the Wise was the Lokanātha, the Exalted Buddha.

Because of his noble renunciation, which was like the Great Renunciation, he fulfilled the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī). Because of his pure conduct and virtue, the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī). Because of his ability to thoroughly dispel sensual thoughts and others, the Perfection of Energy (Viriya-pāramī). Because of reaching the pinnacle of patient restraint, the Perfection of Patience (Khanti-pāramī). Because of practicing in accordance with his promise, the Perfection of Truth (Sacca-pāramī). Because of his unwavering undertaking in all matters, the Perfection of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī). Because of his inclination toward the welfare of all beings, the Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā-pāramī). Because of reaching a state of neutrality toward the actions and ruins of beings, the Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā-pāramī). And Wisdom—which knows which qualities are helpful or unhelpful to those perfections, abandons the unhelpful, and initiates the helpful; which is both a precursor and co-arisen; which is characterized by skill in means; and which accomplishes a life of extreme scrupulousness—is the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī). Thus, these ten perfections are obtained.

However, because of his exceedingly noble inclination toward giving, the teaching was delivered with Generosity (Dāna) as the lead. Therefore, there are also: Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) which is equal toward all welfare; the two accumulations of Merit and Knowledge (Puṇya-ñāṇa-sambhāra); the three good conducts of a Bodhisatta such as good bodily conduct; the four resolves (Adhiṭṭhāna) such as Truth; the four Buddha-grounds (Buddhabhūmi) such as effort (ussāha); the five factors that ripen Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi-paripācanīya-dhamma) such as faith (saddhā); the six inclinations (Ajjhāsaya) of Bodhisattas such as the inclination toward non-greed; the seven dharmas of promise such as “Having crossed over, I shall lead others across”; the eight thoughts of a Great Man (Mahāpurisavitakka) (Dī. Ni. 3.358, A. Ni. 8.30) such as “This Dhamma is for one with few desires, not for one with great desires”; the nine dharmas rooted in wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra); the ten inclinations of a Great Man such as the inclination toward giving; and the ten bases of meritorious action (Puṇyakiriyavatthu) such as giving and virtue. These and many other hundreds and thousands of varieties...
28:
There are the virtues of the Bodhisattas, which are the prerequisites for Omniscience. All those qualities should be extracted and stated here as appropriate.

Indeed, in the conduct of this Akitti Bodhisatta, one should understand the power of the Great Being’s virtues, such as: his departure from home, which was like the Great Renunciation, having abandoned a vast mass of wealth and a large circle of relatives; his lack of attachment to families and groups due to his supreme fewness of wishes, even though he was a person highly esteemed by many after having renounced and gone forth; his absolute loathing for gain, offerings, and fame; his delight in seclusion; his sacrifice of body and life without regard; his sustaining of the body without any physical alteration, being satisfied with the joy born of giving for three whole days even without food; his noble disposition for giving, which accomplished a steadfast manner of sacrifice, thinking, 'I will sustain the body only with the bliss of joy born of giving,' by giving away food in the same manner when a beggar appeared even for a period of one or two months; and his supreme austere livelihood, which was the reason for not seeking food again after giving it away. Therefore, it is said:

'Such are the wonderful and marvelous qualities of the Great Sages, who possess great compassion, who are wise, and who are the sole kin of the entire world.'

'The Bodhisattas, the Great Beings, possess inconceivable power; they always have the True Dhamma as their domain and lead a life of pure austerity.'

'The great ocean, with its rows of waves raised by mighty winds, might overstep its shore, but the Bodhisattas never overstep their nature (Dhamma).'

'Though born and grown in the world, those who have developed what is to be developed are not stained by worldly conditions, just as a lotus is not stained by water.'

'In whatever way their self-love decreases, in that very way their moisture of compassion for beings increases.'
