'Just as the mind is under their control and they do not follow the whims of the mind, so also kamma is under their control and they do not follow the whims of kamma.'

'Those wise and noble persons, while practicing the quest for Bodhi, do not oppress others with anger, nor are they yet able to uproot anger completely.'
29:
'Even a mere clarity of mind towards them can deliver one from suffering; what then need be said of those who follow their example by practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma?'

## In the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary of the Paramatthadīpanī,
## The Explanation of the Akitti Cariyā is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Saṅkha Brāhmaṇa Cariyā

11-12. In this second Saṅkha Brāhmaṇa Cariyā, 'puna aparaṃ' means 'again, another'. The intention is: 'I shall preach not only this Akitti Cariyā, but again another, the Saṅkha Cariyā; listen to it.' This same method should be understood in the subsequent Jātakas as well. 'Saṅkhasavhayo' means named Saṅkha. 'Mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmo' means wishing to cross the great ocean by ship to go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. 'Upagacchāmi paṭṭanaṃ' means 'I go aiming for the port of Tāmalitti.' He is called 'Sayambhū' because he appeared on his own, having attained Paccekabodhi through his self-evolved knowledge. He is called 'Aparājita' (Unconquered) because he was not defeated by anyone, such as the Māra of defilements. It means he stands having crushed the heads of the three Māras. 'Tattāya kaṭhinabhūmiyā' means on the harsh and rough ground, parched by the heat of the sun and filled with gravel and sand.

13. 'Taṃ' refers to that Paccekabuddha. 'Imam-atthaṃ' refers to the meaning beginning with 'Idaṃ khettaṃ' which will be spoken now. 'Vicintayi' means the Teacher (the Buddha) said that the Bodhisatta, who was then Saṅkha the Brahmin, reflected.

In that context, the sequential story is as follows: In the past, this city of Vārāṇasī was named Moḷinī. While King Brahmadatta was reigning in the city of Moḷinī, the Bodhisatta became a Brahmin named Saṅkha, who was wealthy and possessed great riches. He had six alms-halls built at six locations—the four city gates, the center of the city, and the gate of his own residence—and gave great alms to the poor, travelers, and others, spending six hundred thousand daily. One day, he thought: 'If the wealth in my house is exhausted, I will not be able to give alms. While the wealth is not yet exhausted, I will go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi by ship and bring back wealth.' He filled a ship with merchandise, called his wife and children, and instructed them, 'Continue to provide my alms without interruption until I return.' Then, surrounded by slaves and laborers, wearing sandals and carrying a parasol, he set out towards the port village of Tāmalitti.
30:
At that moment, on Mount Gandhamādana, a certain Paccekabuddha, having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) for seven days, emerged from it and surveyed the world. He saw the Brahmin Saṅkha traveling to acquire wealth. He reflected, "This Great Man is going to fetch wealth; will there be danger for him in the Great Ocean or not?" Knowing that there would be danger, he thought, "When this man sees me, he will offer me an umbrella and sandals. By the result of giving sandals, he will find a refuge when his ship is wrecked in the ocean. I shall show him favor." He then traveled through the air, descended not far from the man, and at midday, treading upon the hot sand which was like a bed of embers due to the fierce wind and heat of the sun, he approached him. As soon as the Brahmin Saṅkha saw the Venerable One, he was filled with great joy and thought, "The field of merit for planting seeds of goodness has come to me. Today, it is fitting for me to plant the seed of merit in this Venerable One." Therefore, it was said: "Seeing him on the way, I reflected on this matter," and so forth.

In that verse, the words "idaṃ khettaṃ" (this field) and so forth show the manner of his reflection. "Khetta" (field) is so called because it protects the sown seed by causing it to yield great fruit; it is the ground where various grains grow. In this context, however, it is called a field because it is like a field—referring to the Paccekabuddha, who is the supreme recipient of offerings. For this reason, it was said: "To a being desiring merit."

"Mahāgamaṃ" means obtaining extensive benefits, the ability to provide abundance of attendants and wealth. "Bījaṃ na ropeti" means not planting the seed (not giving).

"Khettavaruttamaṃ" means the most excellent even among the noble fields (recipients). Indeed, the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) are called noble fields; the Paccekabuddha, being even more supreme than those noble disciples, is called "khettavaruttama" (the most excellent field). "Kāraṃ" refers to honor and offerings. The phrase "If I do not perform" should be connected. The meaning is this: "Having obtained such an unsurpassed field for planting the seeds of merit, if I do not perform honor and offerings to this Venerable One, I shall not be one who truly desires merit."

16-17. The summary of the two verses beginning with "Yathā amacco" is as follows: For example, if a certain minister or general, who has been appointed by the King to a position of authority and bears the royal seal, does not act according to the King's instructions toward the people in the palace or the troops outside, and does not give them wealth and grain, thus neglecting his duties, that person falls away from his seal (position).
31:
Just as one falls away from the power and wealth obtained through the royal seal, even so, I, being one who delights in meritorious deeds and desires the fruits of merit to be obtained, having seen the extensive benefit by way of making the offering yield great fruit, if I do not give an offering to this noble recipient whom I have found, I shall in the future fall away from merit and the fruits of merit. Therefore, I must certainly perform merit here. Thus he reflected.

Having reflected thus, the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) removed his sandals even from afar, approached quickly, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, out of compassion for me, please come to the foot of this tree." When the Paccekabuddha went to the foot of the tree, he heaped up sand there and spread out his upper robe. While the Paccekabuddha was seated there, he paid homage and washed the Venerable One's feet with water that had been scented and filtered. He anointed them with scented oil. He cleaned his own sandals, anointed them with scented oil, and placed them on the Venerable One's feet, saying, "Venerable Sir, please travel wearing these sandals and holding this umbrella over your head." Thus he offered the umbrella and sandals. The Venerable One, out of compassion for him, accepted the umbrella and sandals, and while the man was looking on to increase his faith, he flew up into the air and went to Mount Gandhamādana. Referring to that event, it was said:

"Having reflected thus, I removed my sandals, paid homage to his feet, and gave the umbrella and sandals."

The Bodhisatta, seeing that event, was filled with an exceedingly devout heart, went to the port, and boarded a ship. Then, while he was crossing the Great Ocean, on the seventh day, the ship sprang a leak. They were unable to bale out the water. The people, terrified by the fear of death, paid homage to their respective deities and cried out loudly. The Bodhisatta took one attendant, anointed his whole body with oil, and ate as much as he desired of sugar-cakes along with ghee. He also made the attendant eat. Together with him, he climbed to the top of the mast and, determining the direction, said, "In this direction lies our city." Protecting himself from the danger of fish and turtles through an act of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), he leaped with the attendant, clearing a distance of about one usabha, and began to swim across the ocean. The rest of the people, however, perished right there. While he was swimming, seven days passed. Even during that time, he rinsed his mouth with salt water and remained one who observed the Uposatha.
32:
At that time, a daughter of the gods named Maṇimekhalā, who had been appointed by the Four Great Kings (Lokapālas) to protect such noble men, had been negligent for seven days due to her celestial pleasures. On the seventh day, she saw that virtuous man and thought, "If this man were to die here, it would be a great reproach to me." With a heart moved by trepidation and compassion, she filled a golden bowl with divine food and, arriving swiftly, said, "Brahmin, eat this divine food."

Looking up at her, the virtuous man refused, saying, "I will not eat, for I am observing the Uposatha." Wishing to question her, he spoke this verse:

"You who look upon me with a pleasant countenance,
And say to me, 'Eat this food';
I ask you, O lady of great power,
Are you a goddess or a human woman?"

She replied to him:

"I am a goddess of great power, O Saṅkha,
Who has come here to the midst of the ocean's waters.
I have compassion for you and no ill-will in my heart;
It is for your benefit alone that I have come here.

Here are food, drink, beds, and seats,
And various kinds of vehicles, O Saṅkha;
I shall provide all of these for you,
Whatever your heart desires."

Thus she spoke these verses. Hearing her words, the Great Being thought, "This daughter of the gods says to me in the middle of the ocean, 'I will give you this and that.' Whatever she gives me must be due to my own merit. Does she know of my merit or not? I will first ask her." Wishing to question her, he spoke this verse:

"Of whatever sacrifice (yiṭṭha) or offering (huta) I have made,
You are the mistress of it all, O fair-bodied one.
O goddess with beautiful hips, beautiful brows, and a slender waist,
Of what kamma of mine is this the result?"
33:
In that verse, 'yiṭṭha' refers to a sacrifice made through the power of giving. 'Huta' refers to an offering made through the power of hospitality to guests. 'Sabbassa no issarā tvaṃ' means, "Regarding all our meritorious deeds, you, O goddess, are capable of (the mistress of) explaining, 'This result is from this merit, and that result is from that merit.'" 'Sussoṇī' refers to a goddess with beautiful hips (or shanks). 'Subbhūrū' refers to a goddess endowed with beautiful brows and thighs. 'Vilaggamajjhe' refers to a goddess with a slender and beautiful waist. 'Kissa me' means, "Of which of the deeds I have performed is this the result, that I now find a support in the supportless great ocean?"

Hearing these words, the goddess thought, "This Brahmin asks as if he does not know the wholesome kamma he performed; I will tell him." Wishing to explain that the merit of giving a parasol and sandals to a Paccekabuddha on the day he was to board the ship was the cause of this result, she spoke the verse:

"O Brahmin, on a scorching path, to a lone monk,
Whose feet were blistered, who was thirsty and weary,
You, Saṅkha, provided sandals;
That gift (dakkhiṇā) is today your wish-fulfiller."

In that verse, 'eka-bhikkhu' refers to a single Paccekabuddha. 'Ugghaṭṭapādaṃ' means one whose feet are injured and painful due to the hot sand. 'Tasitaṃ' means one who is thirsty. 'Paṭipādayī' means he gave or provided. 'Kāmaduhā' means a gift that yields all that is desired.

Hearing this, the Great Being (Bodhisatta) was delighted in heart, thinking, "Even in such a supportless great ocean, the gift of a parasol and sandals I gave has become the giver of all my desires. Oh, how well-given it was!" and he spoke the verse:

"Let that ship be equipped with planks,
Let it be leak-proof and guided by the wind;
No other vehicle has a place here,
This very day, bring me to the city of Molinī."
34:
In that verse, 'phalakūpapannā' means being equipped with many planks because it is a large ship. It is 'anavassutā' (leak-proof) because there are no holes for water to enter. It is 'erakavātayuttā' because it is joined with a wind that takes it well along its course.

Hearing his words, the goddess was greatly delighted and created a ship made of the seven jewels, eight usabhas in length, four usabhas in width, and twenty yaṭṭhis in depth. She also created the mast, oars, and rudder made of sapphire, gold, silver, and so on, and filled it with the seven jewels. Then, embracing the Brahmin, she placed him on the ship. However, she did not look at his servant. The Brahmin shared the portion of the merit he had performed with the servant, and the servant rejoiced, saying "Sādhu." Then the goddess embraced the servant as well, placed him on the ship, and took the ship to the city of Molinī. After depositing wealth in the Brahmin's house, she returned to her own abode. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"She, being glad, happy, and satisfied there,
Having created a magnificent ship,
Taking Saṅkha along with his man,
Brought them to the pleasant and beautiful city."

Indeed, due to the perfection of the Great Being's intention and the fact that the gift was given to a Paccekabuddha who had just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the first of the seven thought-moments (javana) became kamma to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya kamma), yielding an exceedingly noble result. This result should be understood as only a small fruit of that gift. In truth, that gift, being a requisite for enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra), has immeasurable fruit. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Because of that very deed, with a hundredfold qualities,
I was delicate and grew up in comfort;
Moreover, fulfilling the perfection of giving,
Thus did I give to him."

In that verse, 'tena' means because of that gift to the Paccekabuddha. 'Sataguṇato' means that I, who was Saṅkha at that time, was delicate and grew up in comfort due to many qualities. Therefore, 'sukhedhito' means having grown up in happiness. The Teacher revealed the nobility of his own inclination toward giving (dānajjhāsaya) by showing that even though he experienced such present results, he gave the parasol and sandals to that Paccekabuddha without regard for his own physical suffering, solely with the aim of fulfilling his perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī).
35:
The Bodhisatta, while living his entire life in a house of immeasurable wealth, gave alms excessively and observed the precepts. At the end of his life, he, along with his retinue, filled the city of the devas (was reborn in the celestial realm).

At that time, the daughter of the devas became the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, the serving man became the Elder Ānanda, and the Brahmin Saṅkha was I, the Lord of the World (the Buddha).

For that Brahmin Saṅkha, the Bodhisatta, the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī) was attained by virtue of his very pure daily precepts and Uposatha precepts. The Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī) was attained through the power of wholesome states, because of his liberation from unwholesome states which are contrary to giving and observing precepts. The Perfection of Energy (Viriya-pāramī) was attained through the power of great exertion to accomplish giving and so forth, as well as through the power of his effort in crossing the great ocean. The Perfection of Patience (Khanti-pāramī) was attained through the power of endurance to fulfill those perfections. The Perfection of Truthfulness (Sacca-pāramī) was attained by practicing in accordance with his promise. The Perfection of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī) was attained through the power of unwavering undertaking in all matters. The Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā-pāramī) was attained through the power of his desire for the welfare of all beings. The Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā-pāramī) was attained by reaching a state of neutrality towards the misconduct (saṅkhāra) of beings. Wisdom, which knows the factors that are helpful and unhelpful to all perfections, abandons the unhelpful factors, and is the forerunner in establishing the helpful factors—being co-nascent and consisting of skill in means—is called the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī). In this way, these perfections are also obtained.

However, because his inclination toward giving (dānajjhāsaya) was exceedingly noble, the teaching was delivered by way of the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī). Since all ten perfections are obtained in this birth story, the qualities of the Bodhisatta such as Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) mentioned above should also be extracted here as appropriate. Likewise, the qualities of the Great Being (Mahāsatta) should be understood through such acts as: crossing the ocean to collect the resources for giving with Great Compassion, regardless of his own wealth and comfort, thinking "I shall fulfill the Perfection of Giving"; his determination to observe the Uposatha even while fallen into that ocean; and his refusal to take food even when approached by the daughter of the devas, for fear of breaking his precepts. From now on, in the remaining conducts (cariyā) to be told, the extraction of qualities should be understood in this same manner. I shall mention only the special features in each respective birth story. Therefore, it is said:

"Thus, these perfections of the Great Sage (Mahārisi) are marvelous and unprecedented...
What then can be said of their practice in accordance with the Dhamma, following the Dhamma?"

## The Explanation of the Conduct of Saṅkha the Brahmin is finished.
36:
## 3. Kururājacariyāvaṇṇanā

Regarding the third perfection, "Tatiye Indapatthe puruttame" means in the noble city called Indapattha, the preeminent city of the Kuru kingdom. "Rājā" means he is called a king because he delights the assembly of people through righteous and impartial rule and the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). "Kusale dasahupāgato" means he was endowed with the ten wholesome states; the meaning is that he was possessed of the ten bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu) such as giving, or the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha).

"Kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayā" means from the region known as the Kaliṅga kingdom. "Brāhmaṇā upagañchu maṃ" means eight Brahmins urged by the King of Kaliṅga approached me. Having approached, they begged me for the state elephant, the "Mahānāga." "Dhanyaṃ" means glorious, having reached the pinnacle of splendor, and endowed with auspicious marks. "Maṅgalasammataṃ" means highly esteemed by the people as a cause of auspicious prosperity because of being endowed with such marks.

"Avuṭṭhiko" means being devoid of rain. "Dubbhikkho" means food being difficult to obtain. "Chātako mahā" means a great affliction of hunger is occurring. "Dadāhi" means please give. "Nīlaṃ" means blue-black in color. "Añjanasavhayaṃ" means to be called by the name Añjana; the meaning is named Añjana. This is what is meant: "O Great King, our Kaliṅga kingdom is without rain, and thus a great famine and a great fear of hunger have now arisen there. To appease that, please give your auspicious state elephant named Añjana, which resembles Mount Añjana. For if this elephant is brought there, the rain god will send rain, and by that, all fears will be appeased." In this matter, the sequence of the story is as follows:

In the past, in the city of Indapattha in the Kuru kingdom, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the Kuru King. When he gradually reached the age of discretion, he went to Takkasilā, learned the arts related to architecture and various branches of knowledge (mantras and medicine), and returned. He was appointed to the position of sub-king (uparāja) by his father. Later, upon the passing of his father, he attained the kingship and ruled righteously according to the ten royal virtues without violation, by the name of Dhanañjaya. He had six alms-halls built—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the palace gate—and gave alms, spending six hundred thousand daily, causing the entire Jambudīpa to be in an uproar (of celebration). His inclination toward giving and his delight in giving spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
37:
At that time, in the kingdom of Kalinga, three perils arose: the peril of famine, the peril of starvation, and the peril of pestilence. All the citizens went to the city of Dantapura and cried out at the palace gate, "O Lord, make it rain!" Hearing this, the King asked his ministers, "Why are these people lamenting?" The ministers reported the matter to the King. The King asked, "What did the righteous kings of old do when it did not rain?" They replied, "Intending for it to rain, they would give alms, observe the Uposatha precepts, enter the auspicious royal chamber, and lie upon a bed of grass for seven days." Hearing this, the King did exactly so. However, it did not rain. The King said, "I have performed my duty, yet it does not rain. What shall we do?" They replied, "O Lord, if the auspicious state elephant of the Kuru King named Dhanañjaya in the city of Indapatta is brought here, it will rain." The King asked, "That king is endowed with great military strength and is difficult for others to overcome; how shall we bring his elephant?" They replied, "Great King, there is no need for war with him. That king has a disposition for giving and delights in charity. If asked, he would even cut off his decorated head, pluck out his clear eyes, or hand over his entire kingdom. There is no need to mention an elephant; if asked, he will surely give it." When asked, "Who is capable of making the request?" they replied, "Brahmins are capable, Great King." The King summoned eight Brahmins, honored them, provided travel expenses, and sent them to request the elephant. Those Brahmins traveled swiftly, staying only one night at each place, and arrived within a few days. They refreshed themselves by eating at the alms-halls at the city gate and waited at the East Gate, watching the path where the King would come to the alms-hall.

The Bodhisatta, having bathed early in the morning and anointed himself with perfumes, adorned with all ornaments, mounted the back of his noble, decorated elephant. With great royal majesty, he went to the alms-hall, dismounted, and gave alms with his own hands to seven or eight people. After instructing, "Give in this same manner," he remounted the elephant and headed toward the South Gate. The Brahmins, unable to find an opportunity at the East Gate due to the heavy guard, went to the South Gate. Watching for the King's arrival, they stood on high ground not far from the gate. When the King arrived, they raised their hands and hailed him with cries of victory. The King turned the elephant with his vajira-goad, approached the Brahmins, and asked, "What do you desire?" The Brahmins replied, "The kingdom of Kalinga is oppressed by the perils of famine, starvation, and pestilence. If this auspicious state elephant of yours..."
38:
The Brahmins continued, "...is taken there, the peril will be appeased. Therefore, please give us this collyrium-colored elephant to us." To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the verse: "In the realm of Kalinga... [etc.] ...named Añjana." The meaning of that verse should be understood as previously stated.

Then the Bodhisatta thought, "It is not proper for me to cause disappointment to the seekers or to break my undertaken vow." He descended from the elephant's back. Thinking, "If there is any part not yet decorated, I shall decorate it and then give it," he looked all around. Seeing no part undecorated, he took the trunk, placed it in the hands of the Brahmins, and poured water scented with flowers and perfumes from a jeweled pitcher, thus making the gift. Regarding this, it was said:

"When a seeker has approached me, refusal is not fitting.
Let not my vow be broken; I shall give the magnificent elephant."

"Taking the noble elephant by its trunk, and pouring water from a jeweled pitcher into their hands, he gave the elephant to the Brahmins."

In those verses, "yācakam-anuppatte" means when seekers have arrived. "Anucchavo" means fitting or proper. "Mā me bhijji samādānaṃ" means: "For the sake of Omniscient Wisdom, let not my resolution be broken—the resolution to fulfill the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) by giving whatever blameless thing is desired to all seekers." Therefore, saying "I shall give the magnificent elephant," he gave this auspicious state elephant. "Adāṃ" means he gave.

When the elephant had been given, the ministers said to the Bodhisatta, "Great King, why did you give away the auspicious elephant? Should not another elephant have been given? A king who desires sovereignty and victory should not give away such an auspicious state elephant used for riding." The Great Being (Mahāsatta) replied, "I give only what the seekers ask for. If they were to ask for my kingdom, I would give the kingdom as well. To me, Omniscient Wisdom is dearer than even my kingdom or my life. That is why I gave that elephant." Thus, he spoke the verse beginning with "Tassa nāge padinnamhi." In that verse, "tassa" means by that king.

"Maṅgalasampannaṃ" means endowed with auspicious qualities. "Saṅgāmavijayuttamaṃ" means the noble elephant that is supreme in achieving victory on the battlefield. How so?
39:
He showed that if that noble state elephant were to go elsewhere, how could kingship serve you? It would no longer be able to carry out the duties of a king, and the kingship itself would simply vanish.

'I would even give my entire kingdom' means: let alone the state elephant, which is but an animal, I would give even this entire Kuru kingdom to those who ask. 'I would even give my own body' means: what need is there to mention giving away the kingship? I would give even my own body to those who ask. Indeed, I have already relinquished all my possessions, both internal and external, solely for the benefit of the world. He showed that he donated that elephant because he cherished Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and because Omniscience cannot be attained without fulfilling all the Perfections (Pāramīs), beginning with the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī).

Even though that elephant was brought in this manner, it still did not rain in the kingdom of Kalinga. The King of Kalinga asked, 'Even now it does not rain; what could be the reason?' Having learned that 'The King of Kuru observes the Garudhamma (the Weighty Dhamma); therefore, in his kingdom, it rains once every fortnight or every ten days. This is the power of the King's virtues and not the power of this animal elephant,' he thought, 'We too shall observe the Garudhamma. Go to King Dhanañjaya Koravya, have those teachings written on golden plates, and bring them back.' Thus, he dispatched his ministers. The Five Precepts are called the Garudhamma. The Bodhisatta observed those precepts with great purity. Just as the Bodhisatta observed them, so did the Queen Mother, the Chief Queen, the younger brother who was the Viceroy (Uparāja), the Brahmin Chaplain (Purohita), the courtier who measures fields with a string (Rajjuggāhaka), the Charioteer, the Treasurer (Seṭṭhi), the Grain Measurer (Doṇamāpaka), the Gatekeeper (Dovārika), and the Courtesan (Gaṇikā) who graces the city. Therefore, it was said:

'The King, the Mother, the Chief Queen, the Viceroy, the Chaplain,
The Land Surveyor, the Charioteer, the Treasurer, the Measurer, the Gatekeeper,
And the Courtesan—these eleven persons
Are established in the Garudhamma.'

Those ministers approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and informed him of the matter. The Great Being said, 'I have scruples (kukkucca) regarding my Garudhamma; however, my mother observes it well. Take it from her.' When the ministers pleaded, 'Great King, scruples arise in one who loves the training and practices austerity; please give it to us,' he had it written on golden plates: 'One should not kill living beings, one should not take what is not given, one should not commit sexual misconduct, one should not tell lies, and one should not drink intoxicants.' Then he said, 'Even so, take it from my mother as well.'
40:
The messengers paid homage to the King, went to the Queen Mother, and said, "O Queen, we hear that you observe the Garudhamma; please give that Dhamma to us." The Bodhisatta's mother also spoke of having scruples herself, but being entreated by the messengers, she gave it. Likewise, the Chief Queen and the others also gave it. The messengers had the Garudhamma written on golden plates in the presence of all of them, went to the city of Dantapura, gave them to the King of Kalinga, and reported the matter. That King also, abiding in that Dhamma, fulfilled the Five Precepts. From that time on, it rained throughout the entire kingdom of Kalinga. The three fears were calmed, and the kingdom became secure and prosperous. The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving throughout his life, filled the heavenly realm along with his followers.

At that time, the courtesan and others became the Arahant nun Uppalavaṇṇā and others. Thus it was said:

"The courtesan was then Uppalavaṇṇā, the gatekeeper was then Puṇṇa,
The land surveyor was Kaccāna, and the grain measurer was Kolita.

Sāriputta was then the treasurer, and Anuruddha was the charioteer,
The Brahmin was the Elder Kassapa, and the Viceroy was the wise Ānanda.

The Chief Queen was the mother of Rāhula, the Mother was Māyādevī,
The King of Kuru was the Bodhisatta; thus you should remember the Jātaka."

In this Jātaka, the remaining qualities such as the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī) should also be determined in the manner already stated.

## The Explanation of the Conduct of the Kuru King is finished.

## 4. Mahāsudassanacariyāvaṇṇanā

In the fourth [section], the Explanation of the Conduct of Mahāsudassana, the phrase "In the city of Kusāvatī" means in the city named Kusāvatī, the place where Kusinārā is situated today. "Lord of the Earth" (Mahīpati) refers to the kshatriya named Mahāsudassana. "Universal Monarch" (Cakkavatti) is so called because he causes the Wheel-Treasure to turn, or because he conducts himself according to the four Wheels of Prosperity (Sampatti-cakka) and causes others to do so as well, or because he possesses the conduct of the wheels of postures (iriyāpatha) for the benefit of others.

Alternatively, he is called Cakkavatti because he possesses the four wonderful qualities and the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), and because he possesses the turning of the wheel of authority (āṇā-cakka) which cannot be overcome or transgressed by others.
41:
He is called 'Great Power' (Mahabbala) because he was endowed with the strength of a great army, led by the precious counselor and including the precious elephant and others, which arose through the power of his merit, as well as his own physical strength. The phrase 'When I was' refers to the connection of the words. In this context, this is the sequential account (anupubbikathā):

In the past, counting back three lives from the existence of Mahāsudassana, the Great Being was born into a householder's family. During the dispensation of the living Kassapa Buddha, while entering the forest on his own business, he saw a certain forest-dwelling elder sitting at the foot of a tree. Thinking, 'It is proper for me to build and offer a leaf hut to the venerable one here,' he abandoned his work, cut building materials, and constructed a leaf hut suitable for residence. Having fitted a door and made a wooden floor, he sat to one side, thinking, 'Will the venerable one use it or not?' The elder returned from the village, entered the leaf hut, and sat on the wooden floor.

The Bodhisatta then approached him and asked, 'Venerable sir, is the leaf hut comfortable?' When the elder replied, 'Lay follower, it is comfortable and suitable for a renunciant,' he requested, 'Venerable sir, please reside in this hut.' The elder accepted, saying, 'Very well, lay follower.' Knowing by the manner of acceptance that he would reside there, the lay follower invited him, saying, 'Please come to my house door regularly,' and provided him with daily meals at his own home.

In the leaf hut, he spread a mat and arranged a couch and a stool. He provided a backrest and a footstool. He dug a pond, made a walkway, and scattered sand. To ward off dangers, he surrounded the leaf hut with a thorn fence. Likewise, he enclosed the pond and the walkway. At the edge of the inner fence, he planted rows of palm trees. Having completed the dwelling in this manner, he offered all the requisites of a monk, starting with the three robes. At that time, there was no item used by renunciants that the Bodhisatta did not offer to the elder, such as the three robes, alms-food, bowl, cup, water-filter, ladle, utility vessel, umbrella, sandals, water-jug, needle, walking staff, pen-knife, nail-clipper, lamp, and so forth. Observing the five precepts and keeping the Uposatha, he attended to the elder for the rest of his life. The elder, residing there, attained Arahantship and passed into Parinibbāna.

The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, was reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from there and coming to the human world, he was born in the royal city of Kusāvatī as the Universal Monarch named Mahāsudassana. The majesty of his sovereignty should be understood from the passage: 'In the past, Ānanda, there was a king named Mahāsudassana...'
42:
"...a kshatriya, duly anointed,' and so forth, as it appears in the Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta). That King Mahāsudassana possessed eighty-four thousand cities led by the royal city of Kusāvatī, eighty-four thousand palaces led by the Dhamma Palace, and eighty-four thousand gabled houses led by the Mahāvyūha gabled house. All these blessings arose as a result of the single leaf hut offered to that elder. The eighty-four thousand thrones, eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, and eighty-four thousand chariots arose as a result of the couch and stool offered to him. The eighty-four thousand gems arose as a result of the lamp offered to him. The eighty-four thousand ponds arose as a result of the single pond [previously offered]. The eighty-four thousand women, eighty-four thousand sons, and eighty-four thousand householders arose as a result of the offering of monastic requisites such as bowls and cups. The eighty-four thousand milch cows arose as a result of the offering of the five products of the cow. The eighty-four thousand storehouses of cloth arose as a result of the offering of garments and robes. The eighty-four thousand pots of milk-rice arose as a result of the offering of food.

That king, becoming a king of kings endowed with the seven treasures and four psychic powers, lived having righteously conquered the entire earth bounded by the ocean. He had alms-halls built in countless places and established great charity. Three times a day, he had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming, 'Whoever desires anything, let them come to the alms-halls and take it.' Therefore, it was said: 'Then, three times a day, I had it proclaimed here and there,' and so forth.

In that context, 'there' (tattha) means in that city. There is also a reading 'tadāhaṃ', meaning 'then I' (at the time of being Mahāsudassana). 'Here and there' (tahiṃ tahiṃ) means in various places, specifically inside and outside the various walls. 'Who desires what?' (ko kiṃ icchati) means whoever among brahmins and others desires any of the gifts such as food. 'Wishes for' (pattheti) is a synonym for 'desires' (icchati). The statement 'To whom should what wealth be given?' is mentioned to show that the proclamation of charity was carried out many times in various ways. By this, the nature of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) is shown. For the perfection of giving of Bodhisattas is devoid of discrimination regarding the gift or the recipient.

Now, to show the mention of persons suitable for each gift in the proclamation of charity, the words 'Who is hungry?' (ko chātako) and so forth are spoken.
43:
In this verse, 'chātaka' means one who is hungry (one who wishes to eat). 'Tasita' means one who is thirsty. In the phrase 'ko mālaṃ ko vilepanaṃ', the word 'icchati' (who desires?) should be brought in and connected as: 'Who desires a garland? Who desires unguent?' 'Nagga' means one who is naked, implying one who is in need of clothing. 'Paridahissati' means 'he will wear [it].'

'Ko pathe chattamādeti' means: 'Which traveler on the road takes a parasol to protect himself from rain, wind, and the heat of the sun?' or 'Who desires a parasol?' 'Kopāhanā mudū subhā' means: 'Who takes the sandals—called "subha" because they are beautiful to look at, and "mudu" (soft) because they are pleasant to the touch—to protect one's feet and eyes?' or 'Who desires those sandals?' In the phrase 'sāyañca pāto ca', the word 'ca' includes the noon time as well. This is because it is stated, 'He caused a proclamation to be made three times a day.'

The construction of 'na taṃ dasasu ṭhānesu' means that this almsgiving was prepared not only in ten places, but in more than hundreds and thousands of places. 'Yācake dhanaṃ' means wealth was prepared and set out specifically for the sake of the beggars. In the city, which was twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width, there were seven rows of palm trees within the seven walls; among those rows of palm trees, there were 84,000 lotus ponds, and at the bank of each pond, a great almsgiving was established. Regarding this, the Blessed One taught thus:

'Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana established such almsgiving at the banks of those ponds: food for those desiring food, drink for those desiring drink, clothing for those desiring clothing, vehicles for those desiring vehicles, beds for those desiring beds, women for those desiring women, silver for those desiring silver, and gold for those desiring gold.'

The manner of that almsgiving was as follows: The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) had ornaments suitable for both women and men made; he kept the women only for attendance and prepared all other gift-objects for distribution, then had a drum beaten to proclaim, 'King Mahāsudassana is giving alms; enjoy them as you please.' Many people went to the banks of the ponds, bathed, put on clothes, and enjoyed the great prosperity. Those who already had such clothes discarded their own and departed. Those who had no clothes took them and departed. Some rode on elephant-vehicles and so on, wandering about as they pleased, and [lying on] noble beds...
44:
(Those who had clothes discarded them and) departed. Those who had no clothes took them and departed. Some, riding on elephant-vehicles and so forth, wandered about as they pleased, slept on noble beds, enjoyed prosperity, experienced pleasure with women, adorned themselves with the seven kinds of jeweled ornaments, and having enjoyed such happiness, took whatever objects they desired and departed. Those who had no need for them left them behind and departed. That almsgiving was also carried out daily with continuous effort. At that time, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa had no other work; they spent their time wandering about, partaking of the royal alms and enjoying prosperity. There was no time limit to that almsgiving. Whether by night or by day, whenever those in need came, the alms were given. In this way, the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) maintained the great almsgiving throughout his life, making the entire Jambudīpa festive and bustling. Therefore, it was said: 'Whether by day or by night, if a beggar should come,' and so forth.

In that verse, the phrase 'Whether by day or by night, if [he] should come' shows the timely nature of his giving. The very time when beggars approach desiring a gift is indeed the time for almsgiving for Bodhisattas. 'Vanibbaka' means a beggar (yācaka). The phrase 'having obtained the desired wealth' shows giving with great delight and affection. Whatever gift-object a particular beggar desired, the Bodhisatta gave that very thing to that person. He did not entertain thoughts of opposition regarding the high value or rarity of those objects. The phrase 'he goes with full hands' shows almsgiving to the full extent of the beggar's desire. The Great Being (Mahāsatta) gave as much as the beggars desired, without any reduction, because of his noble disposition and his great power.

The word 'lifelong' shows the absence of a time limit for the almsgiving. From the time they properly undertake the practice, Great Beings do not set a time limit in the middle until the fulfillment of the Perfections. Since there is no shrinking back in accumulating the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), and because they reach a state of non-cessation in between, it is not interrupted even by death. This is because they continue to practice in the same way even beyond that. However, the word 'lifelong' is spoken in terms of the conduct of King Mahāsudassana. 'I do not give wealth that I dislike' means that in giving such a great alms, he does not take wealth out of the palace thinking, 'This particular wealth is disagreeable to me.' 'Nor is it that I have no accumulation' means it is not that there is no accumulation or storage of wealth with me; nor am I one who does not provide support and assistance, like a monk who lives a life of austerity. This was said to show the disposition with which he maintained this great almsgiving.
45:
Now, to clarify this matter with an analogy, the verse beginning with "Yathāpi āturo nāma" is spoken. To show the meaning in connection with the analogy in that verse: For example, a sick person afflicted by disease, wishing to free himself from that disease, satisfies and pleases a physician with wealth such as gold and silver, and by following the prescription accordingly, is freed from that disease.

In the same way, I too, wishing to free all the people of the world who are afflicted by the disease of defilements and the disease of all the suffering of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), and understanding that this renunciation of all possessions is the way of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) for that liberation, gave such a great gift to the beggars and supplicants. This was done to fulfill the aspirations of beings through a great gift without remainder, by way of the things to be given and the recipients, and also to fulfill the mind that arose thinking, "My perfection of giving is not yet complete; therefore, I shall fulfill this deficient mind." In giving thus, there was no lingering attachment, longing, or expectation regarding that gift or its results; it was given solely for the purpose of attaining Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and reaching Enlightenment (sambodhi).

Thus, after performing the great gift, the Great Being (Mahāsatta) ascended the Dhamma Palace (dhamma-pāsāda) produced by the power of his own merit. Right at the gate of the gabled chamber, he suppressed sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) and the like. Sitting on the golden throne there, he attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and direct knowledges (abhiññā). Departing from there, he entered the golden gabled house, and sitting on the silver throne there, he developed the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), spending eighty-four thousand years in meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti). At the time of death, to Queen Subhaddā and the eighty-four thousand ladies of the court and ministers who had come to see him, he gave this advice with the verse:

"Impermanent indeed are conditioned things, subject to arising and passing away; having arisen, they cease; their calming is bliss."

Having given this advice, at the end of his life, he was destined for the Brahma world.

At that time, Queen Subhaddā became the mother of Rāhula, the eldest son (parināyaka-ratana) became Rāhula, the rest of the assembly became the Buddha's assembly, and King Mahāsudassana was I, the Lord of the World.
46:
In this birth story of King Mahāsudassana the Wheel-turning Monarch, the ten perfections (pāramī) are also found in their specific forms. However, because the aspiration for giving was so noble and intense, only the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) appears in the Pali text. The remaining perfections are to be understood in the same manner as mentioned below. Furthermore, even while ruling over the four islands, shining with the seven noble treasures, he did not indulge in such sensual pleasures. Instead, he discarded sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) and the like from afar. While performing such great gifts, he spent eighty-four thousand years in meditative attainments. Even while delivering Dhamma discourses connected with impermanence and so on, he remained diligent in insight (vipassanā). His qualities and powers, such as non-attachment to all things, should be noted.

## The Explanation of the Conduct of Mahāsudassana is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Conduct of Mahāgovinda

In the fifth [story], the Conduct of Mahāgovinda, "the chaplain of seven kings" means the chaplain who gave counsel in all matters to the seven kings, beginning with Sattabhū. "Honored by gods and men" means he was honored with the four requisites and with respect and reverence by those seven kings as well as by all the other Khattiya kings in the Rose-apple Island (Jambudīpa). "The Brahmin Mahāgovinda" refers to the Brahmin who acquired the name "Mahāgovinda" because of his great power and because he was consecrated with the Govinda-consecration. From the time of his consecration, this name became well-known for the Bodhisatta; his original name, however, was Jotipāla.

It is said that on the day he was born, all weapons shone brightly. The King, seeing his own auspicious weapon blazing at dawn, was frightened and asked the chaplain, the Bodhisatta's father, who had come to attend him. The chaplain comforted him, saying, "Do not fear, Great King. Because my son was born, the weapons in the whole city, not just in the palace, are blazing due to his power. There is no danger to the King because of him. In the whole world, there will be no one equal to him in wisdom. This is the omen of his future." The King, being delighted, gave a thousand [pieces of money], saying, "Let this be for the child's milk-money," and added, "Show him to me when he reaches maturity." When the youth grew up, he became one who saw what was beneficial and what was not, and became the advisor in all matters to the seven kings. Later, he renounced the world and became a monk, protecting beings from harm in the present life and the life to come, and establishing them in what is beneficial. Because he shone in this way...
47:
Because of his ability to protect, they named the boy "Jotipāla." Therefore, it was said (in the Dīgha Nikāya), "By name, he was called Jotipāla."

At that time, the Bodhisatta became the son of the Brahmin Govinda, who was the chaplain to the king named Disampati. After his father and the king passed away, he established the king's son, Reṇu, and his six friends—Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū, Bharata, and the two Dhataraṭṭha kings—in their respective kingships so that these seven kings would not quarrel with one another. Teaching them the Dhamma and worldly affairs, he was respected, honored, revered, and worshipped by all kings throughout the land of Jambudīpa, as well as by other Brahmins, devas, nāgas, and householders, reaching a state of supreme honor. Because of his skill in Dhamma and worldly affairs, the name "Mahāgovinda" became famous. As the Blessed One said: "Friends, the Brahmin is indeed Govinda; friends, the Brahmin is indeed Mahāgovinda." Therefore, it was said:

"Once again, at another time, I was the chaplain of seven kings, the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, honored by gods and men."

Then, prompted by the power of the Bodhisatta's merit, the kings, their retinues of princes, Brahmins, householders, and people of the market towns and countryside brought immeasurable and noble offerings from all directions, overwhelming like a great flood. This was due to his accumulation of vast merit over countless lives, his noble birth, his pure conduct and virtue, his mastery of all arts, and his tender heart filled with great compassion for all beings as if they were his own children. The Bodhisatta thought: "Now I am receiving great gain and honor. It would be well if I were to fulfill the Perfection of Giving by satisfying all beings with these possessions." He had six alms-halls built—one in the center of the city, four at the gates, and one at the door of his own house—and practiced great charity by giving away immeasurable wealth daily. Whatever gifts were brought to him, and whatever items were prepared for his own use, he sent them all to those alms-halls. Even though he practiced such great renunciation day after day, there was no sense of satiation or contentment in the Bodhisatta's mind, let alone any stinginess. Because of the crowds of people coming to receive gifts, those departing with offerings, and those praising the virtues of the Great Being, within the city...
48:
...and around the outside of the city, there arose a tumultuous roar like the great ocean stirred by the fierce winds at the end of an aeon. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Then, in the seven kingdoms, whatever gifts I received, with those I gave a great gift, unshakable and like the ocean."

In that verse, "Tadāhaṃ" means "at that time when I was the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, the chaplain of the seven kings." "Sattarajjesu" means "in the kingdoms of the seven kings, such as Reṇu and the others." "Akkhohbaṃ" means a gift that cannot be shaken or obstructed by any internal or external enemies. There is also a variant reading "Accubbhaṃ," which means extremely full, due to the noble and vast nature of the objects of charity and the intention for supreme giving. "Sāgarūpamaṃ" means like the ocean; just as the water in the ocean cannot be exhausted even if all the people in the world were to take it, so too the offerings in Mahāgovinda's alms-halls could not be exhausted. In the final verse, "Varaṃ dhanaṃ" refers to noble or desired wealth. The rest is to be understood as previously explained.

Thus, while the Bodhisatta was occupied with giving, causing a great rain of charity to fall without distinction like a great cloud at the beginning of an aeon, he still diligently taught the Dhamma and worldly affairs to the remaining seven kings. He taught the arts and sciences to seven Brahmin Mahāsālas and instructed seven hundred Snātakas in the mantras. Later, a good reputation spread concerning Mahāgovinda: "The Brahmin Mahāgovinda truly sees Brahmā; the Brahmin Mahāgovinda discusses, speaks, and consults with Brahmā." He thought: "Now this false reputation has spread about me, saying 'He sees Brahmā, he discusses, speaks, and consults with Brahmā.' It would be well if I were to make this reputation true." Having asked permission from the seven kings, the seven Brahmin Mahāsālas, the seven hundred Snātakas, and his wife and children, he resolved, "I will strive to see Brahmā," and devoted himself to the meditation on the Brahma-vihāras for the four months of the rainy season. Knowing his thoughts with his own mind, Brahmā Sanatkumāra appeared before him. Upon seeing the Brahmā, the Great Being questioned him.
49:
“O friend, you are endowed with beauty, you are endowed with fame, and you are endowed with splendor. Who are you? Not knowing you, we ask. How may we know you?” (Thus he asked).

The Brahma, wishing to make himself known, said:
“They know me in the Brahma-world as Sanantana (Sanaṅkumāra). All the devas and Brahmas know me. O Govinda, know me thus.”

When he had spoken thus, Govinda the Brahmin said:
“For the Lord Brahma, a seat, water for the feet, a foot-towel, and honeyed vegetables are prepared. May the Lord favor us by accepting our offering.”

Although he had no need for the offering, in order to gladden the heart of Govinda the Brahmin and to establish a friendly acquaintance, the Brahma accepted it, saying, “O Govinda, I accept the offering you speak of.” Then, wishing to grant an opportunity for questioning, he said:
“For the sake of welfare in this life and happiness in the life to come, the opportunity is given. Ask whatever you desire.”

Then the Great Being (Govinda the Brahmin), regarding only the benefit concerning the hereafter, asked:
“Desiring to be free from doubt regarding things made known by others, I ask the Brahma Sanaṅkumāra: Established in what Dhamma, and training in what manner, can a mortal reach the deathless Brahma-world?”

The Brahma, wishing to answer him, said:
“O Govinda the Brahmin, having abandoned the craving for ‘I’ and ‘mine’ among men, being one-pointed in mind, intent on compassion (karuṇā), free from the stench of defilements, and abstaining from sexual intercourse—established in this Karuṇā-jhāna and training herein, a mortal can reach the deathless Brahma-world.” Thus he taught the path leading to the Brahma-world.
50:
In those verses, ‘Maṃ ve kumāraṃ jānanti’ means they truly know me as ‘Kumāra’. ‘Brahmaloke’ means in the noble world. ‘Sanantanaṃ’ refers to an ancient, long-standing practice. “O Govinda, mark me thus” is the meaning.

“This is the seat prepared for the Lord Brahma to sit upon. This water is for washing the feet. This drinking water is for quenching thirst. This foot-oil is for relieving fatigue. This ‘madhusāka’ refers to vegetables boiled in water without acidity, salt, or spices.” Indeed, at that time, the Bodhisatta’s four-month holy life was of the highest austerity and noble conduct. “Having made all these noble offerings to the Brahma, I request: May the Lord accept this offering as worthy.” Thus, although the Great Being (the Bodhisatta) knew that Brahmas do not consume such things, he spoke thus to fulfill the duty of hospitality, which was his habit. The Brahma, knowing the Bodhisatta’s intention, said, “O Govinda, I accept your offering as you have said.”

The meaning of those words is: “Let it be as if I have sat in that seat of yours, as if my feet have been washed with the water, as if the drinking water has been drunk, as if the feet have been anointed with the oil, and as if the vegetables have been consumed.”

‘Kankhī akankhiṃ paravediyesu’ means “Though I have doubts, I am without doubt regarding the problems made known and clearly explained by others.”

‘Hitvā mamattaṃ’ means abandoning the craving for requisites (upakaraṇa-taṇhā) that arises as “This is mine, this is my self.” ‘Manujesu’ means among beings. The word ‘Brahme’ is used to address the Bodhisatta. ‘Ekodibhūto’ is called such because it arises alone; it shows physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). Alternatively, it is called ‘ekodibhūto’ because of reaching noble concentration (samādhi), meaning well-concentrated through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Wishing to show this one-pointedness by way of the Brahma-vihara of compassion, he said ‘Karuṇedhimutto’. It means having a mind inclined toward Karuṇā-jhāna, having produced that jhāna. ‘Nirāmagandho’ means being free from the stench of defilements (kilesa). ‘Etthaṭṭhito’ means established in those dhammas, having fulfilled those dhammas. ‘Ettha ca sikkhamāno’ means in those dhammas...
51:
The being who practices means one who develops this meditation on the divine abidings (brahmavihāra-bhāvanā). This is just a summary here. The details should be understood as they appear in the Pali texts (such as the Dīgha Nikāya).

Then, the Great Being, having heard the words of that Brahma and feeling revulsion for the 'raw smells' (āmagandha) of defilements, said, 'I shall renounce the world right now.' The Brahma also said, 'Great Being, it is well; renounce. If you do so, my coming to you will indeed be a good coming. Dear son, you are the foremost man in the whole of Jambudīpa, and while in the prime of youth, to renounce such great wealth and power is extremely noble, like a great scent-elephant breaking its iron shackles and entering the forest. This is the tradition of the Bodhisattas.' Having spoken these words to strengthen the Great Bodhisatta's resolve, he returned to the Brahma realm.

The Great Being also thought, 'It is not proper for me to leave this house and renounce yet. I am the one who advises the royal families on their welfare. I should inform them. If they also renounce, it is well; if not, I shall renounce after handing over the position of chaplain (purohita).' First, he informed King Reṇu. Although the king repeatedly enticed him with sensual pleasures, he declared the cause of his sense of urgency (saṃvega) and his absolute desire to renounce. The king then said, 'If you, teacher, renounce, I too shall renounce.' Accepting this with 'Very well,' he similarly informed the six kings beginning with Sattabhū, seven great wealthy brahmins, seven hundred learned scholars (snātakas), and his own wives. To look after their minds, he stayed for seven days and then departed in a renunciation similar to the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) and became a monk.

Following that Govinda, the multitude led by the seven kings also renounced. That assembly was very large. Surrounded by an assembly extending many leagues (yojanas), the Great Being traveled through villages, market towns, provinces, and royal capitals, preaching the Dhamma. He established the multitude in merit. Wherever he went, there was an uproar like the appearance of a Buddha. When people heard, 'Pandit Govinda is coming,' they built and decorated pavilions in advance, went out to meet him, invited him into the pavilions, and served him with various delicious foods. Great gain and honor arose, overwhelming like a great flood. The Great Being established the multitude in the perfection of virtue (sīla-sampadā), restraint of the senses, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the preliminary work for kasinas, the meditative absorptions (jhānas), the super-knowledges (abhiññā), the eight attainments (samāpatti), and the divine abidings (brahmavihāra). It was just like the time of a Buddha's appearance.
52:
The Bodhisatta, fulfilling the perfections throughout his life, spent his time in the bliss of meditative attainments and, at the end of his life, was reborn in the Brahma realm. That holy life (brahmacariya) of the Bodhisatta Mahāgovinda was successful, prosperous, widespread, popular, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans, lasting for a very long time. All those who fully understood his teaching, after the breaking up of the body, after death, were reborn in a happy destination, the Brahma realm. Among those who did not fully understand, some were reborn in the company of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. Some were reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas... pe... the Tusita devas, the Yāma devas, the Tāvatimsa devas, and the Cātumahārājika devas. Those who were the lowest of all filled the host of Gandhabbas. Thus, the multitude for the most part became those who went to the Brahma realm or the heaven realms. Therefore, the heaven and Brahma realms were full, and the four woeful states (apāya) were as if empty.

In this Mahāgovinda Jātaka, as in the Akitti Jātaka, the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) should be extracted. At that time, the seven kings became the Great Elders (Mahātheras), the rest of the assembly became the Buddha's assembly, and Mahāgovinda was I, the Lord of the World (Lokanātha). Likewise, one should clearly understand the following qualities and powers: establishing the seven kings such as Reṇu in their respective kingdoms without conflict; his diligence in advising those kings on welfare and Dhamma in those seven vast kingdoms; his practice of the supreme holy life for four months to make the reputation 'he converses even with Brahma' true to reality; the arrival of Brahma himself to him due to that practice; his renunciation, after standing in the advice of Brahma, by discarding the gain and honor offered by the seven kings and the whole world like a lump of spit, followed by an immeasurable assembly of khattiyas, brahmins, and others; and the long-lasting continuity of his teaching like the dispensation (sāsana) of the Buddhas.

## Mahāgovindacariyā-vaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

## 6. Nimirājacariyā-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth verse beginning with 'Mithilāyaṃ puruttame,' Mithilā refers to the noble city of the Videhans. The Great King named Nimi was so named because he was born like one joining a wheel rim (nemi). That king, through great and special qualities such as giving and virtue, and through great...
53:
Because he is endowed with the great power of a king, he is called a Great King (Mahārāja). A wise person who desires merit is one who seeks wholesome merit for the benefit of both himself and others.

In the past, in the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, our Bodhisatta was a king named Maghadeva. For eighty-four thousand years he spent his time in youthful play; for eighty-four thousand years he served as viceroy; and while ruling as king for eighty-four thousand years, he told his barber, "When you see grey hairs on my head, please inform me." Later, when the barber saw grey hairs and informed him, the king had them removed with golden tweezers and placed upon his palm. Looking at the grey hair, he was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "The divine messenger has indeed appeared to me." He thought, "Now it is time for me to renounce the world," and granted a choice village yielding a revenue of one hundred thousand to the barber. He then summoned his eldest son and said to him:

"These grey hairs growing on my head have appeared;
They lead me toward old age.
The divine messengers have manifested;
It is time for my renunciation."

Having thus spoken and having well-instructed his son in kingship, even though he still had another eighty-four thousand years of life remaining, he regarded himself as if standing in the presence of Death. With a stirred heart, he delighted in the state of renunciation. Therefore, it was said:

"Seeing a grey hair on his head, the wise King Maghadeva, lord of the directions, attained spiritual urgency and truly delighted in renunciation."

That King Maghadeva exhorted his son, "You should practice in this same manner as I have practiced. Do not be the last man in our lineage." Having thus advised him, he departed from the city and became a monk. For eighty-four thousand years, he spent his time in meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti), and at the end of his life, he was destined for the Brahma realm. His son also ruled righteously for many thousands of years, renounced by the same means, and was destined for the Brahma realm. Likewise his son, and his son—in this way, eighty-four thousand kings (less two) renounced the world upon seeing grey hair on their heads. Then the Bodhisatta, while staying in the Brahma realm, reflected, "Is the good practice I established in the human world still continuing, or is it not?"...
54:
(The Bodhisatta Brahma) saw: "My lineage has continued for this long; now it will no longer continue." He thought, "I shall not allow my lineage to be broken," and took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the king born in his own lineage, appearing as if joining the rim (nemi) of his own lineage. Therefore, he received the name "Nimi," with the meaning "one who appeared as if joining the rim."

Indeed, on the day of the prince's naming, the father brought in experts in marks. After observing the marks, they prophesied, "Great King, this prince will uphold your lineage; he will possess greater power and greater merit than even his father and grandfather." Hearing this, the king named him "Nimi" for the reason mentioned. From his youth, Prince Nimi was constantly devoted to the practice of virtue and the Uposatha. Later, his father, seeing grey hair in the same manner as before, gave a choice village as a reward to the barber, instructed his son in kingship, departed from the city to renounce, developed jhānas, and was destined for the Brahma realm.

King Nimi, being naturally inclined toward giving, had five alms-halls built—at the four city gates and in the center of the city—and established great almsgiving. He sacrificed five hundred thousand daily, spending one hundred thousand for each alms-hall. He observed the five precepts and undertook the Uposatha virtue on fast days. He also encouraged the multitude in meritorious deeds such as giving. He spoke of the path to the heavenly realms, warned them with the fear of hell, and restrained them from evil. Abiding by his advice, the people performed merits such as giving and, when they passed away from that life, were reborn in the heavenly realm. The heavenly realm became full, and the hell realm became as if empty. Then the Blessed One, wishing to make known his great inclination for giving and his special fulfillment of the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī), said:

"At that time, having had built four halls with four entrances, I established almsgiving there for birds, beasts, and humans."

In that verse, "Tadā" refers to the time when he was King Nimi. "Māpayitvāna" means having had them built. "Catussālaṃ" refers to halls connected in the four directions. "Catummukhaṃ" refers to a hall equipped with four doors in the four directions. Because the alms-hall was so vast and the gifts and seekers were so numerous, it was impossible to distribute all the gifts through a single door.
55:
Since it was not possible to complete the distribution of gifts through a single door, and it was not easy to exhaust the offerings, he had four great gates constructed at the four directions of the hall. In that hall, gifts were piled up from the doorway to the corners. He conducted the charity from dawn until the usual time of sleep. During other times at night, hundreds of lamps were kept burning. Whenever those in need arrived, gifts were given. This charity was not only for the poor, travelers, and beggars, but also for the wealthy, similar to the charity of King Mahāsudassana. By renouncing such noble and exquisite gifts, all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa received and enjoyed them. Indeed, making the whole of Jambudīpa like a sacrificial pavilion, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) then performed a great almsgiving (Mahādāna). Just as he gave to humans, he also provided charity for animals, starting with beasts and birds, at a suitable place outside the alms-hall. Therefore, it was said: 'There he performed charity for beasts, birds, humans, and others.' Not only for animals, but he also shared merit daily with the petas (hungry ghosts). Just as charity was performed in one alms-hall, it was likewise performed in all five alms-halls. However, in the Pali text, it is mentioned as if there were only one, saying, 'Then I created a four-faced hall,' referring to the alms-hall in the center of the city.

Now, wishing to show a portion of the gifts in that charity, he said: 'Clothing and bedding, food, drink, and nourishment.'

In that verse, 'clothing' (acchādana) refers to various types of garments and robes such as fine linen (khoma). 'Bedding' (sayana) refers to various types of sleeping requisites such as couches, thrones, and ornate rugs (gonaka). Here, it should be understood that 'seating' (āsana) is also included by the term 'bedding.' 'Food, drink, and nourishment' refers to rice of various flavors, beverages, and other diverse types of food as desired by various beings. 'Having performed it without interruption' means performing it day and night without break from the beginning until the end of his life.

43-4. Now, wishing to show how that charity was performed as a Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) aimed at Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), and to illustrate his disposition (ajjhāsaya) at that time with a simile, he said: 'Just as a servant,' and so on. The meaning is: For example, a servant man, having approached his master from time to time...
56:
...by way of service, for the sake of obtaining wealth, pleases that master in every way through body, speech, and mind—through bodily, verbal, and mental actions—and seeks only to please him; in the same way, I, being a Bodhisatta, desiring to serve the state of the incomparable Buddha, who is the Lord of the world including the devas, for the sake of pleasing all people, in every existence wherever I am born, by the power of fulfilling the Perfection of Giving, satisfying all beings with material things, I shall seek and search for the Omniscience (Sabbaññutaññāṇa) named 'Bodhi-ja' (born of enlightenment) because it arises from the Noble Path-knowledge (Ariya-magga-ñāṇa) known as Bodhi, in every way and through various means. I desire and greatly long for that supreme Bodhi, the Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), by performing any act such as the sacrifice of life. (Thus he thought).

In this way, in this Cariyāpiṭaka text, the teaching is given only by the power of the Perfection of Giving to show the nobility of the intention to give. In the Nimi Jātaka, however, the fulfillment of other perfections such as the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī) is also made clear. For indeed, having adorned himself with virtues such as morality in the manner mentioned above, and establishing the multitude of people in those virtues, the devas who were reborn in the celestial realm by abiding in his instruction assembled in the divine assembly hall named Sudhammā and praised the virtues of the Great Being, saying: 'Oh, because we relied on King Nimi, we have attained this prosperity. Indeed, such wonderful persons, who perform the work of a Buddha (Buddhakicca) for the multitude even before a Buddha has arisen, appear in the world!' Thus they spoke clearly in praise. Therefore, it was said:

'Truly a wonder in the world, the wise ones appear;
When the wise King Nimi, seeker of merit, arose,
What a wonder it was then!' (Jā. 2.22.421) etc.

Hearing that praise, all the devas, headed by Sakka, the king of devas, desired to see the Bodhisatta. Then one day, while the Great Being, King Nimi, was observing the Uposatha and sitting cross-legged in the late watch of the night in his noble palace, a reflection arose in his mind: 'Is the merit of giving superior, or is the observance of the holy life (brahmacariya) superior?' The king was unable to cut off his doubt. At that moment, Sakka's stone throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting on the cause and seeing the Bodhisatta's thought, said, 'Now I shall cut off his doubt,' and came to stand before him. When asked by the king, 'Who are you?', he declared his status as the king of devas and asked, 'Great King, what thought are you pondering?' The king then told him the matter. Sakka, wishing to show that the holy life (brahmacariya) alone is superior...
57:
Sakka, having revealed his identity as the King of Devas, asked, “Great King, what are you thinking about?” King Nimi then explained the matter to him. Sakka, wishing to show that the holy life (brahmacariya) is indeed supreme, said:

“By a low holy life, one is reborn among the Khattiyas;
By a medium one, to the state of a deva;
And by a supreme one, one is purified.

These bodies (realms) are not easily obtained by any kind of begging (or sacrificing);
Those who are reborn in these bodies are the homeless ascetics.”

In that verse, among the many views of the sectarians (titthiyas), mere abstinence from sexual intercourse is called ‘low brahmacariya,’ and by that practice, one is reborn in a Khattiya family. Mere access concentration (upacāra) of jhāna is called ‘medium,’ and by that practice, one reaches the state of a deva. However, the attainment of the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) is called ‘supreme,’ and by that practice, one is reborn in the Brahma realm. Since those outside the Dispensation call that Brahma realm ‘Nibbāna,’ it is said that ‘one is purified.’

In the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha, however, for a monk of pure virtue who aspires to a certain group of devas, his intention for the holy life is called ‘low’ due to its inferiority; by that practice, he is reborn in the deva world he desired. The attainment of the eight meditative attainments by one of pure virtue is called ‘medium,’ and by that practice, he is reborn in the Brahma realm. But for one of pure virtue to develop insight (vipassanā) and reach Arahatship, it is called ‘supreme,’ and by that practice, he is purified (from defilements). Thus Sakka praised: “Great King, compared to giving, the practice of the holy life is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold more fruitful and superior.”

‘Kāyā’ refers to the hosts of Brahmas. ‘Yācayogena’ means associated with begging. There is also a Pali reading ‘yājayogena,’ which means associated with sacrificing or giving. ‘Tapassino’ refers to those devoted to austerities. By this verse, he demonstrates the great power of the practice of the holy life.

After speaking thus, he gave advice, saying: “Great King, although the holy life is more fruitful than giving, both of these are deeds to be performed by Great Men. Therefore, being heedful in both, give gifts and also guard your virtue,” and then he returned to his own place in the deva world.

Then the host of devas asked, “Great King, where did you go?” Sakka explained the matter, saying, “I went to Mithilā to sever the doubts of King Nimi,” and he praised the virtues of the Bodhisatta in detail. Upon hearing this, the devas said, “Great King, we wish to see King Nimi; please have him summoned.” Sakka consented, saying “Very well,” and addressed the celestial charioteer Mātali: “Go, seat King Nimi upon the Vejayanta chariot and bring him here.”
58:
“Bring him here,” (Sakka commanded). Mātali the celestial charioteer accepted, saying “Very well,” and went with the chariot. Having seated the Great Being in the chariot, and being requested by King Nimi, he showed and explained the places of those who committed evil deeds and those who performed meritorious deeds according to their karma, and gradually brought him to the deva world. The devas, hearing that “King Nimi has arrived,” took divine scents and flowers in their hands and went out to welcome him as far as the gates of Cīttakūṭa. Honoring the Great Being with divine scents and so forth, they led him to the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall. The King descended from the chariot, entered the assembly hall, and sat on the same seat as Sakka. When invited by Sakka with divine sensual pleasures, he refused, saying, “Great King, I have no need for these sensual pleasures which are like borrowed goods,” and he preached the Dhamma in many ways. Having stayed for seven human days, he said, “I shall go to the human world; there I will perform meritorious deeds such as giving.” Sakka then commanded Mātali, “Take King Nimi back to Mithilā.” Mātali seated King Nimi upon the Vejayanta chariot and reached Mithilā from the eastern direction. The great multitude, seeing the divine chariot, went out to welcome the King. Mātali let the Great Being down at the lion-window (siha-pañjara), took his leave, and returned to his own place. The multitude surrounded the King and asked, “Sire, what is the deva world like?” The King praised the prosperity of the deva world and preached the Dhamma, saying, “You all should also perform meritorious deeds such as giving; by doing so, you will be reborn in that deva world.” Later, as mentioned before, upon seeing a grey hair, he handed over the kingdom to his son, renounced sensual pleasures, became an ascetic, and having developed the four Brahma-vihāras, he became one who reached the Brahma realm.

At that time, Sakka became Anuruddha. Mātali became Ānanda. The eighty-four thousand kings became the Buddha’s assembly. King Nimi became the Lord of the World (the Buddha).

In this Nimi Jātaka, the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) of the Bodhisatta should be extracted in the same manner as mentioned below. Furthermore, one should extract and note his glorious virtues and power, such as: his rebirth in the human world out of great compassion, thinking, “I shall continue the good practice I performed in the past,” even after renouncing the bliss of the Brahma realm; his noble inclination toward giving; his practice of giving and so forth in accordance with that inclination; his establishing the multitude in merit; the spreading of his fame among devas and humans; the great wonder of his approach to Sakka, the King of Devas; his return to the human world to further increase his store of merit without delighting in the divine prosperity even when invited by Sakka; and his total lack of attachment to all kinds of gains and prosperity.

## The Explanation of the Conduct of King Nimi is finished.
59:
## 7. Canda-Kumāra-Cariyā-Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh commentary on the conduct of Canda-Kumāra, 'Ekaraajassa atrajo' means the son born of the breast of the King of Kāsi named Ekarāja. 'Nagare Pupphavatiyā' means in the city named Pupphavatī. 'Candasavhayo' means one who is to be called by the name Canda, meaning one named Canda.

In the past, this city of Vārāṇasī was known as Pupphavatī. There, King Ekarāja, the son of King Vasavatti, reigned. The Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of Queen Gotamī, the chief consort of King Ekarāja. They named the boy 'Canda-Kumāra'. When Canda-Kumāra was able to walk, another son was born, and they named him 'Suriya-Kumāra'. When Suriya-Kumāra was able to walk, a daughter was born, and they named her 'Selā'. They also had two half-brothers named Bhaddasena and Sūra.

As the Bodhisatta grew up, he mastered all arts and sciences to the end. The King brought a suitable princess named Candā and appointed the Bodhisatta as the Viceroy (Uparāja). A son was born to the Bodhisatta, and they named him 'Vāsula'.

The King had a chaplain (purohita) named Khandahāla, whom the King appointed to the position of judge. This Khandahāla was a bribe-taker; by taking bribes, he would make the non-owner the owner and the rightful owner the non-owner. One day, a man who had lost his case came out of the court crying out. Seeing the Bodhisatta going to attend upon the King, he fell at his feet and lamented, "My lord, Khandahāla is destroying justice by taking bribes in the court. I have lost my case because he took a bribe." The Bodhisatta consoled him, saying, "Do not fear," and took him back to the court, where he decided the case in favor of the rightful owner. The multitude shouted "Sādhu" with a great sound.

When the King heard that the Bodhisatta had judged the case well, he summoned him and said, "Dear son, from today onwards, you yourself shall decide the judicial matters." Thus, he handed over the judicial authority to the Bodhisatta. Khandahāla's income was cut off. From then on, Khandahāla bore a grudge against the Bodhisatta and looked for an opportunity to harm him. That King Ekarāja was weak-minded and easily persuaded. One day, having seen the celestial realm in a dream, he desired to go there...
60:
The King said to the chaplain, "Tell me the path leading to the Brahma world." The chaplain replied, "If you wish to give the most noble gift, perform a sacrifice by gathering everything in groups of four." When asked by the King, "What is the most noble gift?", the chaplain explained, "Taking your beloved sons, beloved wives, beloved daughters, wealthy merchants, auspicious elephants, horses, and so on, in groups of four, and sacrificing these two-legged and four-legged creatures by offering their throat blood—this is called the most noble gift (atidāna)."
