In this way, while saying "I will tell you the path to heaven," he actually told him the path to hell.

The King, perceiving the chaplain as a wise man and believing that "the method he spoke of is the path to heaven," desired to practice it. He had a great sacrificial pit prepared and ordered, "Bring the four princes, starting with the Bodhisatta, and all the two-legged and four-legged creatures mentioned by Khandahāla to the place of sacrifice." All the preparations for the sacrifice were made ready. Hearing this, the people made a great uproar. Although the King felt remorse and wanted to release them, he was urged on by Khandahāla and gave the order again. The Bodhisatta, realizing, "Khandahāla, having lost his position in the court, has borne a grudge against me and, desiring my death, has brought about this great calamity for the people," tried to dissuade his father the King from that wrong view through various means, but was unsuccessful. The people lamented; it was a great, pitiful sight. Even as the people were weeping, all the tasks at the sacrificial pit were completed. They brought Prince Canda-Kumāra, bent his neck, and made him sit. Khandahāla brought a golden bowl near, held a sword, and stood ready, saying, "I will cut the prince's neck."

Seeing this, Princess Candā, the consort of the prince, thought, "I have no other refuge; I will ensure the safety of my lord through the power of my truth." With joined palms, she walked through the crowd and declared, "This act which Khandahāla is performing, calling it the path to heaven, is indeed an evil deed. By this word of truth of mine, may my lord be safe!

"All the deities who are in this world have gone to their refuge.
Protect me, who am helpless; save my husband (to be safe)."

Thus she performed an Act of Truth (saccakiriya). Sakka, the King of Devas, hearing her cry and knowing the situation, arrived holding a flaming iron sledgehammer. He threatened the King and ordered everyone to be released. Sakka then revealed his divine form, brandished a flaming thunderbolt, and said, "O wicked king, O foolish king, when have you ever seen anyone reach a happy destination by killing others?" and to Prince Canda-Kumāra...
61:
Sakka threatened them and caused everyone to be released. At that time, Sakka revealed his divine form and stood in the sky, brandishing a flaming, blazing thunderbolt, saying, "Hey, you wicked and foolish king! When have you ever seen anyone reach a happy destination (sugati) by taking the lives of living beings? Release Prince Candakumāra and all these people from their bonds. If you do not release them, I will split the heads of both you and this wicked brahmin right here." Seeing this wonder, the king and the brahmin quickly released everyone from their bonds.

Then, the great multitude raised a loud shout and suddenly rushed into the sacrificial arena. They pelted the brahmin Khaṇḍahāla with stones, one after another, causing him to meet his end right there in the sacrificial pit. They then began to try to kill the king as well. The Bodhisatta, however, stood embracing his father first and prevented them from killing him. The people said, "We shall grant this wicked king his life, but we will not give him the white parasol or the shade of the palace, nor the right to live in the city. We shall make him an outcast (caṇḍāla) and have him live outside the city." They stripped him of his royal attire, dressed him in saffron-dyed robes, wrapped his head with an old turmeric-stained cloth, made him an outcast, and sent him to a caṇḍāla village. All those who performed the animal sacrifice, caused it to be performed, or rejoiced in it, were destined for hell. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Having committed such evil, all of them are established in hell; for having done an evil deed, it is not possible to go from here to a happy destination."

Then, the entire royal assembly, the city dwellers, and the country folk gathered together and consecrated the Bodhisatta as king. That Prince Candakumāra, ruling righteously, remembered the calamity and ruin that had arisen without cause for himself and the people. Filled with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he exerted himself exceedingly in meritorious deeds, establishing great charity, observing the precepts, and undertaking the Uposatha duties. Therefore, it was said:

"Then, I was released from the sacrifice and emerged from the sacrificial arena; having generated spiritual urgency, I established great charity."
62:
## Commentary on the Conduct of Candakumāra (Candakumāracariyāvaṇṇanā)

Reflecting on the nature of such impending ruin, he became filled with spiritual urgency and exerted himself exceedingly in meritorious deeds, establishing great charity. He guarded the precepts and well-undertook the Uposatha duties. Therefore, he spoke the verse beginning with: "Then, I was released from the sacrifice and emerged from the sacrificial arena; having generated spiritual urgency, I established great charity."

In that verse, "released from the sacrifice" (yajanā mutto) means being freed from the danger of being killed in the sacrificial procedure arranged by the brahmin Khaṇḍahāla, in the manner already described. "Emerged from the sacrificial arena" (nikkhanto yaññavāṭato) means departing from that sacrificial ground along with the great multitude who were eager to perform the consecration. "Having generated spiritual urgency" (saṃvegaṃ janayitvāna) means having produced an intense sense of urgency, thinking, "Living together in this world is indeed full of danger." "Established great charity" (mahādānaṃ pavattayiṃ) means causing six alms-halls to be built and, by relinquishing much wealth, giving a great gift similar to the charity of King Vessantara. By these words, he shows how the great charity of Prince Candakumāra began from the time of his consecration.

"Without giving to those worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyye adatvāna) means without relinquishing the gift to persons worthy of offerings (while not consuming it himself). "Even for five or six nights" (api chappañca rattiyo) shows that sometimes for as long as five or six nights, he did not partake of his own drinks, hard food, or soft food.

At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta made the entire island of Jambudīpa like a ploughed field and established great charity like a great cloud raining down. Although in those alms-halls, excellent and refined food, drinks, and so forth were given daily to beggars according to their desire, he would not eat the food prepared for himself—food fit for a king—without first giving it to the beggars. Referring to this, he said, "I do not drink," and so forth.

Now, wishing to show the reason for giving to beggars in such a way, he brings forth an analogy beginning with "Just as a merchant..." Its meaning is: Just as a merchant goes to a place where goods are found, buys many goods with a small capital, and having made a vast accumulation of goods, knows the place and time where his profit and gain will be great, and then carries, brings, or sells those goods at that place and time.

"Even than what is consumed by oneself" (sakabhuttāpi) means even more than what is enjoyed by oneself. (There is also a variant reading "sakaparibhuttāpi," but the meaning is the same.) "To others" (pare) means to another person who is a recipient. "A hundredfold portion" (satabhāgo) means it will become a portion many hundreds of times over in future existences. The point is: Just as the goods bought by a merchant do not yield a great profit if sold right there, but yield great profit and vast fruit when sold in a suitable place and time, even so, wealth that is not enjoyed by oneself but given to a recipient person will have great fruit and become a portion many hundreds of times over.

Therefore, it should only be given to others without consuming it oneself. Regarding this matter, the Blessed One spoke in detail: "If one gives to animals, a hundredfold benefit is to be expected; if one gives to immoral commoners, a thousandfold benefit is to be known." Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, if beings knew the fruit of giving as I know it, they would not eat without having given to others. The stain of stinginess would not take root in their hearts and obsess them. Even if it were their last morsel, their last mouthful, they would not eat without having shared it."
63:
Even if one does not consume it oneself, it should indeed be given to others. Regarding this matter, the Blessed One said in detail: "By giving a gift to an animal, a hundredfold reward is to be expected. By giving a gift to an immoral worldling, a thousandfold reward is to be known" (M. Ni. 3.379). Furthermore, it was said: "Monks, if beings knew the result of sharing gifts as I know it, they would not eat without giving, nor would the stain of stinginess persist in obsessing their hearts. Even if it were their last morsel, their last mouthful, they would not eat without having shared it" (Itivuttaka 26), and so forth.

"Etamatthavasaṃ ñatvā" means knowing this reason, which is characterized by the nature of the great fruit of giving and the nature of being a condition for Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). "Na paṭikkamāmi dānato" means not retreating even slightly from the perfection of giving (dānapāramī), but only advancing. For what purpose does he not retreat? "Sambodhimanupattiyā" means for the purpose of attaining, that is, to realize, the omniscience known as Supreme Enlightenment.

At that time, when he was Canda Kumāra, the people sent his father, the Emperor, to a Caṇḍāla village, and the Bodhisatta caused to be given the necessary provisions and garments for both undergarments and upper robes. That king, being unable to enter the city, would approach the Bodhisatta when he went outside for activities such as playing in the garden. With the perception of him as a son, he did not bow or perform the salutation with joined palms, but merely said, "Master, live long." The Bodhisatta also showed extraordinary respect on the days they met. Thus, having ruled the kingdom righteously, at the end of his life, he filled the celestial realm along with his retinue.

At that time, the brahmin Khaṇḍahāla became Devadatta. Queen Gotamī became Mahāmāyā. Princess Candā became the mother of Rāhula. Prince Vāsula became Rāhula. Princess Selā became Uppalavaṇṇā. Prince Sūra became Mahākassapa. Prince Bhaddasena became Mahāmoggallāna. Prince Suriya became Sāriputta. King Canda became the Buddha, the Lord of the World (Lokānātha).

In this Jātaka as well, the remaining perfections (pāramīs) of Prince Canda Kumāra should be extracted accordingly, following the same method mentioned previously. Furthermore, even while knowing the cruel and harsh nature of the brahmin Khaṇḍahāla, he remained indifferent and decided the legal cases with justice and equity. Even while knowing the sacrificial arrangement of Khaṇḍahāla, who wished to kill him, there was no irritation of mind toward him. Although he was capable of taking his own retinue and becoming an enemy to his father, he reflected, "It is not proper for one like me to oppose elders like my father," and thus, making himself a human sacrifice, he remained obedient to the command of his father who wished to have him killed. Taking the sword from the scabbard...
64:
...towards the chaplain, his own father, who was making an effort to cut off his head, and towards his own son and all beings, he maintained an evenness of mind through the radiation of loving-kindness (mettā). While the people were making an effort to kill his father, he himself embraced him and gave him the gift of life. Although he gave a great gift daily, similar to the giving of King Vessantara, he remained insatiable in giving. He supported his father, who was made to live among the Caṇḍālas by the people, by giving him what was appropriate to be given. He established the people in meritorious deeds. Such powers of virtue should be extracted.

## The Commentary on the Conduct of Canda Kumāra is finished.

## 8. Sivirājacariyāvaṇṇanā

In the eighth [chapter], the Commentary on the Conduct of King Sivi, "Ariṭṭhasavhaye nagare" means in the city named Ariṭṭhapura. "Sivi nāmāsi khattiyo" means there was a king of that name from the Sivi clan.

In the past, while King Sivi was ruling in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the kingdom of Sivi, the Great Being was reborn as his son. They gave him the name "Sivi Kumāra." When he reached the proper age, he went to Takkasilā, and having learned the arts, he returned and demonstrated his skills to his father. He received the position of viceroy, and later, upon his father's passing, he became king. Abandoning the four wrong paths (agati), he ruled the kingdom without violating the ten royal virtues (dasa-rājadhamma). He caused six alms-halls to be built—at the four gates of the city, in the center of the city, and at the palace gate—and maintained a great alms-giving by sacrificing six hundred thousand [pieces of money] daily. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days (Uposatha days), he would go to the alms-halls himself to inspect the distribution of alms.

One day, early in the morning on a full-moon day, while sitting on the royal throne under the raised white parasol, he reflected on the gifts he had given. Seeing no external object (bāhira-vatthu) that he had not given, he thought: "My gift of external objects does not please my heart as much as an internal gift (ajjhattika-dāna). Oh, when I go to the alms-hall, may some beggar ask me for an internal gift instead of an external object! If someone were to ask for the flesh of my body, or blood, or my head, or the flesh of my heart, or my eyes, or half my body, or even my entire self as a slave, I would be able to give it to fulfill their wish."

In the Pali text, however, the giving of eyes is primarily mentioned. Therefore, he spoke the verse: "Nisajjapāsādavare... dadeyyaṃ avikappito." The meaning of that verse is: "Sāriputta, at that time, while sitting upon the excellent palace, I had such a thought. At that time, there was no gift among humans that I had not given. Should anyone come to ask for my eye, I would give it without hesitation."

In that verse, "mānusaṃ dānaṃ" refers to the food, water, etc., given by ordinary people. Thus, when the Great Being's noble desire for giving arose, the Sakka's Pandukambala marble throne showed signs of heat. When that Sakka reflected on the cause...
65:
"I am able to give, fulfilling the desires of various supplicants," thought King Sivi. In the Pāḷi text, however, it is mentioned specifically in terms of eyes. Therefore, it is said:

"Sitting then in the magnificent palace, I thought thus:
'There is no gift given by humans that I have not given. If someone were to ask me for my eye, I would give it with an unwavering mind.'"

In that verse, "mānusaṃ dānaṃ" refers to gifts given by ordinary people, such as food, drink, and so on. Thus, when the noble intention of giving arose in the Great Being (Bodhisatta), Sakka's Paṇḍukambalasilāsana (Pandukambala stone throne) showed signs of heat. When Sakka reflected on the cause and saw the Bodhisatta's intention, he told the assembly of gods, "Today, if the supplicants who arrive ask King Sivi for his eyes, he is thinking, 'I will pluck out my eyes and give them to them.'" He then thought, "Will he be able to give that gift or not? I will first test him."

While the Bodhisatta, having bathed with sixteen jars of scented water, adorned with all ornaments, and mounted upon a noble decorated elephant, was going to the alms-hall, Sakka took the form of an old, decrepit, blind Brahmin. He stood in the king's line of sight on a piece of high ground, stretching out both hands and hailing the king with cries of victory. The Bodhisatta urged his auspicious elephant toward the Brahmin and asked, "Brahmin, what do you desire?" The Brahmin replied, "The fame arising from your noble intention to give has spread continuously throughout the whole world. I am blind, and therefore I beg of you," and approaching him, he asked for one eye. Therefore, it is said:

"Sakka, the Lord of Gods, knowing my thought, sat in the midst of the assembly of gods and spoke these words:
'Sitting in his magnificent palace, the powerful King Sivi, while contemplating various gifts, sees nothing that should not be given.
Is this matter true or false? Come, I shall test him. Wait for a moment until I know his mind.'
'Trembling, with grey hair and wrinkled skin, afflicted by old age and appearing blind, he approached the King.'"
66:
Then, raising his left and right arms and placing his hands together in reverence on his head, the Brahmin spoke these words:

“O Great King, righteous one who increases the welfare of the kingdom, I beg of you. Your fame, delighting in giving, has spread among gods and men.

Both my eyes, my guides, are destroyed and blind. Give me one eye; you too may get along with one.”

In those verses, “cintentō vividhaṃ dānaṃ” means contemplating the various gifts he had given, or contemplating the various external objects of donation (bāhiraṃ deyyadhammaṃ) he had given. “Adeyyaṃ so na passati” means that, just like external objects, he sees nothing among internal objects (ajjhattikavatthu) that cannot be given or that he is unable to give; the meaning is that he thought, “I will even pluck out my eyes and give them.” “Tathaṃ nu vitathaṃ netaṃ” means whether this thought—seeing even internal objects as things to be given rather than things not to be given—is true or false. “So tadā paggahetvāna vāmaṃ dakkhiṇabāhu ca” means at that time raising both the left and right arms. “RaṭṭhavaḍḎana” means the King who makes the country prosper. “Twampi ekena yāpaya” means “O King, looking at what is even and uneven with one eye, sustain your own existence (attabhāva); I too shall get along with the one eye received from your lordship.”

Hearing these words, the Bodhisatta, with a delighted heart, thought, “Just now, while sitting in the palace, I came here having thought thus. And this person asks for my eye as if he knows my mind. Oh, what a gain for me! Today my desire will reach its pinnacle; I shall give a gift never given before,” and he became filled with enthusiasm. To clarify this matter, the Blessed One said:

“Sāriputta, hearing his words, I was joyful and moved by spiritual emotion (saṃvega); with hands joined in reverence and filled with joy, I spoke these words:

'O supplicant, just now, having thought in the palace, I came here. You have come to ask for my eye as if you knew my mind.'”
67:
“My heart's desire is accomplished; my aspiration is fulfilled. Today, I shall grant to the beggar a noble gift never before given.”

In this verse, ‘tassa’ refers to Sakka, who has assumed the form of an old brahmin. ‘Haṭṭho’ means having a joyful and delighted mind. ‘Saṃviggamānaso’ means having a stirred mind, thinking, “This brahmin asks for my eyes as if he knows my mind; for so long a time, I have been negligent, not having conceived such a thought.” ‘Vedajāto’ means that joy and rapture have arisen. ‘Abravi’ means he spoke. ‘Mānasam’ refers to the mental disposition for giving (dānajjhāsaya) that has arisen in the mind, specifically the thought, “I shall give my eyes.” ‘Saṅkappo’ means the heart's desire (manoratha). ‘Paripūrito’ means being fulfilled (paripuṇṇa).

Then the Bodhisatta thought: “This brahmin asks me for my eyes, which are difficult to give, as if he knows the conduct of my mind. Could it be that he was urged by some deity? I will first question him.” Having thought thus, he questioned the brahmin. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Jātaka teaching:

“By whom were you urged to come here, O beggar, to ask for my eyes?
You ask for my supreme organ, which is very hard to give,
that which people say is difficult for a man to surrender.”

Hearing this, Sakka, in the guise of a brahmin, said:
“He who is called Sujampati, the husband of Sujā, among the gods,
and who is called Maghavā in the world of men—
urged by him, I have come here as a beggar to ask for your eyes.

My request is supreme; give me your eyes as I ask.
Give me the supreme eyes, which people say are difficult for a man to surrender.”

The Great Being said:
“O Brahmin, for whatever purpose you have come,
and whatever goal you desire and pray for,
may those various aspirations of yours be fulfilled.
Receive the eyes.”
68:
“To you who ask for one eye, I give both. Go, endowed with sight, while the multitude of people look on. Whatever you desire, may that be fulfilled for you.”

In this verse, ‘vanibbaka’ is an address to the brahmin. ‘Cakkhupathāni’ is a name for the eyes themselves, as they are the pathways (causes) of seeing. ‘Yamāhū’ refers to that which is said in the world to be ‘hard to give.’ ‘Vanibbato’ means to the one who begs. ‘Vaniṃ’ means the act of begging. ‘Te te’ refers to those aspirations of yours, the blind man. ‘Sa cakkhumā’ means you, being endowed with sight through my eyes. ‘Tada te samijjhatu’ means may that which you desire from me be fulfilled for you.

After the King had spoken these words, he thought, “This brahmin says he has come here urged by Sakka; through this means, his sight will surely be restored.” Thinking, “It is not appropriate for me to pluck out my eyes and give them here,” he took the brahmin and went into the inner palace. Sitting on the royal throne, he summoned the physician named Sīvaka.

Then, a great clamor arose throughout the entire city: “It is said that our King wishes to pluck out his eyes and give them to a brahmin!” Then the King's relatives, generals, and other ministers dear to the King, attendants, citizens, and the women of the harem all gathered and tried to dissuade him by various means. The King, however, did not follow their wishes and restrained them. Therefore, [the Buddha] said:

“O Lord, do not give your eyes; do not abandon us all.
Great King, there are many pearls and lapis lazuli; give wealth instead.

O Lord, give chariots yoked with noble horses and well-adorned.
Great King, give elephants covered with golden trappings.

O Chief of Charioteers, give such a gift that all the Sivi people,
along with their vehicles and chariots, may always surround you.”

Then the King spoke three verses:
“He who, having said ‘I will give,’ then sets his mind on not giving,
is like one who places a snare lying on the ground around his own neck.”
69:
Whoever says 'I will give' and then sets his mind on not giving, becomes worse than the wicked and reaches the hell under the authority of Yama.

One should give exactly what is requested; one should not give what is not requested. Therefore, as this Brāhmaṇa asks me for my eyes, I shall give him those very eyes.

In those verses, in the phrase 'Mā no deva', 'no' is merely a particle. It means 'O King, do not give your eyes.' 'Mā no sabbe parākarī' means 'Do not abandon us all.' For if your eyes are given, you will no longer be able to rule; thus, by giving your eyes, it would be as if you have abandoned us—this is the intent of their plea. 'Pariquireyyum' means they would surround or attend to you. 'Evaṃ dehi' means 'Give in such a way that the Sivi people may long attend to you with your eyes unimpaired; give him only wealth, not your eyes; for if your eyes are given, the Sivi people will no longer attend to you'—this is what is shown.

'Paṭimuñcati' means responding again. 'Pāpā pāpataro hoti' means becoming especially more wicked than the wicked. 'Sampaṭṭo yamasādhanam' means one who has reached the Ussada Niraya, the place where the authority of Yama prevails. 'Yañhi yāce' means if a beggar asks for a certain object, the donor should give only that requested object and not what is unasked. It means, 'This Brāhmaṇa asks for my eyes, not for wealth such as pearls; therefore, I shall give only the eyes he requested.'

Then the ministers asked, 'O King, desiring what benefit among long life and so forth do you give your eyes?' The Great Being replied, 'I do not give desiring the prosperity of this life or the next. Indeed, the fulfillment of the Perfection of Giving (Dāna Pāramī) is the ancient path of the former virtuous ones, which Bodhisattas have always practiced.' Thus, he spoke these words:

'O Great King, lord of men, do you desire long life, or beauty, or happiness, or strength? Desiring what do you give? Why does the King, supreme among the Sivi, give his eyes for the sake of the next world?'

'I do not give this gift of eyes desiring fame, nor do I desire a son, nor wealth, nor a kingdom. It is only the practice of the ancient Dhamma observed by the virtuous of old. For this reason alone, my mind delights in giving.'
70:
In that verse, 'Paralokahetu' means: 'O Great King, for what reason does a wise man like you renounce present sovereignty, which is like the prosperity of Sakka, and give your eyes for the sake of the next world?'

'Na vāhaṃ' means: 'Indeed, I do not give these eyes for the sake of divine or human power. Rather, it is because the ancient Dhamma of the virtuous Bodhisattas, which brings about Buddhahood, has been practiced, trained in, and fulfilled by me; for this reason alone, my mind is always delighted in such giving.'

Having spoken these words and informed the ministers, King Sivi commanded the physician named Sivaka: 'Friend Sivaka, come. To give both my eyes to this Brāhmaṇa, quickly extract them and place them in my hands.' Therefore, it was said:

'Come, Sivaka, arise, do not delay, do not tremble,
Extract both eyes and give them to the beggar.'
Then Sivaka, who followed my words, being urged by me,
Extracted and gave the eyes to the beggar, like taking out the kernel of a palm fruit.

In that verse, 'Uṭṭhehi' means 'make an effort to arise; assist me in this gift of eyes.' 'Mā dandhayi' means 'do not delay.' The meaning is: 'I have obtained this supreme opportunity for giving, which is extremely rare and which I have long desired; let not that opportunity be missed.' 'Mā pavedhayi' means 'do not tremble due to shock of mind, thinking "I must extract the eyes of our King"; do not let the body fall into trembling.' 'Ubho pi nayanaṃ' refers to both eyes. 'Vanibbake' means to the beggar. 'Mayhaṃ' means by me (or to me). 'Uddharitvāna pādāsi' means that the physician extracted both eyes from the King's sockets and placed them in the King's hands.

In giving, he did not extract them using a small knife. This is because the physician thought, 'It is not proper for a well-trained physician like me to use a knife on the King's eyes.' Therefore, he ground medicines, infused a blue lotus with the medicinal powder, and had the right eye smell it. Then the eye rotated, and intense pain arose. The physician again infused the medicine and had him smell it; the eye loosened from the socket, and even more intense pain arose. On the third time, he infused a stronger medicine and applied it; by the power of the medicine, the eyeball whirled around, came out of the socket, and remained hanging by the sinews.
71:
Intense pain arose; blood flowed out, and the robes he wore were soaked with blood. The women of the harem and the ministers fell at the King's feet and wailed loudly, saying, "O Lord King, do not give your eyes! O Lord King, do not give your eyes!"

The King endured the pain and said, "Friend, do not delay." The physician replied, "Very well, your majesty," and holding the eye with his left hand, he took a small knife with his right hand, severed the ocular nerves, took the eye, and placed it in the hand of the Great Being (Mahāsatta). The King, looking at the right eye with his left eye, experienced the painful sensation while being overwhelmed by the joy of renunciation. He called the Brahmin, saying, "Come, O Brahmin!"

He then said, "I love Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), which can see all around, a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold more than this eye of mine. May this gift of my eye be a support for the attainment of Omniscience," and he gave the eye to the Brahmin. The Brahmin took the eye and placed it in his own eye socket. By the power of Sakka, it appeared like a blooming blue lotus. Seeing that eye of the Brahmin with his left eye, the Great Being thought, "Oh, how well I have given the eye!" and with joy welling up within him, permeating his entire body, he gave the other eye as well. Sakka did the same with that eye, and while the multitude watched, he departed from the royal residence, left the city, and returned to the celestial realm.

Before long, the King's eye sockets, instead of remaining as hollows, were filled with rising lumps of flesh like balls of red wool and healed like a painted image; the pain subsided. Then, the Great Being stayed in the palace for two or three days and thought, "What is the use of kingship to a blind man?" He decided to hand over the kingdom to the ministers, go to the park, ordain as a hermit, and practice the Dhamma of a recluse (Samaṇadhamma). He informed the ministers of this matter and said, "Let there be only one man near me to provide for washing my face and such, and tie ropes for me in the places for bodily needs." He then went by palanquin and sat on the royal throne by the side of a lotus pond. The ministers paid homage and departed. The Bodhisatta reflected on his gift. At that moment, Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. Seeing this, Sakka thought, "I will grant a boon to the King and restore his eyes to their original state." He went near the Bodhisatta and made the sound of footsteps. When the Great Being asked, "Who is this?"—
72:
“I am Sakka, the Lord of Devas; I have come to your presence. O Royal Sage, choose whatever boon you desire in your heart.”

When Sakka said this, the King replied:
“O Sakka, I have abundant wealth, an army, and a vast treasury. But now that I am blind, I only desire death.”

When he said this, Sakka asked, “King Sivi, why do you wish to die? Is it because you are blind?” “O Lord of Devas, it is because I am blind,” he replied. Sakka said, “O King, giving is not done for the sake of the future life alone; it also becomes a cause for benefit in the present life. Therefore, perform an Act of Truth (Saccakiriya) depending on the merit of your gift. By the power of that truth, your eyes will arise again.” Then the King said, “In that case, I have given the great gift well,” and performing an Act of Truth, he said:

“Whatever beggars of various lineages come to me to ask, whoever among them asks of me, that person is dear to my heart. By this word of truth, may my eye arise.”

In that verse, “Ye maṃ” means among those who come to ask of me, the one who utters the words “Give me this thing” and asks of me is dear to my heart. “Etena” means if it is true that all beggars are dear to me, and this which I have spoken is the truth, by this word of truth, may one eye arise (or let it arise).

Immediately upon his words, the first eye appeared. Then, for the sake of the second eye arising, he said:

“That Brahmin who came to ask of me, saying ‘Give me your eye,’ to that Brahmin beggar, I gave my eyes.
Great joy and happiness entered me even more. By this word of truth, may my second eye arise.”

In that verse, “Yaṃ maṃ” means the one who; “so” means that Brahmin who asked for the eye; “āgā” means came; “vanibbato” refers to the one who asks. “Maṃ āvisī” means after giving the eyes to the Brahmin...
73:
After giving his eyes to the Brahmin, even in the state of blindness, without minding such pain, I reflected, "Oh, well given is my gift!" and a surpassing joy (pīti) entered me. Boundless happiness (somanassa) arose. (I made an Act of Truth:) "If it is true that such boundless joy and happiness arose in me then, by this word of truth, let a second eye arise for me."

At that very moment, the second eye appeared clearly. Those eyes of the King were neither natural eyes nor divine eyes. It is impossible to make a natural eye again once it has been given to the Brahmin Sakka, and for one whose eyes are destroyed, what is called a divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) does not arise. However, according to the method mentioned, because they were born through the power of the diffusion of joy, based on his own joy of giving which was consistent in the beginning, middle, and end, they are called "Eyes of the Perfection of Truth" (Saccapāramitā-cakkhūni). Therefore, it is said:

"While preparing to give, while giving, and after the gift was given, there was no change in my mind, solely for the sake of Enlightenment."

In that verse, 'dadamānassa' refers to the time when the physician was extracting the eyes to be given. 'dentassa' refers to the time when the extracted eyes were being placed in the hand of the Brahmin Sakka. 'dinnadānassa' refers to the time after the gift of eyes had been given. 'cittassa aññathā' refers to the change of the disposition of giving to another state. 'bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā' means that the gift was solely for the cause of Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

To show that "I performed this gift which is so difficult to perform because Omniscient Knowledge is very hard to attain, and not because I disliked my eyes or even my body," he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Na me desso." In that verse, in the phrase 'attā na me na dessiyo', the first 'na' is merely a particle. The meaning is: "I should not be angry with myself, it is not that I do not love myself." There is also a reading 'attānaṃ me na dessiyaṃ'. The meaning of that reading is: "I should not be angry with myself, I do not deserve to be angry, that body should not be the object of my anger." They also read 'attāpi me na dessiyo'. 'adāsahaṃ' means "I have given." There is also a reading 'adāsihaṃ'.

Then, when the eyes appeared due to the Bodhisatta's Act of Truth, the entire royal assembly gathered by the power of Sakka. Then Sakka, standing in the sky in the midst of the great crowd—
74:
“O Great King, who increases the prosperity of the Sivis, these verses spoken according to the Dhamma are your eyes; they appear again like divine eyes. Surpassing walls, surpassing rocks, and surpassing mountains, your eyes can experience sight for a hundred yojanas all around.” Having offered praise with these verses, Sakka went back to the celestial realm. The Bodhisatta, surrounded by a great multitude and with great honor, entered the city and sat upon the royal throne under the raised white parasol in the great pavilion well-prepared at the palace gate. Wishing to preach the Dhamma to the citizens, the country folk, and the royal assembly who had come to see him, being exceedingly joyful and delighted due to the recovery of his sight—

“Who in this world, when asked, would not give their wealth, even if it is excellent and very dear to them? Come then, all you Sivis who have gathered, behold my divine eyes today. Surpassing walls, surpassing rocks, and surpassing mountains, my eyes experience sight for a hundred yojanas all around. There is nothing superior to the measure of giving in the lives of mortals here. By giving human eyes, I have obtained non-human eyes. Seeing this benefit, O Sivis, give gifts and enjoy them. Having given and enjoyed according to your ability, reach the heavenly realm, being blameless.”

Thus he preached these verses. In those verses, ‘dhammena bhāsitā’ means: O Great King, these verses of yours are spoken by the very nature of truth. ‘Dibbāni’ means: endowed with divine power. ‘Paṭidissare’ means: they appear again. ‘Tirokuṭṭaṃ’ means: beyond a wall. ‘Tiroselaṃ’ means: beyond a rock. ‘Samatiggayha’ means: having surpassed. The eyes can accomplish the seeing of forms for a hundred yojanas all around in the ten directions. ‘Ko nīdha’ means: who here in this human world. ‘Api visiṭṭhaṃ’ means: even if it is noble. ‘Na cāgamattā’ means: there is no other superior Dhamma than the measure of sacrifice. ‘Idha jīvite’ means: in this life of mortals.
75:
In this world of living beings. Some also read it as "idha jīvatan," meaning those living in this world. "I have obtained the divine eye, which is not found among humans; for this reason, it should be known that 'there is nothing superior to generosity (cāga).'" The phrase "having seen this as well" means having seen this divine eye that I have obtained.

Thus, with these four verses, he preached the Dhamma not only at that moment but also by gathering the great multitude on every Uposatha day twice a month. Having heard that Dhamma, the multitude performed meritorious deeds such as giving and were destined for the heavenly realm.

At that time, the physician was Elder Ānanda, Sakka was Elder Anuruddha, the rest of the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and King Sivi was the Lord of the World, the Buddha.

The perfections (pāramīs) of King Sivi should be extracted appropriately according to the method mentioned in this Jātaka. Although he practiced immeasurable great charity daily so that there was no external gift (bāhira-deyyadhamma) he had not given before, he was not satisfied with that charity and thought: "How shall I give a gift of my internal organs? When will someone come and ask me for an internal gift? If a beggar should desire my heart, I will extract my heart, dripping with drops of blood, like one pulling a lotus with its stalk from clear water, and give it. If he should desire my flesh, I will peel off my flesh like one peeling the skin of a palm fruit. If he should desire my blood, I will fill a vessel brought to me by piercing myself with a sword or by falling into the mouth of a machine and give the blood. If someone should say, 'Work in my house is not progressing, serve as a slave there,' I will set aside my royal attire, surrender myself to him, and serve as a slave. If someone should desire my eyes, I will pluck out my eyes like extracting the pulp of a palm fruit and give them to him." Thus, such noble thoughts arise only in Great Bodhisattas who have attained mastery (vasībhāva) unique to them. Even when restrained by ministers and attendants upon finding a beggar for his eyes, he did not heed their words but experienced supreme joy (pīti) from practicing according to his resolve. Relying on the truth of that joyful mind, he performed an Act of Truth (saccakiriyā) in the presence of Sakka, and by that truth, his eyes were restored to their original state, and those eyes were like those of divine power. Thus, the qualities and power of the Great Being should be understood.

## The Explanation of the Conduct of King Sivi is finished.

9. Explanation of the Conduct of Vessantara. In the ninth story, in the phrase "yā me ahosi janikā," the word "me" is spoken by the Teacher referring to himself when he was King Vessantara. Therefore, he said, "The khattiya lady named Phussatī," and so on. At that time, the mother of King Vessantara was a princess named Phussatī. "In past births" (atītāsu jātīsu) means in the birth immediately preceding that one. Here, the plural is used in the sense of the singular. The meaning is the birth immediately before the life as King Vessantara.
76:
## 9. Explanation of the Conduct of Vessantara

In the ninth [story], the Explanation of the Conduct of Vessantara, in the phrase "yā me ahosi janikā," the Teacher speaks referring to himself as King Vessantara. Therefore, he said, "The khattiya lady named Phussatī," and so on. At that time, the mother of King Vessantara was a princess named Phussatī. "In past births" (atītāsu jātīsu) means in the birth immediately preceding that one. Here, the plural is used in the sense of the singular. It should be connected as: she was the beloved chief queen of Sakka.

Alternatively, it means: she who is my mother, Queen Māyā, in this final birth, was named Phussatī in a past birth. Having been a princess in that past birth, I was conceived in the womb of Queen Phussatī as King Vessantara; in the birth immediately preceding that, she was the beloved celestial queen of Sakka. This is the sequential account of that story:

Ninety-one aeons (kappas) from this Bhadda-kappa, the Teacher named Vipassī appeared in the world. While the Buddha Vipassī was residing in the Khema Deer Park near the city of Bandhumatī, King Bandhumā gave a precious piece of sandalwood, sent by another king, to his eldest daughter. The princess had that sandalwood ground into fine powder, filled a casket with it, went to the monastery, and honored the golden-hued body of the Teacher. She scattered the remaining scented powder in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, in the future, may I be the mother of a Buddha like you." When she passed away from that life, as a result of the offering of sandalwood powder, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans with a body as if sprinkled with red sandalwood water, and was reborn as the chief queen of Sakka, the king of gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Then, when the signs of her passing (pubbanimitta) appeared near the end of her lifespan, Sakka, the king of gods, knowing that her life was exhausted, said out of compassion, "Sister Phussatī, I grant you ten boons; choose them." Therefore, the verse beginning with "tassā āyukkhayaṃ ñatvā" was spoken.

Knowing the end of her life, the Lord of Gods said this:
"I give you ten boons; choose, O auspicious one, whatever you desire."

In that verse, "varā" means choose the boon you desire. "Bhadde yadicchasi" means "O Phussatī, whatever you desire, whatever is dear to you, choose and accept as a boon in ten parts."

"Punidamabravī" means that once again, the goddess, not knowing her nature of passing away, asked, "What fault is there in me?" and so on. Indeed, being heedless, she did not know her life was ending, and when Sakka said, "Take a boon," she thought he wanted her to be [reborn] in some place and thus spoke. In that speech, "aparādhatthi" is asking "Is there a fault?" "Kiṃ nu doso atthi me tavā" means "Why is there a fault in me?"
77:
That goddess Phussatī, not knowing that her life span was exhausted, when Sakka said, "Accept a boon," thought, "He desires my birth in some place," and spoke thus. In that context, "aparādhatthi" means "Is there a fault?" She meant, "Why have I become one who is to be angered at or one who is unloved by you? You are making me depart from this delightful heavenly world." It is a question to Sakka, asking for what reason he wishes to make her depart from this heaven, just as a strong wind uproots a tree from its roots.

"Tassidaṃ" refers to these words spoken to her. "You have indeed committed no evil," meaning he shows that it is not because of a fault that he wishes her to pass away. "And you are not unloved by me," meaning, "I do not have anger toward you."

Now, desiring to show his intention to grant the boons, he said, "Your life is only this much; the time for passing away has come," and urging her to accept the boons, he said, "Accept the ten excellent boons given by me." In that context, "varuttame" means the most excellent among boons, the supreme boons.

"Dinnavarā" refers to one who has been granted boons according to the promise, "I shall give boons." "Tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā" means pleased (tuṭṭhā) due to the satisfaction of obtaining the desired gain, and joyful (haṭṭhā) due to the mirth from seeing Sakka for the last time. "Pamoditā" means delighted with great joy. "Mamaṃ abbhantaraṃ katvā" means "including me among those boons." That goddess Phussatī, knowing that her life span was exhausted, when the opportunity was given by Sakka to grant boons, surveyed the entire surface of Jambudīpa. Seeing the palace of the Sivi King which was suitable for her, she chose these ten boons: to be the chief queen of that king, to have dark eyes, to have dark eyebrows, to have the name Phussatī, to obtain a son endowed with special qualities, to have a belly that is not protuberant, to have breasts that do not sag, to not have grey hair, to have delicate skin, and to have the power to release those condemned to death.

Thus, having accepted the ten boons, she passed away from the heavenly world and was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Madda. When she was born, her body appeared as if sprinkled with sandalwood powder. Therefore, on the day of her naming, they gave her the name "Phussatī." That maiden Phussatī grew up with a great retinue, and when she reached the age of sixteen...
78:
(She) became one possessed of excellent beauty. Then, in the city of Jetuttara, the Great King Sivi brought that maiden Phussatī for his son, Prince Sañjaya, and having raised the white parasol, he established her in the position of Chief Queen, making her the head of sixteen thousand court ladies. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

## “Passing away from that heaven, that Phussatī was born into a royal family;
## In the city of Jetuttara, she was united with King Sañjaya.”

That Phussatī became the beloved and pleasing queen of King Sañjaya. Then, when Sakka, the King of Devas, was reflecting, he saw, “Of the boons I gave to Phussatī, nine boons have been fulfilled; the boon to obtain an excellent son has not yet been fulfilled. I shall fulfill that for her as well.” Having thought thus, he saw the Bodhisatta in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven whose life-span was exhausted. He went to the Bodhisatta and said, “Friend, it is proper for you to take conception in the womb of the Chief Queen of King Sañjaya, the son of King Sivi, in the human world.” Having obtained the promise from that Bodhisatta and from sixty thousand other deities who were also about to pass away, he returned to his own place.

The Great Being also passed away from that heaven and was conceived in the womb of that queen. The remaining deities were born in the houses (the wombs of the wives) of sixty thousand ministers. When the Great Being was conceived, Queen Phussatī developed a pregnancy craving to give alms, having six alms-halls built at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the palace gate, and spending six hundred thousand (pieces of money) daily. The King, hearing of the Queen's craving, summoned the soothsaying Brahmins and inquired of them. Upon hearing, “Great King, a noble being delighted in giving has arisen in the Queen's womb; he will never be satiated with giving,” he was delighted and arranged the almsgiving as described. He fully satisfied the ascetics, Brahmins, the aged, the sick, the destitute, travelers, and beggars. From the time the Bodhisatta took conception, the King’s gains, tributes, and revenues increased beyond measure. Due to the power of the Great Being’s merit, kings throughout the whole of Jambudīpa sent gifts and offerings. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

## “When I entered the womb of Phussatī, my dear mother;
## Through my power, my mother then became delighted in giving.”
79:
“He gives gifts to the poor, the sick, the aged, the beggars, the wayfarers, the ascetics, the Brahmins, and those who are destitute and without possessions.”

In that verse, “mama tejena” means by the power of my intention to give. “Khīṇe” refers to those whose wealth and property are exhausted and have come to ruin. “Akiñcane” refers to those who have no possessions to keep. In all these words, the locative case (sattamī vibhatti) is used in the sense of support (ādhāra). Indeed, the poor and others are the objects (visaya) for the occurrence of the practice of giving.

Queen Phusatī, carrying the womb with a great retinue, when ten months were full, desired to see the city and informed the King. The King had the city decorated like a celestial city, placed the Queen on a noble chariot, and had her circumambulate the city. When she reached the middle of the merchants' street (Vessa-vīthi), the winds of karma (labor pains) moved. The ministers informed the King. He had a birth-house built right there in the merchants' street and provided protection. There she gave birth to a son. Therefore, the Buddha said:

“Having carried me for ten months, while circumambulating the city,
In the middle of the merchants' street, Phusatī gave birth to me.
My name is not from my mother's side, nor is it of paternal origin.
Because I was born here in the merchants' street, I was named Vessantara.”

In that verse, “karonte puraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ” means while King Sañjaya was taking the Queen and circumambulating the city. “Vessānaṃ” means of the merchants. “Mattikaṃ nāmaṃ” means a name descended from the mother, grandmother, etc. “Pettikasambhavaṃ” means ‘pettika’ because it belongs to the father, and ‘sambhava’ because it originates from that father; thus, a name originating from the father. It shows that the name was not given in connection with the parents. “Jātettha” means born here. There is also a reading “Jātomhi”. “Tasmā Vessantaro ahū” means because he was born in the merchants' street at that time, he became known as Vessantara; the meaning is they named him Vessantara.

When the Great Being came out of his mother's womb, he was pure and came out with his eyes open. As soon as he was born, he stretched out his hand to his mother and asked, “Mother, I wish to give a gift. Is there anything to give?” Then his mother said, “Dear son, give as you wish,” and placed a bag of a thousand coins near his hand. Indeed, the Bodhisatta...
80:
In the Mahosadha Jātaka, in this Vessantara Jātaka, and in the final existence—in these three places, the Bodhisatta spoke as soon as he was born. King Sañjaya appointed sixty-four nurses for the Great Being, who were free from defects such as being too tall and who had sweet milk. He also provided nurses for the sixty thousand children born at the same time as the prince. He grew up with a great retinue along with those sixty thousand children. The King had an ornament for a child made, worth a hundred thousand, and gave it to him. At the age of four or five, he took it off and gave it to the nurses; even when the nurses tried to give it back, he would not take it. Hearing this, the King said, “What is given by my son is well given,” and had another ornament made. He gave that one away too. Thus, even in his childhood, he gave ornaments to the nurses nine times.

At the age of eight, while sitting on his couch, he thought: “I give external gifts, but they do not satisfy me. I desire to give internal gifts. If someone were to ask for my heart, I would pull out my heart and give it. If they were to ask for my eyes, I would pluck out my eyes and give them. If they were to ask for the flesh or blood of my whole body, I would cut the flesh from my whole body or pierce it with a sword to give the blood. Furthermore, if someone were to say, ‘Be my slave,’ I would declare myself to him and give myself.” While he was thinking of this natural disposition of his, this great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, shook as far as the water's edge. Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, bowed and stood facing the city of Jettuttara. Therefore, it was said:

“When I was a child, eight years of age by birth,
Then sitting in the palace, I reflected on giving gifts.”

“I would give my heart, my eye, and also my flesh and blood;
I would give my body, declaring myself a slave, if anyone should ask of me.”

“As I was reflecting on my nature, unshaken and firm,
The earth, with Sineru and the forests as its crest, then trembled.”

In that verse, “sāvetvā” means declaring the state of being a slave, saying, “From today onwards, I am the slave of this person.” “Yadi koci yācaye mamaṃ” means if anyone should ask of me. “Sabhāvaṃ cintayantassa” means of him who was reflecting on his own true nature, which is not contrary to reality...
81:
To me, who was contemplating according to my own desire without being satisfied, means 'while I was contemplating.' *Akampita* means being free from trembling. *Asaṇṭhita* means being without hesitation. The reason is that when those who are not Bodhisattas give away their eyes and so forth, there might be trembling, known as mental terror, and hesitation, known as shrinking back, due to greed and such; it means being free from those [greed, etc.]. *Akampī* means unmoving. *Sineruvana-vaṭaṃsakā*: the forest of wish-fulfilling trees such as Nandana, Phārusaka, Missaka, and Cittalatā that have arisen on Mount Sineru is called *Sineruvana*. Alternatively, the forest on Mount Sineru and the delightful forests in Jambudīpa and elsewhere are called *Sineruvana*; because those forests and mountains incline towards that perfection of giving, it is called *Sineruvana-vaṭaṃsakā*.

While the earth was thus trembling, a sweet and deep cloud thundered and a momentary rain fell; streaks of lightning flashed; the great ocean surged; Sakka, the king of gods, clapped his hands; the Great Brahmā gave a shout of approval; and there was a single tumult as far as the Brahma-world. Even at the age of sixteen, the Bodhisatta reached the completion of all arts. His father, wishing to give him the kingship, consulted with the mother, brought the princess named Maddī, the daughter of his maternal uncle from the Madda royal family, and having appointed her as the chief queen among sixteen thousand women, consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingship. From the time the Bodhisatta was established in the kingship, he spent six hundred thousand [pieces of money] daily, maintaining a great almsgiving, and he would go to inspect the almsgiving once every half-month. Later, Queen Maddī gave birth to a son. Because they received the son with a golden net, they named him "Prince Jāli." When Prince Jāli was able to walk, Queen Maddī gave birth to a daughter. Because they received the daughter with a black antelope skin, they named her "Kaṇhājinā." Therefore, it was said:

"Once every half-month in succession, and on the fifteenth day, the full-moon Uposatha day,
Having mounted the elephant named Paccaya, I went to give gifts."

In that verse, *anvaddhamāse* means once every half-month in succession. *Puṇṇamāse* means on the full-moon day; it is connected as 'on the fifteenth day, endowed with the fullness of the month and the fullness of the moon, I went to give gifts.' The grammatical construction there is: Having mounted the elephant named Paccaya, I went to the alms-hall to give gifts every half-month. While going thus, when I went to give gifts on one fifteenth day, the full-moon Uposatha day, then the brahmins from the kingdom of Kaliṅga...
82:
In that verse, 'approached me' (*upagañchu maṃ*) means they approached the auspicious state elephant named 'Paccaya.' On the day the Bodhisatta was born, a female elephant that travels through the sky brought a completely white young elephant, regarded as highly auspicious, placed it in the stable for the state elephant, and departed. Because that elephant was obtained on account of (*paccaya*) the Great Being (the Bodhisatta), they named it 'Paccaya.' Having mounted that state elephant named Paccaya, he approached to give gifts. Therefore, it was said:

'Brahmins from the kingdom of Kaliṅga approached me;
They asked me for the noble elephant, regarded as auspicious and glorious.
"The country is without rain; there is a great famine and hunger.
Please give the excellent elephant, the all-white noble beast."' 

In that verse, the stanza beginning with 'Kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayā' has already appeared in the *Kururājacariya* mentioned below; therefore, the meaning and the sequence of words of those verses should be understood in the same way as stated in that *Kurudhamma Jātaka*. Here, however, because the auspicious elephant is pure white, it is said, 'the all-white noble beast' (*sabbasetāṃ gajuttamaṃ*). While the Bodhisatta was on the back of the noble elephant:

'The brahmins ask me for whatever elephant, I give it and do not tremble;
I do not hide what I have; my mind delights in giving.'

Wishing to make known his delight in giving:

'When supplicants have reached me, refusal is not proper.
Let not my undertaking be broken; I will give the magnificent elephant.'

Having thus made the vow, he descended from the elephant's back and went around to look for a part that was not decorated, but finding no undecorated part, he took a golden water-vessel filled with scented water mixed with flowers and said, 'Sirs, come here.' Placing the elephant's trunk, which was like a decorated silver garland, into the hands of those brahmins, he poured the water and gave the decorated noble elephant. Therefore, it was said:

'Taking the elephant by its trunk, and pouring water from the jewel-adorned golden vessel into the hands of the brahmins, I gave the elephant,' thus he said.
83:
In those verses, 'santā' means the existing gift-object. 'Nappaṭigūhāmi' means I do not hide [it]. One who thinks of his own property, "Let it be mine alone," or who refuses a person who comes to beg, is said to be hiding it in effect, even if it is right in front of the beggars. The Great Being, however, is one who wishes to give even internal gifts (ajjhattika-dāna), starting with his own head; how then could he refuse an external gift (bāhira-dāna)? Therefore, he said, "I do not hide the existing gift-object." For that very reason, he said, "My mind delights in giving." The rest of the words have the same meaning as stated below.

The ornaments adorned on the four legs of that elephant are worth four hundred thousand. The ornaments adorned on the two sides are worth two hundred thousand. The rug spread under the belly is worth one hundred thousand. The three nets on the back—the pearl net, the ruby net, and the golden net—are worth three hundred thousand. The ornaments adorned on the two ears are worth two hundred thousand. The rug spread on the back is worth one hundred thousand. The ornament on the frontal globe (kumbha) is worth one hundred thousand. The three crest flowers are worth three hundred thousand. The ear-tip ornament is worth one hundred thousand. The ornaments for the two tusks are worth two hundred thousand. The ornament wrapped around the trunk is worth one hundred thousand. The tail ornament is worth one hundred thousand. The mounting ladder is worth one hundred thousand. The drinking trough for the elephant is worth one hundred thousand. Setting aside the priceless items, this much of the value amounts to two million four hundred thousand (24 lakhs). The ruby fixed on the umbrella socket, the crest-gem, the pearl strings, the ruby fixed on the goad, the pearl strings wrapped around the elephant's neck, and the ruby placed on the elephant's frontal globe—these six ornaments are priceless. The white elephant treasure itself is also priceless. Thus, including the white elephant treasure, there are seven priceless things. He gave all those treasures to the brahmins. Furthermore, he gave the five hundred families who were the elephant's attendants, along with the elephant trainers and keepers. Simultaneously with the gift, earthquakes and other phenomena occurred in the manner stated below. Therefore, it is said:

"Furthermore, when I was giving the supreme elephant, entirely white, even then the earth trembled, and the forests and Mount Sineru bowed."

In the Vessantara Jātaka, it is also said:

"Then there was a terrifying event; then there was a hair-raising experience; when the noble elephant was given, the earth trembled violently."
84:
"By giving that elephant" means by the relinquishing of that auspicious state elephant, which was complete with the six priceless treasures and the ornamental items worth two million four hundred thousand. "Sivayo" means the Sivi princes and the inhabitants of the Sivi kingdom. This word "Sivayo" is the head of the teaching (the principal subject). Among those Sivi people, all except King Sañjaya, Queen Phusatī, and Queen Maddī—including the ministers, courtiers, brahmins, householders, merchants, country folk, and city dwellers—were included. "Became angry" means they were angry at the Bodhisatta due to the instigation of the deities. "Assembled" means they gathered together in unity. It is said that when those brahmins received the elephant, they mounted it, entered through the great gate, and went through the center of the city. When the people asked, "O brahmins, why are you riding our elephant?", they went along provoking them with hand gestures and such, saying, "King Vessantara gave this elephant to us; who are you?"

Then, with the ministers at their head, the people gathered at the palace gate and complained, "A king should only give wealth, grain, fields, lands, male and female slaves, and attendants to brahmins. Why does King Vessantara give the auspicious state elephant, which is worthy only of kings? We will not allow him to destroy the kingdom in this way now." Having complained thus, they informed King Sañjaya of the matter. Although the king tried to persuade them, they did not listen and went away. However, they said:

"Do not oppress that king with sticks or weapons; he is not one who deserves bonds. Banish him from the kingdom; let him live on Mount Vaṅka."

Therefore, it was said, "They banished him from their own kingdom; let him go to Mount Vaṅka." In that statement, "banished" means they made an effort to have him live outside the kingdom. The king also thought, "This opposition is very powerful; let my son live outside the kingdom for a few days," and said:

"If this is the will of the Sivis, we do not reject that will. Let him stay this night and enjoy sensual pleasures. Then, at the end of the night, towards sunrise, let the united Sivis banish him from the kingdom."
85:
(The King) spoke thus and sent a minister to his son. "Go and inform my son of this matter," he said as he sent him. That minister did as (the King) had commanded.

The Bodhisatta, upon hearing those words, asked the reason:
"Why are the Sivi people angry with me?
I do not see any evil deed that I have committed.
O minister, explain this clearly to me:
Why are they banishing me?"

When the minister replied, "It is because you, Prince, gave away the noble white elephant," he became joyful and said:
"I would give even my heart or my eyes;
What use to me is external wealth?
Whether it be silver or gold, pearls or cat's-eye gems.

Seeing a beggar approach, I would give my right arm,
(or my left arm);
I shall not waver in giving; my mind delights in alms-giving.

Let all the Sivi people banish me or kill me as they wish,
I shall never refrain from giving;
Let them cut me into seven pieces if they wish."

Then he said, "Let the people grant me the opportunity to give alms for just one day. I shall give alms tomorrow and depart on the third day." He sent the minister to the people. Then he commanded the minister in charge of all affairs, saying, "Tomorrow I shall give the great alms-giving known as the Sattasataka (the Gift of Seven Hundreds). Prepare seven hundred elephants, seven hundred horses, seven hundred chariots, seven hundred women, seven hundred male slaves, seven hundred female slaves, and seven hundred milch cows. Prepare also all kinds of food, drink, and everything suitable for giving."

He went alone to Queen Maddī’s residence and encouraged her in giving, saying, "Dear Maddī, if you wish to store up the treasure (of merit) that follows one to the next life, give to those possessed of virtue." He then told her the reason for his departure and said, "I am going to live in the forest. You stay here without being distressed." The Queen replied, "Great King, I cannot live even for a single day without you."

On the second day, he performed the great alms-giving of seven hundreds. While he was giving alms, evening arrived. He went to his parents' residence in a decorated chariot and requested their permission, saying, "I shall depart tomorrow." He paid homage to his parents, who were weeping with tears against their will, circumambulated them, and then (departed).
86:
Having left (the palace) that day, he stayed at his own house, and on the following day, saying "I shall depart," he descended from the palace. Although Queen Maddī was pleaded with and restrained by her parents-in-law in various ways, she did not heed their words. She paid homage to them, circumambulated them, took leave of the remaining women, took her two children, and went ahead of King Vessantara to stand in the chariot.

The Great Being ascended the chariot and, standing there, took leave of the multitude. He gave them this advice: "Be diligent and perform meritorious deeds such as alms-giving," and then he departed from the city. The Bodhisatta's mother, thinking, "My son delights in giving; let him give alms," sent carts filled with the seven kinds of jewels along with ornaments on both sides. The King gave away even the ornaments he was wearing on his body to the beggars who arrived, doing so eighteen times, and then gave away all that remained. As soon as he left the city, he felt a desire to turn back and look. Then, through the power of his merit, the earth at the spot where the chariot was broke and turned around, making the chariot face the city. The King looked at his parents' residence. Due to that pathos, the earth trembled. Therefore, it was said, "Tesaṃ nicchubhamānānaṃ," and so on.

89-90. In that verse, "nicchubhamānānaṃ" means when those Sivis are expelling or being expelled. Or it means when they are departing. "Mahādānaṃ pavattetuṃ" means to give the great alms-giving of seven hundreds. "Āyācissaṃ" means I requested (asked permission). "Sāvayitvā" means having proclaimed. "Kaṇṇဘေရိံ" refers to a pair of large drums. "Dadāmahaṃ" means I give.

Then, in that alms-hall where alms were being given, "tumūlo" means a great commotion arose, which was "bheravo," inspiring fear. Indeed, except for the Great Being (the Bodhisatta), that sound generated fear in others. To show the manner in which that fear arose in the multitude, it was said, "Dāနေနိမံ" and so on. Because of this alms-giving, the Sivi people are driving this Great King Vessantara out of the country and banishing him; yet, he gives such an alms-giving once again.

92-94. Now, to show that alms-giving, he spoke the verse beginning with "Hatthiṃ." In that verse, "gavaṃ" refers to milch cows. In the phrase "catuvāhiံ rathaṃ datvā," because they carry the load, they are called "vāhino," meaning four thoroughbred Sindh horses...
87:
It means that the four well-bred Sindhu horses and the chariot were given to the Brahmins. Indeed, as the Great Being was leaving the city, sixty thousand ministers born on the same day and the rest of the people followed him with tearful faces. He turned them back and, while driving the chariot, said to Queen Maddī, 'Sister, if any seekers come from behind, please observe and inquire.'

Queen Maddī sat watching. Then, four Brahmins who had not arrived in time for the Great Gift of Seven Hundreds (Sattasataka Mahādāna) arrived and asked, 'Where is King Vessantara?' When told, 'He has given his gifts and left by chariot,' they followed him, saying, 'We shall ask for the horses.'

When Queen Maddī saw those Brahmins coming, she informed him, 'Great King, seekers are coming.' The Great Being stopped the chariot. Those Brahmins arrived and asked for the horses, and the Great Being gave the horses to them. The Brahmins took the horses and departed.

After the horses were given, the chariot pole remained suspended in the air. Then, four deities (devaputtas) came in the form of red deer (rohita-miga), took hold of the chariot pole, and pulled it along. The Great Being, knowing they were deities, said to Queen Maddī:

'Sister Maddī, look and take note; it appears like a wondrous form.
In the form of deer, these beings carry me like well-trained horses.'

In that passage, 'cittarūpaṃ va' means like a wondrous form. 'Dakkhiṇassā' means they carry me like well-trained horses.

As they were traveling thus, another Brahmin came and asked for the chariot. The Great Being made his wife and children get down from the chariot and gave the chariot away. After the chariot was given, the deities disappeared. From that time on, they all traveled only on foot.

Then the Great Being said, 'Sister Maddī, you carry Kaṇhājinā; I shall carry Prince Jāli.' Thus, both of them carrying the two children in their arms, speaking pleasant words to each other, asking people they met on the way for the road to Mount Vaṅka, and giving the children fruits from the fruiting trees that bent down of their own accord, they reached the Ceta kingdom on that very day because the deities, wishing for their welfare, shortened the journey. Therefore, it was said, 'Having given the chariot drawn by four...' and so on.

In that passage, 'ṭhatvā cātummahāpathe' means standing at the four-way crossroads, because it was the place where the path he was traveling and the path from which that Brahmin came intersected.
88:
Standing at the main road where four ways meet, he gave the chariot to that Brahmin. 'Ekākiyo' means being alone, without companions such as ministers or servants. For that reason, he said 'adutiyo' (without a second). He spoke these words to Queen Maddī.

96–99. 'Padumaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ vā' means like a red lotus or like a white lotus. 'Kaṇhājinaggahī' refers to Queen Maddī carrying the young girl Kaṇhājinā. 'Abhijātā' means those of noble birth. 'Visamaṃ samaṃ' refers to uneven ground and even ground. 'Entī' means they come. In the phrase 'anumagge paṭipphathe', it should be understood that the word 'vā' (or) is elided (meaning either along the path or in the opposite direction). 'Karuṇaṃ' is a neuter verbal usage, meaning a compassionate manner. 'Dukkhaṃ te paṭivedentī' means: 'These delicate ones travel on foot; Mount Vaṅka is still far from here.' At that time, out of pity for us, those people feel suffering themselves, or it means they experience the suffering that has arisen within them.

100–1. 'Pavane' means in the great forest. 'Phaline' means among the fruiting trees. 'Ubbiddhā' means trees that have grown high upwards. 'Upagacchanti dārake' means the fruits come to a position within the children's reach; in this way, the trees themselves bend their branches and approach the children.

'Acchariyaṃ' means something marvelous, worthy of snapping one's fingers. 'Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtaṃ' means an unprecedented, extraordinary wonder (abbhuta). It is called 'lomahaṃsanaṃ' (hair-raising) because it has the power to make one's hair stand on end. 'Sāhukāraṃ' is simply the act of giving praise (sādhukāra). She is called 'sabbaṅgasobhanā' because, as a jewel of a woman, she is beautiful in all her limbs and parts.

103–4. 'Accheraṃ vatā' means 'Oh, how wonderful!' 'Vessantarassa tejenā' means by the power of King Vessantara's merit. 'Saṅkhipiṃsu pathaṃ yakkhā' means the deities, urged by the power of the Great Being's merit, brought that journey to an end, making it short. This was done as if out of compassion for the children, as stated in the words 'anukampāya dārake' (out of compassion for the children). In reality, from the city of Jetuttara to Suvaṇṇagiritala Mountain is 5 yojanas; from there to the Kontimārā River is 5 yojanas; from there to Marañjanāgiri Mountain is 5 yojanas; from there to the village of Daṇ膽abrāhmaṇa is 5 yojanas; and from there to the city of Mātula is 10 yojanas. Thus, it is 30 yojanas from the city of Jetuttara to that kingdom. The deities, urged by the power of the Great Being's merit, caused them to complete that entire journey in a single day. Therefore, it is said, 'nikkhantadivaseva cetaraṭṭhamupāgamuṃ' (they reached the Ceta kingdom on the very day they departed).
89:
The deities, urged by the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, shortened the journey. They traversed the entire distance of thirty yojanas in a single day. Therefore, it is said: "On the very day of their departure, they arrived at the kingdom of Ceta."

Thus, the Great Being reached the city of Mātula in the kingdom of Ceta in the evening and stayed in a rest-house near the city gate. Then, Queen Maddī wiped the dust from King Vessantara’s feet and massaged them. Thinking, "I shall make known the arrival of King Vessantara to the people," she left the rest-house and stood at the doorway within the sight of the public. Women entering and leaving the city saw Queen Maddī and surrounded her. The people, seeing Queen Maddī, King Vessantara, and their children arriving in such a manner, informed the kings. Sixty thousand kings came to King Vessantara, weeping and lamenting. After relieving his travel fatigue, they asked the reason for his arrival.

The Great Being recounted everything, beginning with the gift of the white elephant. Upon hearing this, the kings invited him to take their throne. The Great Man, King Vessantara, said, "Let it be as if I have accepted your kingdom, but my father the King has banished me from the country; therefore, I shall go only to Mount Vaṅka." Although the kings pleaded with him in various ways to stay in that city, he had no desire for the royal splendor. Taking the protection provided by those kings, he stayed that night in the rest-house. Early the next morning, after consuming food of various exquisite flavors, he departed surrounded by the kings. Having traveled fifteen yojanas, he stopped at the entrance of the forest and sent the kings back. He then proceeded the remaining fifteen yojanas according to the landmarks indicated by them. Therefore, it is said:

"At that time, sixty thousand maternal uncles lived in Mātula;
They all approached him with palms joined, weeping.

Having engaged in conversation there with the Cetas and the Ceta princes,
They departed from that place and went to Mount Vaṅka."

In those verses, "tattha vattetvā sallāpaṃ" means having engaged in joyful conversation with the assembly of kings in that place. "Cetaputtehi" means with the princes of the Ceta kingdom. "Te tato nikkhamitvāna" means having sent those kings back from the entrance of the forest. "Vaṅkaṃ agamu pabbataṃ" means the four of us headed towards Mount Vaṅka.
90:
Then, the Bodhisatta, traveling along the path indicated by the princes of Ceta, reached Mount Gandhamādana and stayed there for that day. From there, heading north and traveling along the foot of Mount Vipulla, he sat by the banks of the Ketumatī River. After eating delicious meat given by a forest hunter, he gave the hunter a golden pin. Having bathed and drunk water, his fatigue was relieved, and he crossed the river. After sitting for a while at the foot of a banyan tree situated on a mountain ridge, he rose and continued, passing around Mount Nālika until he reached Lake Mucalinda. Reaching the northeast corner along the lake's shore, he entered the thicket via a single-file path. Passing through that, he reached a square lotus pond in front of difficult mountain passes and river sources.

At that moment, Sakka, the King of Gods, reflecting [on the situation], thought: "The Great Being has entered the Himālaya; it is proper that he finds a dwelling place." He then sent the celestial architect Vissakamma, saying: "Go, Vissakamma, and create a delightful hermitage in a pleasant spot in the folds of Mount Vaṅka." Vissakamma created two leaf-huts, two walkways, and two quarters for day and night. In various places, he displayed trees adorned with various flowers, fruiting trees, flowering shrubs, banana groves, and so on, and prepared all the requisites for an ascetic. He wrote the words: "Whoever wishes to go forth as an ascetic, let them take these." Then, after driving away non-humans and animals and birds with terrifying sounds, he returned to his own abode in the celestial realm.

The Bodhisatta, seeing the single-file path, thought, "This must be a dwelling place for ascetics." Leaving Queen Maddī and the children there, he entered the hermitage. Seeing the written words, he realized, "Sakka has given this to me," and opened the door of the leaf-hut and entered. He set aside his sword and bow, removed his layman's clothes, donned the garb of a hermit, and taking a staff, he came out. With a composure like that of a Paccekabuddha, he went to the children. Queen Maddī, seeing the Great Being, fell at his feet and wept. She then entered the hermitage with him, went to her own leaf-hut, and took the form of a female ascetic. Later, they made the children young ascetics as well. The Bodhisatta asked a boon from Queen Maddī: "From this day forth, we are those who have gone forth. Women are a stain on the holy life; do not come to me at improper times." She accepted, saying, "Very well," and in turn asked a boon from the Great Being: "My Lord, please stay here in this hermitage and look after the children; I shall search for and bring various fruits." From that day on, Queen Maddī brought fruits from the forest and looked after the three of them. Thus, the four royals lived in the folds of Mount Vaṅka for about seven months. Referring to this, the verses beginning with "Āmantayitvā devindo, vissakammaṃ mahiddhikaṃ" were spoken.
91:
In that verse, 'āmantayitvā' means having called. 'Mahiddhikaṃ' means endowed with great divine power. 'Assamaṃ sukataṃ' means having well-prepared the hermitage. Sakka, the King of Gods, commanded Vissakamma: 'Create well a pleasant leaf-hut suitable for King Vessantara to dwell in.' Vissakamma, the celestial architect, created it well.

111. 'Asuñño' means that by making the hermitage not empty, it becomes not empty. Alternatively, there is a reading 'asuññe'; I dwell in the hermitage which is not empty because of my presence, constantly protecting the children and remaining there. Due to the power of the Bodhisatta's loving-kindness, all animals within a radius of three yojanas also attained a mind of loving-kindness.

While King Vessantara and his family were living there, a Brahmin named Jūjaka, a resident of the kingdom of Kaliṅga, was told by his wife named Amittatāpanā: 'I can no longer constantly perform tasks for you such as pounding grain, fetching water, and cooking gruel and rice. Bring me a male or female slave to be my servant.' Jūjaka the Brahmin replied, 'O Amittatāpanā, I am very poor. Where could I possibly get a male or female slave for you?' She said, 'King Vessantara is living on Mount Vaṅka. Go and ask for his children to be my servants and bring them back.' Jūjaka, being infatuated with his wife through the power of defilements, could not refuse her words. He had provisions prepared and, traveling in stages, reached the city of Jetuttara and asked, 'Where is the Great King Vessantara?'

The people, saying, 'Because of his excessive giving to these beggars, our king was banished from the country. Having destroyed our king in this way, he has now come here again,' took up clods of earth, sticks, and staves, and followed the Brahmin, reviling him. The Brahmin, being misled by the deities, left that city and set out on the road leading to Mount Vaṅka. Reaching the entrance of the forest in due course, he entered the great forest and, wandering about having lost his way, met Cetaputta, who had been stationed by the Ceta princes to guard the Bodhisatta. Cetaputta asked, 'O Brahmin, where are you going?' He replied, 'To the presence of the Great King Vessantara.' Cetaputta thought, 'Surely this Brahmin is going to ask for the king's children or his queen,' and threatened him, saying, 'O Brahmin, do not go there. If you go, I will cut off your head right here and feed it to my dogs.' Jūjaka the Brahmin, fearing death, spoke a lie: 'I am an envoy sent by King Sañjaya, Vessantara's father. I have come to bring him back.' Hearing these words, Cetaputta was greatly delighted, entertained the Brahmin, and told him the way to Mount Vaṅka. Furthermore, as the Brahmin continued his journey, he met the ascetic Accuta and asked the way.
