Following the landmarks pointed out by the ascetic, he arrived in due course near the Bodhisatta's hermitage. While Queen Maddī was away searching for fruit, he approached the Bodhisatta and asked for the two children. Therefore, the Lord uttered the verse beginning with 'Pavane vasamānassa.'

112. Dear Sāriputta, in the forest region...
92:
Cetaputta, having paid honor and respect to the Brahmin, told him the way to Mount Vaṅka. As Jūjaka the Brahmin continued from there, he met an ascetic named Accuta along the way and asked him for directions as well. The ascetic also told him the way. Traveling according to the landmarks described, he arrived in due course near the site of the Bodhisatta's hermitage. While Queen Maddī was away in the forest to gather various fruits, he approached the Bodhisatta and asked for both the son and the daughter. Referring to that event, the Lord said:

'While I was living in the forest, a traveling Brahmin came to me;
He asked for both my young children, Jāli and Kaṇhājinā.'

When Jūjaka the Brahmin thus asked for the children, the Bodhisatta thought, 'It has been a long time indeed since a solicitor has come to me. Today I shall fulfill the Perfection of Giving without remainder,' and he became filled with joy. As if placing a bag of a thousand coins into an outstretched palm, he delighted the Brahmin's heart and, making the entire mountain cleft echo, said: 'I give my young children to you, O Brahmin. However, Queen Maddī went to the forest early this morning for fruit and will return in the evening. When she returns, I will show you the children. You may eat the roots and fruits, stay for one night, and after your fatigue has vanished, you may leave early in the morning.'

Jūjaka the Brahmin thought, 'This King Vessantara may give the children because of his noble intention, but the mother, being strongly attached to her offspring, might return and create an obstacle to the gift. It would be better if I press him, take the children, and leave this very day.' He then said, 'If the children have already been given to me, what is the use of sending them after showing them to their mother? I will take the children and leave this very day.'

The Bodhisatta said, 'O Brahmin, if you do not wish to see the princess, their mother, then take these children and go to the city of Jetuttara. There, King Sañjaya will take the children and give you great wealth. With that wealth, you can buy male and female slaves and live happily. On the other hand, these royal children are very delicate; how could they possibly serve you?'

Jūjaka the Brahmin replied, 'I cannot do that. I fear royal punishment. I will take them only to my own village.' Hearing this conversation between them, the children realized, 'Our father wishes to give us to the Brahmin,' and they ran away, went to the pond, and hid among the lotus bushes. When Jūjaka the Brahmin did not see the children...
93:
“You said, 'I give the children,' and then you let them run away. Is this your conduct of a good man?” the Brahmin said. Then the Mahāsatta (Great Being) immediately rose and searched for his son and daughter. Seeing them hiding in the lotus pond, he said, “Come, my dear children, do not create an obstacle to my perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī). Help me bring my aspiration for giving to its pinnacle. This Brahmin will take you and go to the presence of your grandfather, King Sañjaya. Dear Jāli, if you wish to be free from slavery, give the Brahmin a thousand gold nikkhas and become a free man. Dear Kaṇhājinā, if you wish to be free, give a hundred of each—a hundred male slaves, a hundred female slaves, a hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, and a hundred gold nikkhas—and become a free woman.” Having thus set a price on his children and comforted them, he went to the hermitage, took water with a pitcher, and for the sake of it being a support for the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), he poured the water of donation onto the Brahmin’s hand. Filled with extreme joy and delight, he gave away his beloved children, making the earth resound. In this gift of children as well, the trembling of the earth and other signs occurred just as mentioned before. Therefore, it was said:

“Seeing the beggar approach, joy arose in me;
I took both children and gave them to the Brahmin then.”

“When he gave his own children to the Brahmin Jūjaka,
the earth shook, and Mount Sineru and the forests bowed.”

Then the Brahmin, tying the hands of the children who were unwilling to go with a creeper, dragged them away. At the places where they were tied, the skin broke and blood flowed. That Brahmin dragged them while beating them with a creeper-stick. The children, looking back at their father, said:

“Mother has gone out, and you, Father, are giving us away;
Do not give us away, Father, until Mother returns to us;
Then let this Brahmin sell or kill us as he pleases.”

Having said this, and seeing this man of such terrifying appearance and cruel deeds, they lamented, saying:

“Is this a man or an ogre (yakkha) who eats flesh and blood?
Coming from the village to the forest, he asks for you, Father, for this wealth;
While being led away by a demon (pisāca), why, Father, do you just look on?”

In this context, 'wealth' (dhana) refers to the wealth of children.
94:
The Brahmin Jūjaka, even as the children were lamenting in that way, took them and departed, beating them as he went. Because of the children’s pitiful lamentation and the Brahmin’s lack of compassion, intense grief arose in the Mahāsatta, and remorse also appeared. At that very moment, he remembered the lineage of the Bodhisattas: “All Bodhisattas will become Buddhas after making the five great sacrifices (pañca mahāpariccāga). I am also among them, and the gift of children is one of those great sacrifices. Therefore, Vessantara, it is not fitting for you to feel regret after giving a gift.” Admonishing himself thus, and strengthening his resolve with the thought, “From the time they were given, they no longer belong to me,” he made a firm determination and sat on a stone slab at the door of the leaf-hut, as still as a golden statue.

Then Queen Maddī, returning from the forest after gathering various fruits, was blocked on her path by deities in the form of wild beasts, who thought, “Let there be no obstacle to the Mahāsatta’s gift.” When those beasts departed, she reached the hermitage after a long time. Thinking, “Today I saw a bad dream, and ill omens have appeared; what could it be?” she entered the hermitage. Not seeing her children, she went to the Bodhisatta and said, “Lord, I do not see our children. Where have they gone?” He remained silent. The mother, searching for the children, ran here and there, and not finding them, returned and asked again. The Bodhisatta thought, “I will dispel her grief for the children with harsh words,” and said:

“O beautiful and famous Princess Maddī,
You went out early in the morning to gather food;
Why have you returned thus in the evening?”

Having said this, even though she explained the reason for her delay, he said nothing further regarding the children. Overwhelmed with grief for her children, she searched for them again, wandering through the forests as swiftly as the wind. The area she searched in that single night amounted to about fifteen yojanas. Then, at dawn, she went and stood before the Mahāsatta. Overcome by intense grief at not seeing the children, she fainted and fell to the ground at his feet like a severed plantain tree. Thinking, “She is dead,” he was shaken and felt intense grief, but regaining his mindfulness, he wanted to know, “First, is she alive or not?” Having avoided physical contact for seven months...
95:
Although King Vessantara had not touched a woman's body for seven months, because there was no one else, he lifted Queen Maddī's head, placed it on his lap, sprinkled it with water, and massaged her face and chest. After a short while, Queen Maddī regained consciousness, and establishing her sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, she asked, "Great King, where have those little children gone?" The King replied, "O Queen, I have given them as servants to a Brahmin who came to me and asked for them." When the Queen said, "Great King, why did you not tell me, who have been wandering and weeping all night after you gave the children away?", he replied, "If I had told you at first, your mental suffering would have been great; but now, because of your physical suffering, your mental suffering will be less," and said:

"O Maddī, look only at me, do not look for the children,
Do not weep so bitterly.
If we remain alive, we shall get our children back,
And we shall be free from disease."

After thus comforting her, he said again:

"A virtuous person should give as a gift children,
Four-footed animals, grain, and other wealth in the house,
Upon seeing a beggar who has come.
O Maddī, rejoice in my noble gift of giving the children."

Saying this, he made Queen Maddī rejoice in his gift of the children. She also rejoiced, saying:

"Great King, I rejoice in your noble gift of giving the children.
Having given, let your mind be clear,
And may you be one who can give even more."

While the two royals were thus speaking pleasant words to each other, Sakka thought: "Yesterday, the Great Man gave his children to the Brahmin Jūjaka, making the earth resound. Now, if some base person approaches and asks for Queen Maddī and takes her away, the King will be without support. Let me approach him in the guise of a Brahmin, ask for Maddī, and having brought his perfections to the summit, make her such that she cannot be given to anyone else, and then give her back to him." At the time of sunrise, he went to the King in the guise of a Brahmin. Seeing the Brahmin, the Great Man was filled with joy and delight, thinking, "A guest has come to us again," and after exchanging sweet greetings with him, he asked, "O Brahmin, for what purpose..."
96:
"...have you come to this place?" Thus he asked. Then Sakka asked the King for Queen Maddī. Regarding that, it is said: "Once again Sakka descended, having a form like a Brahmin, and asked me for Queen Maddī, who is virtuous and devoted to her husband."

In that verse, "once again" means after the day the children were given. The meaning is immediately after that. "Descended" means having come down from the celestial realm. "Having a form like a Brahmin" means having an appearance identical to a Brahmin.

Then the Great Being (Mahāsatta), without saying, "Yesterday I gave both my children to a Brahmin, and I am alone in the forest; how can I give you Queen Maddī, who is virtuous and devoted to her husband?", but as if placing a priceless gem in an outstretched palm, without hesitation, without attachment, and without a shrinking mind, being joyful and delighted, thinking, "Today my Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramī) shall reach its summit," and as if making the mountain resound, he said:

"I give, I do not waver, O Brahmin, in what you ask of me;
I do not hide what is present; my mind delights in giving."

Having said this, he quickly took water with a ceremonial pitcher, poured the water into the Brahmin's hand, and gave his wife. Regarding that, it is said: "Taking Maddī by the hand, and filling the [Brahmin's] palm with water, with a clear mind and intention, I gave Maddī to him."

In that verse, "filling the palm with water" means filling the outstretched palm of that Brahmin with the water of donation. "With a clear mind and intention" means having a mind and intention cleared by the arising of faith, thinking, "Surely, by this renunciation, I shall bring the Perfection of Giving to its summit and attain Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi)." At that very moment, all the miracles described above appeared. The hosts of Devas and Brahmas were exceedingly filled with joy and delight, thinking, "Now, the Supreme Enlightenment of this King is not far off." Regarding that, it is said: "When Maddī was being given, the Devas in the sky rejoiced; then the earth, adorned with Mount Sineru and forests, also trembled."
97:
At that time, when Queen Maddī was being given away, she did not weep, nor was she displeased, nor did she even frown. This thought occurred to her: "Whatever the King desires, let him do as he wishes."

She said: "I have been his wife since my youth; he is my lord and master. If he wishes to give me to anyone, let him give me; let him sell me or even kill me."

The Great Man also gave her away, saying: "O Brahmin, I cherish Omniscience far more than Queen Maddī—a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold. May this gift of mine be a support for the penetration of Omniscience." Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One:

"Sāriputta, when I renounced Prince Jāli, my daughter Kaṇhājinā, and the devoted Queen Maddī, I did not hesitate for any reason other than for the sake of Enlightenment.
It was not that my two children were not dear to me, nor was Queen Maddī not dear to me. Omniscience is dearer to me; therefore, I gave away those who were dear."

In that verse, "cajamāno na cintesiṃ" means that while renouncing and giving, he did not think with the power of distress or anxiety, but gave with a released mind.

In this context, an objector asks: "Why did this Great Man renounce his own children and wife, who were of noble birth and royal lineage, into slavery to another? Indeed, is it not true that reducing free people to slavery is not the practice of the virtuous?" The answer is given: It was done according to the natural law (or in accordance with the Dhamma). This is the inherent nature following the qualities that make a Buddha—namely, the complete renunciation of all things possessed as 'mine' without remainder. For Bodhisattas who are striving to fulfill the Perfection of Giving (Dāna Pāramī), free from discrimination regarding the gift and the recipient, it is not improper to give what is possessed as 'mine' to a beggar who asks for it. This natural law is also an ancient one.

For all Bodhisattas, the renunciation of everything is a practice repeatedly and well-cultivated, a lineage and tradition of their family. In that lineage, the renunciation of especially dear things is a distinction. Indeed, some Bodhisattas renounce wealth such as royal power inherited through the lineage, renounce their own limbs such as the head and eyes, renounce their dear life, and renounce a beloved son who establishes the family lineage...
98:
...and renounce a dear wife of pleasing conduct. There has never been a Buddha in the past who did not renounce these five great sacrifices (Mahāpariccāga). For instance, when the Blessed Maṅgala was a Bodhisatta seeking Omniscience, in his third existence counting from his final birth, while living on a mountain with his wife and children, a demon named Khara-dāṭhika heard of the Great Being's inclination toward giving. Approaching in the guise of a Brahmin, he asked the Great Being for his two children.

The Great Being, saying "I give my children to the Brahmin," was exceedingly joyful and gave both children, causing the earth to shake as far as the water's edge. While the Great Being was watching, the demon, leaning against a support board at the end of the walkway, ate the two children like a bundle of lotus stalks. Looking at the demon's face, which was vomiting streams of blood like flames of fire, the Great Being did not allow any thought such as "The demon has surely deceived me" to arise. Because his skill in means was well-developed, because past things have the nature of not reconnecting, and because he had thoroughly contemplated conditioned things (saṅkhāra) through the lens of impermanence and so on, he felt only joy, thinking: "My Perfection of Giving (Dāna Pāramī) is indeed fulfilled; this gift, having accomplished a great purpose for me, will lead to the attainment of Omniscience." Knowing his own unique mental state at that moment, he made an aspiration: "By the result of this, in the future, let rays of light emanate from my body in this very same manner." Due to that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, the radiance from his body always pervaded and remained throughout the ten thousand world systems. In this way, other Bodhisattas also penetrated Omniscience only after renouncing their very dear wives and children.

Furthermore, to give an analogy: suppose a man takes a village or a district from a king for a fee and, while working, due to his own or his disciples' negligence, he carries "rotten wealth" (debt). The king then has him arrested and put in prison. This thought might occur to him: "I have incurred this much debt while doing this king's work; therefore, the king has put me in prison. If I stay here, I myself will die, and my wife, children, and workers will lose their livelihood and fall into great ruin. What if I inform the king and, placing my son or younger brother here in my stead..."
99:
“It would be good if I could depart. Thus, I shall be released from this bond, and before long, having gathered wealth from friends and acquaintances and given it to the King, I shall also release those people from their bonds. Being diligent and by the power of my exertion, I shall restore my own prosperity to its original state.” Thinking thus, that man would act accordingly. The perfection of this simile should be understood in this way. The correlation between the simile and the subject is as follows: Kamma is like the King; Saṃsāra is like a prison; the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) who wanders in Saṃsāra by the power of Kamma is like the man placed in the prison by the King. Just as the man in that prison, by handing over his son or brother to others, effects the release of himself and them from suffering, so too should it be understood that the Great Being, by giving his son and others to others, attains Omniscience (Sabbaññutaññāṇa) and thereby releases all beings from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth (Vaṭṭadukkha). Just as that man, freed from suffering, remains in his desired prosperity along with them, so too should it be understood that the Great Being, freed from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth through the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga), is endowed with the prosperity of Omniscience such as the Ten Powers (Dasabala) through Buddhahood, and causes those who follow his words to be endowed with prosperity such as the Threefold Knowledge (Vijjā-taya). In this way, the renunciation of wife and children by Great Beings is of an irreproachable nature. By this same method, it should be understood that the objection regarding their renunciation of limbs and life is also resolved.

Thus, after the Great Being (Mahāsatta) had given away Queen Maddī, Sakka, the King of Gods, being filled with wonder and amazement, praised the Great Being’s gift by way of appreciation, starting with these verses:

“All your obstacles, both divine and human, have been conquered. The earth has resounded because of your voice, and your fame has reached the heavens.”

“To those who give what is difficult to give, and perform deeds that are difficult to do, the ignoble cannot emulate the Dhamma of the virtuous. The Dhamma of the virtuous is difficult to follow.”

“Therefore, the destination from this world is different for the virtuous and the ignoble. The ignoble go to hell, while the virtuous are destined for heaven.”

In those verses, ‘paccūhā’ means enemies. ‘Dibbā’ refers to those who hinder divine prosperity. ‘Mānusā’ refers to those who hinder human prosperity. Who are these enemies? They are the states of stinginess (macchariya). It is shown that the Great Being, by giving away his wife and children, has conquered all those states of stinginess. ‘Duddadaṃ’ refers to things difficult to give, such as one’s wife and children.
100:
“Other future Disciples and Silent Buddhas cannot emulate such a difficult deed of great renunciation performed by those like you, who give what is difficult for others to give, such as wife and children. How much less can the ignoble and stingy emulate it? They simply cannot. Therefore, the Dhamma which is the practice of the virtuous Great Bodhisattas is extremely difficult for others to follow.”

Thus, Sakka, having praised the Great Being by way of appreciation and wishing to return Queen Maddī, said:

“I give back your wife, Maddī, who is beautiful in all her limbs. May you alone be the one desired by Maddī, and may Maddī remain with you, her husband.”

Having said this and returned Queen Maddī, Sakka stood in the air, shining in his divine form like the young sun. Revealing himself, he said:

“I am Sakka, the Lord of Gods. I have come to your presence. O Royal Seer, choose a boon; I grant you eight boons.”

With these words, he invited him to choose boons. The Bodhisatta then requested these eight boons: “May my father restore me to the kingship once again; may I release the condemned from execution; may I be a refuge for all beings; may I not commit adultery; may I not fall under the influence of women; may my son have a long life; may the objects to be given, such as food and drink, be abundant; may I give those gifts with a clear and devoted mind without them being exhausted; and having given such great gifts and gone to the celestial realm, when I return from there to this human world, may I attain Omniscience.”

Sakka replied, “Before long, your father, King Sañjaya, will come here and restore you to the kingship. All your other desires will also reach their fulfillment. Do not worry; be diligent.” Having given this advice, he returned to his own place. The Bodhisatta and Queen Maddī lived joyfully in the hermitage given by Sakka.

As the Brahmin Jūjaka went away taking the princes, the deities provided protection. Every day, a goddess would come at night in the form of Queen Maddī and care for the princes. Although Jūjaka intended to go to the kingdom of Kalinga, being misled by the deities, he arrived at the city of Jetuttara in half a month. While King Sañjaya was sitting in the hall of judgment, he saw his grandchildren passing through the royal courtyard with the Brahmin and recognized them.
101:
The King summoned the children along with the Brahmin, and upon hearing the account, he gave wealth and purchased his grandchildren exactly as the Bodhisatta had instructed. Then, he had them bathed, fed, and adorned with all kinds of ornaments. King Sañjaya took his grandson Prince Jāli onto his lap, and Queen Phussatī took her granddaughter Kaṇhājinā onto hers, and they inquired about and listened to the news of the Bodhisatta and the Princess.

Upon hearing that news, the King, with a mind full of remorse, thinking, "I have indeed committed a great wrong," immediately prepared an army of twelve akkhobhaṇīs and set out toward Mount Vaṅka together with Queen Phussatī and the grandchildren. Traveling in succession, they met with the son and the daughter-in-law. When King Vessantara saw his beloved son and daughter, he could not contain his grief and fainted, falling right there. Likewise, Queen Maddī, the father, the mother, and the sixty thousand courtiers born on the same day also fell. Seeing that pitiful sight, not a single person could maintain their composure, and the entire hermitage became like a forest of sal trees struck by the Yugandhara wind. Sakka, the King of Devas, in order to dispel their fainting, caused the Pokkharavassa rain to fall. Those who wished to be wet became wet, while for those who did not wish to be wet, the water rolled off like raindrops on a lotus leaf. Everyone regained consciousness. At that time, wonders such as the shaking of the earth appeared as described above. Therefore, he said:

## Once again, meeting with the parents in the great forest, they wept piteously and spoke of their happiness and suffering.

## With great shame and fear of wrongdoing, he approached both parents. At that time, the earth, along with Mount Meru and the forest ranges, shook.

In that verse, "karuṇaṃ paridevante" means that all the people who had arrived, starting with the parents, were weeping piteously. "Sallapante sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ" means asking about each other's well-being and suffering and engaging in conversation as a friendly greeting. "Hirottappena garunā ubhinnaṃ" means that he did not feel anger or resentment, thinking, "These parents listened to the words of the people of Sivi and banished me, who was innocent and established in the Dhamma," but rather approached them just as before, with the shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) that arose from respect for the Dhamma toward both parents. Due to that power of my Dhamma, the earth shook even then.
102: Then, the Great King Sañjaya, having apologized to the Bodhisatta and handed over the kingship, immediately had his hair and beard trimmed, had him bathed, and consecrated the Bodhisatta—who shone like a king of gods adorned with all ornaments—along with Queen Maddī in the kingship. From that moment on, surrounding his son with a fourfold army of twelve akkhobhaṇīs, he had the sixty-yojana road from Mount Vaṅka to the city of Jetuttara decorated, and in two months, he entered the city in comfort. The great multitude experienced grand joy and delight. Activities such as the tossing of garments took place. In the city, the drum of joy was beaten throughout. Even down to those in the prisons, all who were in bondage were released. On the very day he entered the city, at dawn, the King thought: "Tomorrow, when the night has brightened and they hear of my arrival, beggars will come; what shall I give to them?" At that moment, Sakka's stone seat showed signs of heat. Reflecting and knowing the reason, Sakka immediately caused a rain of the seven jewels to fall like a dense cloud, filling the areas to the front and back of the royal palace to waist-height. Throughout the entire city, it rained to knee-height. Therefore— "Again, leaving the great forest with my kinsmen, I entered the delightful city, Jetuttara, the supreme city. Then the seven jewels rained down, a great cloud poured forth; then too, the earth shook, along with Sineru and its forest-wreaths. This inanimate earth, unaware of happiness or suffering, even it shook seven times through the power of my giving," he said. After the rain of seven jewels had fallen, the next day the Great Being had it proclaimed, "Let the wealth that fell in the front and back yards of any family belong to them alone," and having the remaining wealth brought, he had it poured into the granaries along with the wealth in his own palace grounds and performed a great distribution of gifts. "acetanāyaṃ pathavī" means this great primary element, the earth, is devoid of intention, whereas the deities possess intention. "aviññāya sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ" means not knowing happiness or suffering precisely because it is inanimate...
103:
Although encountering the causes of happiness and suffering, the Great Earth (being inanimate) does not experience those effects. The shaking of the earth occurred solely through the power of my generosity. Thus, the Great Earth, characterized in such a way, shook seven times due to the majestic power of my meritorious deeds of giving. These occasions were: when the inclination for giving (dānajjhāsaya) arose at the age of eight with the thought, 'I shall give even my heart and other limbs to those who ask'; the time of giving the auspicious white elephant; the time of being banished to the forest; the time of the Great Gift (Sattasattaka); the time of giving his son and daughter; the time of giving his wife; the time of reuniting with relatives at Mount Vaṅka; and the day of re-entering the city when the rain of seven gems fell. In these places, it shook seven times.

Thus, having performed great acts of giving throughout his life, which were the causes for the manifestation of wonders such as the sevenfold shaking of the Great Earth in a single existence, the Great Being (Mahāsatta) was reborn in the Tusita heaven at the end of his life. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Then the wise Khattiya King Vessantara, having given gifts, passed away and was reborn in heaven.' (Jā. 2.22.2440).

At that time, the brahmin Jūjaka became Devadatta; Amittatāpanā became Ciñcamāṇavikā; the Ceta prince became Channa; the ascetic Accuta became Sāriputta; Sakka became Anuruddha; Queen Maddī became the mother of Rāhula; Prince Jāli became Rāhula; Kaṇhājinā became Uppalavaṇṇā; the parents became the Great Royal Families; the rest of the retinue became the Buddha's retinue; and King Vessantara became the Lord of the World (the Buddha).

In this Jātaka as well, the remaining perfections (pāramīs) should be extracted appropriately according to the method mentioned below. Likewise, the majestic qualities of this Great Man (Mahāpurisa) should be understood as the causes for the manifestation of many wonders, such as the sevenfold shaking of the Great Earth, starting from: the mother's longing (dohala) to give gifts by distributing six hundred thousand [pieces of wealth] daily while the Great Being was in her womb; the fact that the wealth was never exhausted despite such giving; his speaking the words, 'I will give, is there anything [to give]?' while stretching out his hand at the very moment of birth; his lack of desire to take back his ornaments after they had passed into the hands of his nurses at the age of four or five; and his desire to give his own limbs, such as his heart, at the age of eight. Therefore, it is said:

'Such were these wonders and marvels of the Great Sage... even the devotion of the mind toward these [wonders] can liberate one from suffering; how much more so the imitation of their conduct in accordance with the Dhamma!'

## The Description of the Conduct of Vessantara is finished.
104:
## 10. Sasapaṇḍitacariyāvaṇṇanā

125-6. In the tenth [story], beginning with 'When I was a hare,' [the Buddha said]: 'Sāriputta, while I was wandering in search of Omniscience (Bodhi), I was once a wise hare.' Indeed, Bodhisattas, though subject to the power of Kamma, are born in the animal realm to favor and assist such animals. 'Pavanacārako' means one who frequents the great forest. He is called 'tiṇapaṇṇasākaphalabhakkho' because he feeds on grass such as dabba-grass, leaves, vegetables, and fruits fallen from trees. 'Paraheṭhanavivajjito' means being free from harming others. 'Suttapoto' refers to an otter. 'At that time,' when I was a hare, I exhorted those three friends, the monkey and the others.

127. 'Kiriye kalyāṇapāpake' refers to wholesome and unwholesome actions. The word 'pāpāni' shows the manner of exhortation. In that context, 'shun evil deeds' means to avoid these evils starting from taking life up to wrong view. 'Enter into merit' means to direct one's body, speech, and mind toward these good practices, starting from giving and observing virtue up to straightening one's view; it means to practice this wholesome conduct.

Thus, although the Bodhisatta was born in the animal realm, being endowed with wisdom, he became a good friend and preached the Dhamma by way of exhortation to those three individuals whenever they approached him. They, having accepted his exhortation, returned to their respective dwellings. As time passed, the Bodhisatta looked at the sky and, seeing the full moon, exhorted them, 'Observe the Uposatha.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'On the Uposatha day, seeing the moon full,
I told them there: Today is the Uposatha day.
Prepare gifts to be given to a worthy recipient;
Having given a gift to a worthy recipient, observe the Uposatha.'

128-9. In those verses, 'seeing the moon not yet full' means seeing the moon slightly incomplete on the fourteenth day of the waxing moon; it refers to the fifteenth Uposatha day at dawn after that night had passed, when he told those friends, the monkey and others, 'Today is the Uposatha day.' The Bodhisatta explained the duties to be performed on that Uposatha day. In those words, it means: 'Prepare gifts according to your ability; observe the Uposatha for the sake of giving.'
105:
"Today is the Uposatha day for my friends." Therefore, the instructions for the practice on that Uposatha day should be applied with words such as "Prepare the items for alms," and so forth. In that context, "dānāni" refers to the objects to be offered. "Paṭiyādetha" means to prepare them according to one's ability and strength. "Dātave" means for the purpose of giving. "Upavassatha" means to perform the act of observing the Uposatha, to keep the Uposatha precepts; for an offering given while established in virtue is of great fruit. Therefore, it is shown that if a recipient arrives, you should give a portion from the food you are to eat and then eat.

They accepted the Bodhisatta's advice, placing it upon their heads, saying, "Very well," and undertook the factors of the Uposatha. Among them, the otter went to the riverbank early in the morning, thinking, "I will search for food." At that time, a fisherman had pulled out seven rohita fish, strung them together with a vine, buried them in the sand on the riverbank, and went to the lower current of the river to catch more fish. The otter, smelling the scent of the fish, dug up the sand, saw the fish, and pulled them out. After proclaiming three times, "Is there an owner for these?" and seeing no owner, he bit the vine, placed them in his own dwelling bush, and lay down reflecting on his virtue, thinking, "I will eat only when the time is right."

The jackal also went out to search for food and found two meat skewers, a monitor lizard, and a jar of curds in a field-watcher's hut. After proclaiming three times, "Is there an owner for these?" and seeing no owner, he put the rope of the curd jar around his neck, took the meat skewers and the monitor lizard in his mouth, placed them in his own dwelling bush, and lay down reflecting on his virtue, thinking, "I will eat only when the time is right."

The monkey also entered the forest, brought a bunch of mangoes, placed them in his own dwelling bush, and lay down reflecting on his virtue, thinking, "I will eat only when the time is right." For all three of them, the thought arose: "Oh, if only a recipient would come here!" Therefore, it was said:

Saying "Very well" to my words,
According to their ability and strength,
Having prepared the items for alms,
They sought for a worthy recipient.

As for the Bodhisatta, he sat in his own dwelling bush and thought, "I will go out only when the time is right to eat dabba grass and such." He reflected: "The recipients who come to me are not able to eat grass. And as for me, I have no sesame, rice, or such..."
106:
"I have no offerings to give. If a recipient comes to me, I, who subsist on grass, will give the flesh of my own body." Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Sitting down, I thought of a gift worthy of a recipient.
If I should find a worthy recipient, what shall my gift be?

I have no sesame, mung beans, black grams, rice, or ghee.
I subsist on grass alone, and grass is not fit to be given.

If any worthy recipient comes to me for alms,
I shall give my own self; that recipient shall not go away empty-handed."

In those verses, "dānaṃ dakkhiṇanucchavaṃ" means he thought of a gift appropriate for the status of a recipient, an object of offering to be given to a worthy one. "Yadihaṃ labhe" means if I should find any worthy recipient today. "Kiṃ me dānaṃ bhavissati" means what shall my offering be? "Na sakkā tiṇa dātave" means I have no offerings such as sesame or beans to give to a recipient; and as for that grass which is my food, it is not fit to be given to a worthy recipient. "Dajjāhaṃ sakamattānaṃ" means what is the use of my thinking about such offerings? Is there not this body of mine, which is blameless, easily obtained because it does not depend on others, and is fit for others' use? If any worthy recipient comes to me, I shall give this very self of mine to him. In this way, that recipient who comes to me shall not go away empty-handed with empty hands.

While the Great Being was thus reflecting according to the true nature of things, by the power of that reflection, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat of Sakka showed signs of heat. Sakka, upon investigating and seeing this reason, thought, "I will test the King of Hares." He first went to the otter's dwelling place and stood there in the guise of a Brahmin. When asked by the otter, "For what purpose, Brahmin, are you standing there?" he replied, "If I could get some food, I would observe the Uposatha and perform the duties of a recluse." The otter said, "Very well, I will give you food." Therefore, (the Blessed One) said:

"Seven rohita fish have I, taken from the water to the dry land.
O Brahmin, I have this; eat this and dwell in the forest."
107:
The Brahmin said, "Let it be for now; I shall know (take it) later." In the same manner, he went to the jackal and the monkey. When they also invited him with the offerings they had, he said, "Let it be for now; I shall know later." Regarding this, it was said:

"O Brahmin, the field-watcher forgot and left behind for me my dinner: two meat skewers, a lizard, and a pot of curd. This I have, O Brahmin; eat this and dwell in the forest."

"O Brahmin, there are ripe mangoes, the water is cool, and the cool shade is delightful. These ripe mangoes I have, O Brahmin; eat these and dwell in the forest."

In those verses, 'dussa' means he forgot. 'Rattibhattaṃ apābhataṃ' means removed from (brought for) dinner. 'Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhā' refers to two meat skewers roasted on coals and one lizard. 'Dadhivārakaṃ' refers to a pot of curd.

Then the Brahmin went to the Wise Hare (Sasa-paṇḍita). When the Wise Hare asked, "For what purpose have you come?", he replied in the same way as before. Therefore, the verses beginning with "Mama saṅkappamaññāya" were spoken.

In those verses, 'mama saṅkappamaññāya' means knowing the various thoughts mentioned previously. 'Brāhmaṇavaṇṇinā' means with a physical form having the appearance of a Brahmin. 'Āsayaṃ' refers to the dwelling bush.

135-7. 'Santuṭṭho' means satisfied equally in all parts. 'Ghāsahetu' means for the sake of food. 'Adinnapubbaṃ' means never given before by any who are not Bodhisattas. 'Dānavaraṃ' means the noble gift. Having said, "Today I shall give to you," he then said, "You are endowed with the virtue of morality; it is not proper for you to harm others," thus dissuading the Brahmin from taking life. Now, making himself fit for the Brahmin's consumption in order to give, he said, "Come, kindle a fire," and so on.

In that verse, 'ahaṃ pacissamattānaṃ' means "I myself will descend into the pit of coals prepared by you and cook myself." 'Pakkaṃ tvaṃ bhakkhayissasi' means "You shall eat the meat thus cooked."
108:
138-9. 'Nānākaṭṭhe samānayī' means that Sakka, disguised as a Brahmin, appeared as if collecting various kinds of wood. 'Mahantaṃ akāsi citakaṃ, katvā aṅgāragabbhakaṃ' means he made a large pyre, flameless and smokeless, filled with glowing coals within, burning brightly all around, sufficient for my body to be submerged; he created this large pyre instantly by his psychic power. Therefore, it is said: "He kindled the fire there, so that it might quickly become great."

In that verse, 'so' refers to that great fire-heap being kindled so it would quickly grow large. 'Phoṭetvā rajagate gatte' means shaking his body, which was covered in dust, three times, intending: "If there are any insects among my fur, let them not die." 'Ekamantaṃ upāvisi' means since the wood was not yet burning, he sat down nearby for a while, waiting for them to ignite.

140. 'Yဒါ mahākaṭṭhapuñjo, āditto dhamadhamāyati' means when that pile of wood burns all around and makes the sound "dhama-dhama" by the power of the flames rising through the force of the wind. 'Taduppatitvā patati, majjhe jālasikhantare' means at that time, thinking "This mass of coals is capable of consuming my body," he jumped up and, with a joyful heart like a royal swan onto a cluster of lotuses, he gave his whole body as an offering and descended into the midst of that mass of coals within the flames.

141-2. 'Paviṭṭhaṃ yassa kassaci' means just as when someone enters cool water during the summer heat, it calms their distress and fever, and produces pleasure and joy. 'Tatheva jalitaṃ aggiṃ' means likewise, that burning mass of coals did not produce even a trace of heat for me when I entered. On the contrary, due to the joy of giving, there was only the calming of all distress and fever. "For a long time indeed, all my body parts, such as the outer and inner skin, have reached the state of being offered as a gift; my greatly desired heart's wish has reached its pinnacle." Therefore, it is said:

"Skin, hide, flesh, sinew, bone, along with the heart-strings—my entire body I gave to the Brahmin."

In that verse, 'hadayabandhanaṃ' means the piece of heart-flesh. Because it remains as if binding the heart-base (hadayavatthu), it is called 'hadayabandhanaṃ'. Alternatively, 'hadayabandhanaṃ' means the heart and the liver.
109:
The meaning is the flesh of the heart and the flesh of the liver which stands as if binding that heart. "Kevalaṃ sakalaṃ kāyaṃ" means the entire body without exception.

Thus, in that fire, because he was unable to cause heat even in a single pore of his own body, the Bodhisatta felt as if he had entered the interior of a mass of snow. He said to Sakka, who had assumed the form of a Brahmin, “Brahmin, the fire you have made is very cold; why is this?” (Sakka replied), “O wise one, I am not a Brahmin; I am Sakka. I have come to test you and have done this.” The Bodhisatta uttered a brave lion's roar, saying, “Sakka, let that be for a moment; even if the entire world were to test me with almsgiving, they could not in any way arouse in me a desire not to give. Behold this!”

Then Sakka said, “Wise Hare, let your virtues be known throughout the entire aeon.” He squeezed the mountain, took the essence of the mountain, and having drawn the sign of a hare on the orb of the moon, he caused the Bodhisatta to lie down on a couch of young dabba grass in that very thicket in that forest grove, and then returned to his own celestial realm. Those four wise ones also, being united and joyful, fulfilled the permanent virtue and the Uposatha virtue, performed merits as was appropriate, and passed away according to their kamma.

At that time, the otter became the Venerable Ānanda, the jackal became Mahāmoggallāna, the monkey became Sāriputta, and the Wise Hare became the Lord of the World, the Buddha.

The perfections such as virtue of this Bodhisatta should also be extracted here in the appropriate manner, according to the method mentioned below. Even though he was born in an animal state, his virtues should be understood here: his wisdom in knowing wholesome and other states as they truly are; his careful avoidance of unwholesome states by seeing even a minute fault as a danger; his proper establishing of himself in wholesome states; his urging others to abstain from unwholesome states by showing the disadvantages, saying, “These are indeed evil states; if they are grasped thus and practiced thus, they lead to such destinations and such future results”; his establishing others in meritorious deeds by showing the benefits, saying, “This is called giving, this is called virtue, this is called the Uposatha practice; for those established in these, the prosperity of devas and humans is already in their hands”; his disregard for his own body and life; his favoring of other beings; and his noble disposition for giving. Therefore, it is said: “Thus these are wonderful... (etc.) ...due to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.”

## The Explanation of the Sasa-Paṇḍita Cariyā is finished.
110:
Now, he concludes by uttering the ten special conducts already mentioned, starting with "Akitti the Brahmin." In that conclusion, "I myself was then" means that the one who gave those noble gifts, such as Akitti the Brahmin, was I myself at that time, and no other. Thus, although the perfections such as virtue were fulfilled as appropriate in those various existences, he presented the teaching through the power of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), intending the extreme nobility of his disposition toward giving at that time.

In the Akitti Jātaka and others, there were my renunciations of various kinds of gifts, the renunciation of my own limbs, and the renunciation of my children and wife, which reached the ultimate limit. Although these are indeed the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) because they reached the supreme excellence of giving by being embraced by compassion (karuṇā) and skill in means (upāya-kosalla) and by being directed solely toward omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), they are called "requisites of giving" (dāna-parikkhārā) because they are the equipment for my gift which is the ultimate perfection (paramattha-pāramī), and because they were prepared by repeatedly developing the sequence of perfections. To show the person who possesses these requisites, it was said: "Having given his life to the beggar, he fulfilled this perfection."

Here, excluding the Sasa-Paṇḍita Cariyā (Conduct of the Wise Hare), in the remaining nine conducts, the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) and the sub-perfection of giving (dāna-upapāramī) should be understood as appropriate. In the Sasa-Paṇḍita Cariyā, however, it is the ultimate perfection of giving (dāna-paramattha-pāramī). Therefore, it was said:

"Seeing one who had come for alms, I sacrificed myself;
There is no one equal to me in giving; this is my perfection of giving."

Although there is indeed no limit to the number of existences in which the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) fulfilled the perfection of giving during the time of Akitti the Brahmin and others, and at other times such as Mahājanaka and Mahāsutasoma, the fact that it was the ultimate perfection of giving (paramattha-pāramī) during the time of the wise hare should certainly be made clear.

## In the Commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka named Paramatthadīpanī,
## the explanation of the meaning of the First Chapter,
## which summarizes the ten kinds of conduct and specifically clarifies the perfection of giving, is finished.
111:
## 2. Hatthināgavagga
## 1. Mātuposakacariyāvaṇṇanā

In the first Jātaka of the second chapter, 'kuñjaro' refers to an elephant. 'Mātuposako' refers to one who looks after and supports a mother who is blind and infirm with old age. 'Mahiyā' means on the earth. 'Guṇenā' means that by the attribute of virtue (sīla-guṇa), there was no one equal to me in that elephant existence.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the elephant species in the Himalayan region. That noble elephant was entirely white, extremely beautiful, possessed of auspicious marks, and was surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of elephants. His mother, however, was blind. That elephant king would give sweet fruits of various sizes into the trunks of the attendant elephants to be sent to his mother. The elephants who were commissioned, however, would not give them to the mother but ate them themselves. When the elephant king learned of this situation, he thought, "I will leave the herd and support only my mother." During the night, without the other elephants knowing, he took his mother and went to the foot of Mount Caṇḍoraṇa. There, he stayed near a lotus pond and supported his mother by keeping her in a mountain cave.

2-3. 'Pavane disvā vanacaro' means a man who frequented the forest, while wandering in that great forest, saw me. 'Rañño maṃ paṭivedayī' means he informed the King of Bārāṇasī about me.

That man, having lost his way and being unable to determine the directions, wept with a loud voice. The Bodhisatta elephant king, hearing the sound of that man's weeping, thought, "This man is helpless; it is not proper for me that this person should perish in this forest while I am here." He went to the man's presence. Seeing the man fleeing in fear, he asked, "O man, there is no reason to fear because of me; do not run away. Why are you wandering about weeping?" When the man replied, "Lord elephant, I have lost my way, and today is the seventh day," the elephant said, "O man, do not be afraid; I will place you on the path used by humans." He then let the man sit on his back, led him out of the forest, and returned. That wicked man, thinking, "When I reach the city, I will inform the King," went to Bārāṇasī while marking trees and mountains. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī's state elephant had died. That man approached the King and reported that he had seen the Great Being. Therefore, it was said, "O Great King, an elephant worthy of you dwells in the forest," and so on.
112:
In that verse, "tavānuucchavo" means an elephant suitable and fit for the Great King to ride. "Na tassa parikkhāyattho" means that in capturing that noble white elephant, there is no need for the use of pits dug around to cut off movement, nor for using a female elephant with ear-rings, nor for snares thrown while hiding oneself, nor for the tethering post called an 'āḷaka', nor for a deceptive pit from which he could not escape if he entered. "Sahagahite" means at the very moment of being captured (he followed). "Ehiti" means he will come along.

The King of Bārāṇasī, keeping this man as a guide, went to the forest and sent the elephant trainer with an entourage, saying, "Bring the white elephant spoken of by this man." That elephant trainer went with the entourage and saw the Bodhisatta elephant king entering the lotus pond and gathering food. Therefore, it is said:

"Having heard that man's words, the King of Bārāṇasī, with a joyful mind, sent a skilled and well-trained elephant trainer.

When that elephant trainer arrived, he saw the elephant king at the Padumma lotus pond, pulling up lotus stalks and roots to sustain his mother."

In that verse, "chekakācariya" refers to an elephant trainer skilled in the methods of capturing elephants and so on. "Susikkhita" refers to one who has thoroughly learned the art of training elephants to the very end.

"Viññāya me sīlaguṇaṃ" means knowing my attribute of virtue, thinking, "This elephant is a noble breed (ājānīya) and is excellent; he is not foolish, not fierce or cruel, and is endowed only with good habits." How so? "Lakkhaṇaṃ upadhārayi" means that because he possessed well-trained elephant-craft, he extensively examined my auspicious marks. Therefore, that elephant trainer said, "Come, dear son," and took hold of my trunk.

When the Bodhisatta elephant king saw the elephant trainer, he thought, "This danger has arisen because of that man whom I guided and sent. Indeed, I am of great strength; I am capable of destroying even a thousand elephants. If I become angry, I can destroy the entire kingdom along with its army. However, if I were to become angry, the virtue (sīla) I have undertaken would be broken. Therefore, even if I am oppressed with spears, I will not be angry." Having resolved his mind thus, he bowed his head and stood perfectly still. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with, "Yaṃ me tadā pākatikaṃ, sarီrānugataṃ balaṃ."
113:
In this verse, 'pākatika' means being accomplished by nature. 'Sarīrānugata' refers only to the physical strength that follows the body; it does not mean the strength that follows wisdom, known as skill in means (upāya-kusala). 'Ajja nāgasahassānaṃ' means being equal to the collective strength of many thousands of elephants at the present time. It is a true equality with the physical strength of those elephants, not merely a metaphor. This is because the Bodhisatta was born into the Maṅgala elephant family at that time.

28. 'Yadihaṃ tesaṃ pakuppeyaṃ' means: "If I were to become angry with those who approached to capture me, I would be able to crush their lives." Not only them, but I could also strike and grind into powder the entire kingdom from which those men came.

9. 'Api cāhaṃ sīlarakkhāya' means: "Although I am capable in this way, I am like one bound because of guarding the virtue established in myself and being protected by the guardianship of virtue." 'Na karomi citte aññathattaṃ' means: "I do not allow in my mind the act of striking those beings, which would be a deviation from that virtue; I do not even let such an angry thought arise." 'Pakkhipantaṃ mamāḷake' means: "Even upon seeing the one who puts (binds) me to the post." Why is this? It is because of the fulfillment of the Perfection of Virtue. The connection is: "I do not allow a change in my mind toward those people so that for me, who guards virtue without flaw in such situations, the Perfection of Virtue will soon be fulfilled."

10. By the verse 'Yadi te maṃ', he shows the very state of being established in virtue by firmly guarding it. In that verse, 'koṭṭeyyuṃ' means they might destroy or break. 'Sīlakhaṇḍabhayā mamā' means: "I do not get angry because of the fear that my virtue might be broken."

Having thought thus, while the Bodhisatta remained motionless, the elephant trainer descended into the Paduma lotus pond. Seeing the Bodhisatta’s possession of auspicious marks, he said, "Come, my son," and took hold of the trunk, which was like a silver garland. On the seventh day, he reached the city of Bārāṇasī. While still on the way, he sent a message to the King. The King had the city decorated. The elephant trainer, having anointed the Bodhisatta with perfumes and adorned him, led him to the elephant stable, surrounded him with colorful curtains, and informed the King. The King brought food of various excellent flavors and offered it to the Bodhisatta. That Bodhisatta, the elephant king, thought, "I will not take food without my mother," and did not accept the morsel. Even when entreated, he did not take it, saying: "O Great King, my mother is blind and remains lonely along the mountain ranges. Having no one to serve her, she will strike her foot against a stump and fall at Mount Caṇḍoraṇa." Hearing these words, the King of Bārāṇasī said, "O noble elephant, that blind mother of yours who has no one to serve her..."
114:
"That mother of mine is helpless and blind, with no one to lead her. She surely strikes her foot against a stump and falls at the rugged Mount Caṇḍoraṇa."

Hearing this, the King asked: "O noble elephant, who is she to you—that blind one with no one to lead her, who strikes her foot against a stump and falls at the rugged Mount Caṇḍoraṇa?"

When he replied, "She is my mother, O Great King, blind and with no one to lead her, who strikes her foot against a stump and falls at the rugged Mount Caṇḍoraṇa," the elephant king, who had not taken food for seven days, said, "Today is the seventh day that my mother has not obtained food." Therefore, the King said, "Release this noble elephant who supports his mother. Let the elephant reunite with his mother along with all his kinsmen," and he had him released.

"The elephant king, freed from bonds, the tusker freed from the tether, after resting for a moment, went toward the mountain."

In that verse, 'kapaṇikā' means a poor, pitiable person. 'Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭeti' means that due to blindness and the suffering of separation from her son, she wanders lamenting and strikes her foot against various tree stumps. 'Caṇḍoraṇaṃ pati' means facing the rugged Mount Caṇḍoraṇa, wandering at the foot of that mountain. 'Agama yena pabbato' means that the noble elephant, once freed from bonds, rested a little, preached the Dhamma to the King with verses on the Ten Royal Virtues, gave the advice, "O Great King, be diligent," and being honored by the people with perfumes and garlands, left the city. On that very day, he reunited with his mother and told her everything that had happened. She, with a joyful heart, gave a blessing to the King:

"May that King live long, the one who increases the realm of the Kāsīs, who released my son, and who always respects the elders."

The King, being inspired by the virtues of the Bodhisatta, founded a village not far from the lotus pond and arranged for regular service to the Bodhisatta and his mother. Later, when the mother passed away, he performed the funeral rites and then went to the Kuruṇḍaka hermitage. Five hundred ascetics who had come down from the Himalayas lived in that place. The King entrusted the service of those ascetics and had a stone statue made in the likeness of the Bodhisatta, and held great festivals of worship. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa gathered annually and held the elephant festival called 'Hatthimaha'.

At that time, the King became Ānanda. The mother elephant became Mother Māyā. The forest hunter became Devadatta. The elephant king who supported his mother became I, the Buddha.

In this Jātaka, the Perfections such as Generosity are shown accordingly. The Perfection of Virtue, however, is exceptionally sublime.
115:
He established the duty of constantly attending to the Bodhisatta's mother. Later, when the Bodhisatta's mother died, he performed the funeral rites for her body and went to the hermitage of the ascetics named Kurandaka. In that place, five hundred ascetics who had descended from the Himālaya lived. The King of Bārāṇasī, having transferred the duties performed for that elephant to those ascetics, had a stone statue made in the likeness of the Bodhisatta and offered great honor and respect. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa gathered annually and held a festival of worship called the Elephant Festival (Hatthimaha).

At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī became Ānanda. The mother elephant became Mahāmāyā. The forest hunter became Devadatta. The elephant king who cared for his mother was the Lord of the World, the Buddha.

In this Jātaka as well, the perfections such as the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) should be extracted as appropriate. However, because the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī) was exceedingly abundant, that Perfection of Virtue alone was elevated into the discourse and taught. Furthermore, although he was born in the animal realm, in accordance with the state of being praised even by the Omniscient Buddha as a Brahma, a former deity, a first teacher, and one worthy of offerings, he developed a mind of deep respect for his mother. Reflecting that "This mother is of great benefit to her son; therefore, the wise have prescribed the duty of caring for one's mother," even though he was the lord and master of many thousands of elephants and a powerful herd leader, he disregarded the danger of being alone while being surrounded and followed by those elephants. Leaving the herd and becoming solitary, he thought, "I will honor my benefactress mother," and thus cared for his mother. Seeing a man who had lost his way, out of compassion, he took him and brought him to the path used by humans. He endured the wrong committed by that man. Although he was capable of harming those led by the elephant trainer who came to bind him, he thought, "Even by merely threatening them, they will suffer distress, and for me, there would be a breach in my virtue." Thinking thus, he did not do so, but allowed himself to be captured easily like a well-trained state elephant. Thinking, "Without my mother, I will not consume any food," he fasted for seven days. Without harboring any resentment in his mind, thinking "This king caused me to be captured," he radiated loving-kindness (mettā) toward the king. His qualities and power as a Great Man (Mahāpurisa), such as preaching the Dhamma to that king through various methods, should be understood here. Therefore, it was said: "Thus, these wonderful and marvelous qualities of the Great Sage (Mahesī) arose from the practice in accordance with the Dhamma," and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Conduct of the Elephant King Who Cared for His Mother is finished.
116:
## 2. Explanation of the Bhūridatta-cariya

In the second [account], the Bhūridatta-cariya, "Bhūridatta" means Datta who possesses wisdom like the earth. "Datta" was the name given by the Bodhisatta's parents at that time. However, because he could properly resolve problems that arose in the Naga realm, in the realm of the Great King Virūpakkha, and in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, [he was so named]. One day, while the Great King Virūpakkha, who rules over the Nagas, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with a retinue of Nagas and sat surrounding Sakka, a problem arose among the deities. No one was able to speak or solve it. Then, permitted by Sakka, the Great Being himself ascended the noble throne and answered it. Then the king of gods honored that Bhūridatta with divine scents and flowers and said, "O Datta, you are endowed with vast wisdom like the earth; from this day forth, let your name be Bhūridatta." "Bhūri" is a name for the earth; therefore, because he was like the earth, because he delighted in the true meaning, and because he was endowed with great wisdom known as "bhūri," the Great Being became famous as "Bhūridatta." Because he was endowed with the great psychic power of the Nagas, he was also called "Mahiddhika" (One of Great Power).

In the past, in this very eon, the son of the King of Bārāṇasī was exiled from the country by his father and, while living in the forest, cohabited with a certain Naga maiden. Based on that union, two children were born—a son and a daughter. They named the son "Sāgarabrahmadatta" and the daughter "Samuddajā." Later, after the death of his father, the prince went to Bārāṇasī and ruled as king. At that time, a Naga king named Dhataraṭṭha, who was ruling the Naga kingdom in a Naga realm of five hundred yojanas, heard from a tortoise named Cittacūḷa, who was not a speaker of truth, that "The King of Bārāṇasī wishes to give his daughter to you, O Naga King; that princess named Samuddajā is very beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing." Hearing this, Dhataraṭṭha sent four Naga youths. When the King of Bārāṇasī, who did not wish to give his daughter, was threatened by the terrifying forms of the Nagas, he said, "I will give her." Then [Dhataraṭṭha] sent great gifts and, with great Naga power and a large retinue, took the king's daughter to the Naga realm and placed her in the position of Chief Queen.

Later, that Princess Samuddajā, in union with the Naga King Dhataraṭṭha, gave birth to four sons: Sudassana, Datta, Subhoga, and Ariṭṭha. Among them, Datta was the Bodhisatta. As mentioned before, because Sakka had given him the name "Bhūridatta" with a pleased mind, he became famous by the name Bhūridatta. At that time, the father, Naga King Dhataraṭṭha, divided the kingship of one hundred yojanas each to those four sons. There were many attendants. Those four brothers...
117:
He became known only by the name "Bhūridatta." Then, their father, the Naga King, divided the kingdom into portions of a hundred yojanas each and gave them to his four sons. There was great fame and retinue. Sixteen thousand naga maidens attended each of them. The father also had a kingdom of exactly a hundred yojanas. The three sons came to visit their parents every month, but the Bodhisatta came every half-month.

One day, he went with the Great King Virūpakkha to pay respects to Sakka. Seeing the extremely delightful splendor of Sakka—the Vejayanta Palace, the Sudhammā divine assembly hall, the Pāricchattaka-Kovīḷāra tree, the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, and the retinue of celestial nymphs—he thought: "Even such splendor as this is difficult for me to attain while remaining in this naga state; how much more so the Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi)?" Feeling revulsion for his naga state, he thought: "I will go to the naga realm, observe the Uposatha, and cultivate virtue. That virtue will bring the Bodhi-knowledge to maturity and will be the cause for rebirth in this heavenly realm." Having so planned, he went to the naga realm and said to his parents: "Mother and father, I will perform the Uposatha practice." When the parents said, "Observe the Uposatha right here; there is great danger for nagas who go outside," he did so once. However, being disturbed by the naga maidens, the next time, without informing his parents, he called his wife and said: "Dear, I will go to the human world. Near the Yamunā river, there is a great banyan tree. Not far from it, on top of an anthill, I will coil myself and undertake the four-factored Uposatha. I will lie there and perform the Uposatha practice." Leaving the naga realm, he did as he said. Therefore, the verse beginning with "Virūpakkhena mahāraññā, devalokamagañchahaṃ" was spoken.

In that verse, "Virūpakkhena mahāraññā" means with the Great King named Virūpakkha, the lord of the nagas. "Devalokaṃ" means to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. "Agañchahaṃ" means I went, I approached.

12. In that heaven, "passiṃ tvāhaṃ" means I saw; the word "tu" is a mere particle. "Ekantasukhasamappite" means truly and entirely endowed with happiness. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are the six spheres of contact (phassāyatana) called heavens. Monks, it is not easy to describe in words how happy those heavens are..."
118:
"...heavens" (M. Ni. 3.255). "Taṃsaggagamanatthāya" means for the purpose of going to that heaven by way of rebirth. "Sīlabbataṃ" means the practice known as virtue (Uposatha). Alternatively, "sīlabbataṃ" refers to the Uposatha virtue and the practice of undertaking the sacrifice of one's own limbs and body, as in "Let those who desire skin take my skin," and so on.

"Sarīrakiccaṃ" means the care of the body, such as washing the face. "Bhuttvā yāpanamattakaṃ" means having consumed only enough food to sustain the body so as to keep the faculties calm. "Caturo aṅge" means the four factors. "Adhiṭṭhāya" means having undertaken. "Semi" means I lie down.

"Chaviyā" and so forth shows those four factors. Among those four, giving up the outer and inner skin is one factor, and the rest are each separate factors. Here, in the mention of "maṃsa" (flesh), "rudhira" (blood) should also be understood as included. "Etena" means by these (four factors). "Harātu so" means let anyone who has a need for this skin and so forth take all that I have given. "Let him take everything"—thus he makes an invitation (pavāraṇā) without any regard for his own body.

In this manner, while the Great Being was performing the Uposatha practice every half-month, a long time passed. As time went by, one day a Nesāda Brahmin, together with his son named Somadatta, arrived at that place. At the time of dawn, seeing the Great Being surrounded by naga maidens, he approached him. At that moment, the naga maidens dived into the earth and went back to the naga realm. The Brahmin asked the Great Being: "Friend, are you a deva, a yakkha, or a naga?" The Bodhisatta revealed his true self and thought: "If this man goes from here and makes my dwelling place known to the people, it might be an obstacle to my Uposatha practice. I should take him to the naga realm and provide him with great luxury. In that way, he will delight in staying there, and my Uposatha practice will be long-lasting." Then he said to him: "Brahmin, I will give you great glory. Come to the pleasant naga realm; let us go there." The Brahmin replied: "Lord, I have a son; I will come when he arrives." The Bodhisatta said: "Go, Brahmin, bring your son." The Brahmin went, told his son about the matter, and brought him. The Great Being took both of them and, by his psychic power...
119:
[The Nesāda Brahmin] brought [his son] to the Naga realm. For the father and son, a divine-like appearance manifested in that Naga realm. Then, the Bodhisatta gave them divine luxury and four hundred Naga maidens each. The father and son enjoyed great wealth and happiness.

The Bodhisatta, without negligence, performed the practice of Uposatha. Once every half-month, he went to attend to his mother and father, preached the Dhamma, and from there went to the Brahmin to inquire about his health, saying, "What object do you desire? Please tell me your wish." After saying, "May you enjoy yourself without weariness," and exchanging greetings with Somadatta, he returned to his own residence. The Brahmin lived in that Naga realm for a full year, but due to his lack of merit, he became weary. Taking his son, who was unwilling to leave, he took leave of the Bodhisatta. Due to his ill fortune, he did not accept the many riches and the wish-fulfilling gem offered by the Bodhisatta, saying, "I will go to the human world and become a monk." The Bodhisatta commanded the Naga youths to escort the Brahmin and his son to the human world. The father and son took off their divine ornaments and divine clothes and went down into a pond to bathe. At that moment, those divine ornaments and clothes vanished and returned to the Naga realm. Then, they put back on the soiled bark garments they had worn before, and taking bows, arrows, and spears, they went into the forest to kill animals and made their living just as before.

At that time, a certain ascetic gave the Alampāyana mantra, which he had received from a Garuda king, along with the appropriate medicines and ritual procedures for that mantra, to a certain Brahmin who was attending to him. That Brahmin thought, "I have found a means of livelihood," and after staying for a few days, he took leave of the ascetic and departed. In due course, he reached the banks of the Yamunā river and walked along the main road reciting that mantra. At that time, the Naga maidens, who were attendants from the Bodhisatta's residence, had brought that wish-fulfilling gem and placed it on a heap of sand by the Yamunā river, playing at night by the light of that gem. At dawn, hearing the sound of the Brahmin reciting the mantra, they mistakenly thought, "A Garuda is coming!" and being terrified, they abandoned the gem and dived into the earth to return to the Naga realm.

The Brahmin took that gem and proceeded. At that moment, the Nesāda Brahmin, while going into the forest with his son to kill animals, saw the Alampāyana Brahmin's...
120:
(The Nesāda Brahmin) saw that gem in the man's hand and recognized it, thinking, "This is the wish-fulfilling gem of Bhūridatta." Desiring to take that gem, he spoke with the man and, realizing he was a master of spells, said: "If you give me this gem, I will show you a Naga of great power. By capturing that Naga and traveling through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, you will obtain much wealth." When the man said, "If so, show him and take it," the Nesāda led him to the place where the Bodhisatta was observing Uposatha, lying coiled on top of an anthill, and standing not far away, he stretched out his hand and showed him.

The Mahāsatta (Great Being) saw that Nesāda and thought: "This man might endanger my Uposatha virtue. Although I brought him to the Naga realm and established him in great wealth, he did not desire it. After leaving there, wanting to go on his own, he did not desire to take the gem I offered. Now, however, he comes leading a snake-catcher. If I were to get angry with this treacherous friend who betrays kindness, my virtue (sīla) would be broken. I have already resolved upon the Uposatha endowed with four factors; let it remain as resolved. Whether Alampāyana cuts me or not, I will not be angry with him." Thinking thus, he closed his eyes, making the Perfection of Resolve (Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī) his priority, tucked his head into his coils, and lay motionless. The Nesāda Brahmin also said, "O Alampāyana, take this Naga and give me the gem." Alampāyana, seeing the Naga, was delighted and, disregarding everything else, said, "Take it, Brahmin," and tossed it into his hand. As soon as the gem slipped from his hand and fell to the ground, it dived into the earth and returned to the Naga realm. The Nesāda Brahmin was deprived of both the gem and his friendship with Bhūridatta, and he departed without any support.

Alampāyana, having smeared his body with medicines of great power, ate a little, and spread saliva over his body. Reciting a divine mantra, he approached the Bodhisatta, grabbed him by the tail, pulled him, and holding his head firmly, forced his mouth open. Having eaten medicine, he poured it along with saliva into the Naga's mouth. The Mahāsatta, of pure nature, did not open his eyes and did not get angry for fear of breaking his virtue. Then, by the power of the medicinal mantra, the man grabbed him by the tail, held him head-downwards, shook him to make him vomit the food he had eaten, and laid him out lengthwise on the ground...
121:
Having made the Naga King lie down, he kneaded him with his hands as if kneading a Masūraka stone. The bones seemed to be crushed into fine powder. Again, grabbing him by the tail, he beat him against the ground as if washing a cloth. Even though the Bodhisatta experienced such suffering, he did not get angry but reflected only on his virtue (Sīla). Thus, after making the Bodhisatta weak, the Alampāyana Brahmin prepared a basket made of vines and put the Bodhisatta inside. However, because the Naga King's body was very large, it could not fit into the basket, so he forced him in by pressing with his heel. Then, taking the basket, he went to a village, placed it in the middle of the village, and shouted, "Come, those who wish to see the Naga dance!" All the villagers gathered. At that moment, Alampāyana said, "Come out, Great Naga!"

The Bodhisatta thought, "Today, it is proper for me to perform and please the audience. If they are pleased, Alampāyana will receive much wealth and, being satisfied, will release me. Whatever he wants me to do, I will do it." Then, Alampāyana said to the Naga coming out of the basket, "Become large!" and he became large. "Become small, become round, have many hoods, have from one hood up to a thousand hoods, become high, become low, become visible, become invisible, let only half the body be visible, become blue, golden, red, white, and crimson, emit smoke, emit flames, emit water"—whatever forms were commanded, he manifested them and danced. Seeing this, the people were filled with wonder and gave much gold, silver, clothing, ornaments, and so on. Thus, he obtained about a hundred thousand in that village. Although Alampāyana had said when capturing the Bodhisatta, "I will release you when I get a thousand," upon receiving so much wealth, he became greedy and did not release him, thinking, "If I get this much even in a small village, I will surely get much more in the city."

That Alampāyana accumulated wealth in that village, made a basket of jewels, put the Bodhisatta in it, and riding a fine carriage with a large retinue, he made him perform in villages, towns, and royal capitals until he reached the city of Vārāṇasī. He gave the Naga King sweet popcorn and honey-balls, but the Naga King, fearing he would not be released, did not eat. Even though he did not eat, he was made to perform for about a month in various places, starting from the four city gates. Therefore, he spoke the verse beginning with "Saṃsito akataññunā." The meaning of that verse is: The Nesāda Brahmin, who pointed out the location saying he had seen this Naga on an anthill near a banyan tree, who is ungrateful and betrays his friend, captured me by reciting the Alampāyana mantra and makes me perform in various villages, towns, and royal capitals for his livelihood.
122:
In that verse, "Saṃsito" means pointed out by indicating the place, saying, "This Naga is sleeping on top of an anthill near a certain banyan tree." "Akataññunā" refers to the Nesāda Brahmin who does not know the favor done for him and betrays his friend. "Alampāyano" is the snake charmer who obtained this name by reciting the Alampāyana mantra. "Mamaggahī" means he captured me. "Kīḷeti maṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ" means he makes me perform for his own livelihood in various villages, towns, and royal capitals.

"Tiṇato pi lahuko mama" means that giving up one's life appears as light to me as giving up a mere blade of grass. "Pathavī-uppatanaṃ viya" means that transgressing virtue (Sīla) appears to me as a deed even more heavy than the overturning of the great earth, which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick.

"Nirantaraṃ ဇာတိသတံ" means that because of not transgressing virtue continuously for many hundreds of my births, I would give up my life; I am able to give up my life. "နေဝ သီလံ ပဘိန္ဒေယျံ" means I would never break or destroy the virtue I have undertaken, even once. "Catuddīpāna hetū" shows that even for the sake of the sovereign glory of a Cakkavatti, [I would not break my virtue].

Now, to show how he protected his virtue at that time even by sacrificing his life for a certain purpose, and how, because of that protection of virtue, he did not harbor any perversion of mind toward the Nesāda and Alampāyana Brahmins who caused such harm, he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Api ca." That verse has the same meaning as stated below.

Thus, while the Great Being (Bodhisatta) was in the hands of the snake charmer, his mother had a bad dream and, not seeing her son in the Naga realm, was overcome by grief. Then her eldest son, Sudassana, hearing the news, sent Subhoga, saying, "Go to the Himavanta, search for Bhūridatta in the five great rivers and seven great lakes, and return." He sent Kāṇāရိဋ္ဌ, saying, "Go to the Deva realm, and if the deities who wish to hear the Dhamma have taken Bhūridatta there, bring him back from there." He himself said, "I will search in the human realm," and in the guise of an ascetic...
123:
Sudassana departed from the Naga realm. His half-sister named Accimukhī, who had great affection for the Bodhisatta, followed Sudassana. She transformed herself into a small frog and hid within his matted hair. Starting from the place where the Bodhisatta observed the Uposatha, they searched everywhere and eventually reached the city of Vārāṇasī, arriving at the palace gate. At that time, the Brahmin Alampāyana, in the midst of a great crowd in the royal courtyard, opened the basket to show the play of the Bhuridatta Naga to the King, and gave the signal, saying, "Come, O Great Naga!"

When the Bodhisatta put out his head and looked, he saw his elder brother Sudassana. He came out of the basket and went directly toward Sudassana. The great crowd retreated in fear. The Bodhisatta went and paid respectful homage to Sudassana, then turned back and re-entered the basket. Alampāyana, thinking, "This Naga has bitten this ascetic," said, "Do not be afraid, do not be afraid." Sudassana, initiating a dialogue with Alampāyana, said, "What can this Naga do to me? There is no snake charmer like me," and added, "You have captured this Naga and are boasting; if I wish, I shall have this small frog destroy that Naga." He then called his sister and stretched out his hand. Hearing Sudassana's voice, she, who was lying inside the matted hair, croaked like a frog three times, came out, sat on his shoulder, and then jumped onto Sudassana's palm. After letting three drops of poison fall onto his palm, she entered the matted hair once again.

Sudassana showed the drops of poison and said, "If I let these drops of poison fall on the earth, all medicinal plants, grass, and forest trees will be destroyed. If I throw them into the sky, it will not rain for seven years. If I drop them in the water, all aquatic living beings therein will die." To make the King believe him, he had three pits dug: he filled one with various medicines, the second with cow dung, and the third with divine medicines. Then he dropped the poison into the middle pit. At that very moment, smoke arose and flames broke out. The flames spread and caught the pit of cow dung. From there, the flames rose again, spread to the pit filled with divine medicines, consumed them, and then went out.
