While Alampāyana was standing not far from that pit, the poisonous fumes spread and caused his skin to peel off. He became a person afflicted with white leprosy. Terrified by the danger, he cried out three times, "I release the Naga King!" Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta came out of the jeweled basket.
124:
The Bodhisatta created a body adorned with all kinds of ornaments and stood with the appearance of a celestial being. Sudassana and Accimukhī also stood in the same manner.

Then Sudassana informed the King of his status as the King's nephew. Upon hearing this, the King embraced them, kissed their heads, took them into the palace, and accorded them great honor and respect. While exchanging pleasantries with Bhuridatta, the King asked, "Dear son, how could Alampāyana capture you, who are endowed with such great power and majesty?" Bhuridatta explained everything in detail and then preached the Dhamma to his uncle, saying, "Great King, a king should rule the kingdom in this manner."

Then Sudassana requested leave from his uncle, saying, "Uncle, my mother is weary from not seeing Bhuridatta; we cannot delay here any longer." He then returned to the Naga realm together with Bhuridatta and Accimukhī.

There, in the Naga realm, while the Great Being was lying on his sickbed, a large assembly of Nagas came to inquire about his health. While Kāṇāriṭṭha was speaking in praise of the Vedas, sacrifices, and Brahmins, Bhuridatta refuted that doctrine and preached the Dhamma in various ways, establishing them in the perfection of virtue (sīla-sampadā) and the perfection of right view (diṭṭhi-sampadā). He observed the precepts throughout his life, performed the Uposatha duties, and at the end of his life, he filled the heavenly city.

At that time, the parents were the members of the royal family. The hunter Brahmin became Devadatta. Somadatta became Ānanda. Accimukhī became Uppalavaṇṇā. Sudassana became Sāriputta. Subhoga became Mahāmoggallāna. Kāṇāriṭṭha became Sunakkhatta. Bhuridatta became the Lord of the World (Lokanātha), the Buddha.

The remaining perfections of this Bhuridatta should be extracted in the same manner as mentioned below. In this Jātaka, although he resided in the sovereignty of the Naga realm, which was like the glory of the celestial world, being attended by sixteen thousand Naga maidens like a painted scene in his own Naga palace spanning a hundred yojanas, he did not indulge in the pride of sovereignty. He served his parents once every half-month and showed respect to the elders in the family. Whenever problems arose among the entire Naga assembly, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, or the Tāvatiṃsa assembly, he would immediately cut through them with his sword of wisdom—as if cutting a bundle of lotus stalks with a sharp sword—in the midst of those various assemblies, and preached the Dhamma according to their inclinations. Renouncing the wealth and possessions described above, and without regard for his own body or life, he undertook the four-factored Uposatha. Having made that vow...
125:
Out of fear of the danger of breaking his word, he fell into the hands of the snake charmer. Even then, [the snake charmer] spat saliva mixed with poisonous medicine into his mouth, grabbed him by the tail and pulled him repeatedly, dragged him, rubbed him on the ground, trampled him, and beat him. Despite undergoing such great suffering through various forms of maltreatment, and although he was capable of turning that snake charmer into ashes just by looking at him in anger, he reflected on the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī). Fearing the destruction of his virtue, he did not allow even a slight disturbance in his mind. Thinking, "I shall let the snake charmer obtain wealth," he followed the man's will. Even towards the ungrateful and treacherous Nesāda Brahmin, who had been brought back to the Naga realm by Subhoga, he did not get angry, even without formally undertaking the precepts. He refuted the false views spoken by Kāṇāriṭṭha, preached the Dhamma in various ways, and established the Naga assembly in virtue and Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi). These and other attributes and powers of the Bodhisatta should be understood. Therefore, it is said: "Thus, these are wonderful... according to the Dhamma."

## The Explanation of the Conduct of Bhūridatta is finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Conduct of the Naga Campeyya

Regarding the third [story], "Campeyyako": Between the kingdoms of Anga and Magadha, there is a river named Campā. Because the Naga realm beneath that Campā river is not far away, it is also called Campā. The Naga king born there is named Campeyyaka. "At that time also, I was a practitioner of Dhamma" means that during the time I was that Naga king Campeyya, I was one who practiced the Dhamma.

Indeed, the Bodhisatta was then reborn in the Campā Naga realm and became the Naga king named Campeyya, possessing great psychic power and majesty. While ruling as the Naga king there and enjoying sovereign wealth similar to the bliss of the King of Devas, he realized there was no opportunity to fulfill the Perfections. He thought, "What is the use of this animal birth to me? By observing the Uposatha and escaping from this birth, I shall properly fulfill the Perfections." From then on, he performed the Uposatha observance in his own palace. Ornamented Naga maidens would come to him. Thinking, "Here, there will be danger to my virtue," he left the palace and sat in the garden. They came there too. He thought, "Here, my virtue will be defiled. Leaving this Naga realm..."
126:
"...I will go to the human world and observe the Uposatha." From then on, on Uposatha days, he would leave the Naga realm and go to the top of an ant-hill near a road, not far from a border village. Relinquishing his body as a gift, he thought, "Let those who desire my skin and so on take them; let those who wish to make a performing snake do so." He lay there with his coils folded and observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth and fifteenth days. On the first day of the lunar month, he returned to the Naga realm. A long time passed while he was thus observing the Uposatha.

Then, his chief queen named Sumanā said to the Bodhisatta, "O Naga King, you go to the human world to observe the Uposatha, but that human world is suspicious and full of danger." Standing by the bank of the Mangala pond, he told her of three omens: "O sister, if someone beats me and causes me distress, the water in this pond will become turbid. If a Garuda seizes me, the water will boil. If a snake charmer captures me, the water will turn the color of blood." Having informed her of these three omens, he undertook the fourteenth-day Uposatha, left the Naga realm, went to that place, and lay on top of the ant-hill, beautifying it with the splendor of his body. His body was white like a silver garland, and his head was like a red woolen ball. The size of his body was like the head of a plow. During the time of the Bhūridatta birth (Jā. 2.22.784 etc.), it was the size of a thigh; during the time of the Saṅkhapāla birth (Jā. 2.17.143 etc.), it was the size of a single-log boat.

At that time, a young man from Bārāṇasī went to Takkasilā and learned the Alampāyana mantra. While returning to his village by that road, he saw the Great Being (Bodhisatta) and thought, "What is the use of returning to the village empty-handed? I will capture this Naga, make him perform in villages, towns, and royal capitals, and only after earning wealth will I return." Thinking thus, he took divine medicines, recited the divine mantra, and approached the Naga king. From the moment the Great Being heard the divine mantra, it was as if hot iron rods were being thrust into his ears, and as if his head was being crushed by a mountain peak. He raised his head from between his coils, looked to see "Who is this?", and seeing the snake charmer, he thought: "My venom has fierce power. If I get angry and blow out my nasal breath, this man's body will be scattered like a handful of chaff. Then my virtue will be broken. I will not look at him." He closed his eyes and placed his head between his coils.
127:
The snake-charmer Brahmin, having consumed medicine and recited mantras, spat saliva onto the body of the Bodhisatta. Due to the power of the medicine and mantras, wherever the saliva touched, it was as if blisters were breaking out.

Then, the snake charmer grabbed the tail and pulled it, making the Bodhisatta lie down at full length. He oppressed him with a stick shaped like a goat's hoof to weaken him, and then firmly grabbed and squeezed the head. The Bodhisatta had to open his mouth. At that moment, the charmer spat saliva into his mouth and broke his fangs with the power of the medicine and mantras. The mouth became filled with blood. Fearing the breach of his virtue (sīla), the Bodhisatta endured such suffering and did not even open his eyes to look. The snake charmer, thinking, "I will make the Naga King weak," crushed the whole body as if grinding bones starting from the tail, and performed maneuvers known as paṭṭakaveṭhana (coiling), tantamajjita (stretching/massaging), and dussapothana (beating like washing clothes). Although the Bodhisatta's entire body was smeared with blood, he endured the intense pain.

Then, knowing his weakness, the charmer made a basket (peḷā) out of creepers, placed the Naga inside, and took him to a border village to perform in the midst of the people. In colors such as blue and so on, in shapes such as round or square, and in sizes such as small or large, the Bodhisatta danced, performing whatever the Brahmin desired; he even created a hundred or a thousand hoods. The people were delighted and gave much wealth. In a single day, he obtained a thousand kahāpaṇas and requisites worth a thousand. From the beginning, the Brahmin had thought, "I will release him when I get a thousand." However, upon receiving that wealth, he thought, "I have obtained this much wealth even in a border village; how much more would I get if I show him to the King and the King's great ministers?" He then took a cart and a carriage, loaded the requisites onto the cart, and sitting in the carriage, he set out, thinking, "I will have the Bodhisatta perform with a great retinue in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, and after performing before King Uggasena in the city of Bārāṇasī, I will release him." He killed frogs and gave them to the Naga King. The Naga King, thinking, "This man will kill repeatedly because of me," did not eat. Then he gave him honey-coated parched rice. Thinking, "If I take food, I will surely die within this basket," he did not eat those either.
128:
Within a month, the Brahmin reached Bārāṇasī and obtained much wealth while making the Naga perform in the gate-villages. The King also summoned the snake charmer and said, "Make him perform for us as well." He replied, "Very well, O King, I will make him perform for you tomorrow on the fifteenth day (Full Moon)." The King had the drum beaten to announce, "Tomorrow the Naga King will dance in the royal courtyard; let the people assemble and watch," and the next day, he had the royal courtyard decorated and summoned the snake charmer. The snake charmer brought the Bodhisatta in a jeweled basket and sat down, placing the basket on a magnificent rug. The King also descended from the palace and sat on the royal throne surrounded by the multitude. The snake charmer took the Bodhisatta out and made him dance. The Bodhisatta displayed every manner that the Brahmin thought of. The multitude could not contain their emotions. Thousands of turbans and garments were tossed up. A rain of jewels fell upon the Bodhisatta. Therefore, the verse beginning with "Tadāpi maṃ dhammacārī" was spoken.

In that verse, "Tadāpi" means at the time when I was the Naga King named Campeyya, even then. "Dhammacārī" means one who practices only the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action (dasa-kusalakamma-patha) and does not practice even a grain of unrighteousness. "Upavuṭṭhauposathaṃ" refers to the Uposatha observed by way of keeping the eight-factored Noble Uposatha virtue. "Rājadvāramhi kīḷati" means making him perform at the palace gate of King Uggasena in Bārāṇasī.

"Yaṃ yaṃ so vaṇṇaṃ cintayi" means that the snake-charmer Brahmin thought, "Let there be such and such a color, like blue." Therefore, it was said, "Nīlaṃ vā pītalohitaṃ." In that phrase, the word "vā" in "nīlaṃ vā" has an indefinite meaning; it is spoken with a short vowel for the sake of the verse's meter. By that word "vā," it includes other distinct colors like white that remain after those mentioned, as well as distinct shapes like roundness, and distinct sizes like small or large. "Tassa cittānuvattanto" means following the mind of that snake charmer. "Cintitasannibho" means he intended to show that he appeared to the spectators in whatever manner the Brahmin thought of.

Not only was displaying the manner thought of by the Brahmin my power, but furthermore, I could turn land into water and water into land; I could take the great earth which is land and make it water, and take water and make it earth—such was my great power. "Yadihaṃ tassa kuppeyaṃ" means if I were to become angry with that snake charmer, "khaṇe na chārikaṃ kare" means I could turn him into ashes in the very moment of anger.
129:
In this way, the Blessed One, having shown that he was capable of preventing the harm that was to befall him at that time, now spoke the verse beginning with "Yadi cittavasī hessaṃ" to show the purpose for which he did not prevent it.

The meaning of that verse is: "If I, becoming angry and thinking, 'This snake charmer oppresses me excessively; he does not know my power; behold, I shall show him my power,' had acted according to my will even by a mere glance, then in that very moment, that snake charmer would have been scattered like a handful of chaff. I would have fallen away from the virtue (sīla) I had undertaken. If I were thus diminished in virtue and my virtue were broken, that supreme goal of Buddhahood, which I have aspired to since the time at the feet of the Dīpaṅkara Buddha, would not be accomplished."

"Kāmaṃ bhijjatuyaṃ kāyo" means: This body, composed of the four great elements, sustained by rice and gruel, and subject to impermanence, rubbing, massaging, breaking, and dissolution—let it be broken or destroyed if it must. Let it be scattered in this very place like a handful of chaff thrown into a great wind, yet I shall not break my virtue at all. "Vikarante bhusaṃ viya" means: Virtue is the cause for the accomplishment of the supreme goal; even if this physical frame is scattered like a handful of chaff, I shall not break it. Thinking, "I shall fulfill the Perfection of Virtue (sīla-pāramī) without regard for body or life," he showed that he endured such suffering at that time.

Then, a month had passed while the Bodhisatta was in the hands of the snake charmer, and during all this time, he remained without food. The Nāgī Sumanā, thinking, "My lord has been gone for a very long time; what could have happened?" looked at the pond and, seeing the water the color of blood, realized, "He must have been captured by a snake charmer," and departed from the Nāga realm. Going near the anthill and seeing the place where the Bodhisatta was captured and the place where he had suffered, she wept and lamented. She then went to the border village to inquire and, hearing the news, went to Bārāṇasī and stood weeping in the sky at the royal courtyard. While the Bodhisatta was dancing, he looked up at the sky and, seeing Sumanā, felt ashamed and entered the basket to lie down.

When he entered the basket, the King, wondering "What is the reason?" looked here and there and saw her standing in the sky. He asked, "Who are you?" and upon hearing that she was a Nāga princess, he concluded, "Undoubtedly, the Nāga King [entered the basket upon seeing] this..."
130:
When the Nāga King saw [the King], he entered the basket out of shame. The King, concluding, "This displayed psychic power belongs only to the Nāga King and not to the snake charmer," asked, "How did this Nāga King, possessing such great power, come into the hands of this man?" He was told, "This Campeyya Nāga King is a practitioner of Dhamma and is endowed with virtue. While observing the Uposatha on the fourteenth and fifteenth days, he surrendered his body as an act of giving and lay upon an anthill near the main road; it was there that he was captured by this man." Furthermore, he heard, "This Nāga King has thousands of wives resembling celestial nymphs, and the wealth of the Nāga realm is like the prosperity of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. This Nāga King of great psychic power and majesty is capable of overturning the entire earth, yet he endures such perverted suffering only because he fears his virtue might be broken." Upon hearing this, the King was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). At that very moment, he bestowed great wealth, attendants, and authority upon the Brahmin snake charmer and had him release the Nāga, saying, "Here, friend, release this Nāga King."

The Bodhisatta made his Nāga form disappear and stood like a celestial youth in the form of a young man. Sumanā also descended from the sky and stood near him. The Nāga King, with palms joined in reverence to the King, invited him, saying, "Come, Great King, come to see my abode." Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"The released Nāga Campeyya spoke thus to the King:
'Homage to you, O King of Kāsi; homage to you, O Multiplier of Kāsi.
I join my palms in reverence to you; please come to see my abode.'"

Then the King gave permission to go to the Nāga realm. The Bodhisatta took the King and his retinue to the Nāga realm, showed them his sovereign wealth, and after having them stay there for a few days, had a drum beaten to announce: "Let all the King's attendants take as much wealth, such as gold and silver, as they desire." He also sent wealth for the King in hundreds of carts. The Nāga King exhorted the King with the Ten Royal Virtues (dasa-rājadhamma), saying, "Great King, a king must give alms, guard virtue, and provide righteous protection and ward in all things," and then sent him back. The King departed from the Nāga realm with great glory and returned to Bārāṇasī. It is said that from that time on, gold and silver became abundant on the surface of Jambudīpa. The Bodhisatta, guarding his virtues and observing the Uposatha once every fortnight, reached the heavenly city along with his followers.

At that time, the snake charmer became Devadatta. The Nāga princess Sumanā became the mother of Rāhula. King Uggasena became the Elder Sāriputta. As for the Nāga King Campeyya, he became I, the Buddha, the refuge of humans. In this Jātaka, the remaining perfections of the Nāga King Campeyya should be noted as appropriate. The wonderful psychic powers of the Bodhisatta in this Jātaka are just as described in the Bhūridatta Jātaka, which will be mentioned below.

The practice of the Perfections of the third, the Nāga King Campeyya, is finished.
131:
The snake charmer became Devadatta; the Naga princess Sumana became the mother of Rāhula; King Uggasena became the Elder Sāriputta; and the Naga King Campeyya became the Lord of the World (the Buddha). In this birth also, the remaining perfections of that Naga King Campeyya should be extracted and noted as appropriate. In this birth, the wonderful and marvelous powers of the Bodhisatta are just as described previously in the Bhūridatta Jātaka.

## The Explanation of the Conduct of the Naga Campeyya is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Conduct of Cūḷabodhi

In the fourth [section], the explanation of the conduct of Cūḷabodhi: The name "Cūḷabodhi" is metaphorically applied in this birth based on his existence as the wandering ascetic Mahābodhi. It should be understood that he is not called Cūḷabodhi because there is an elder brother named Mahābodhi in this Jātaka. "Susīlavā" means one who has good virtue, one endowed with virtue. "Bhavaṃ disvāna bhayato" means seeing existence, such as sensual existence (kāmabhava), as something to be feared. In the word "nekkhammaṃ," it should be noted that the word "ca" is elided; by that "ca," the word "disvāna" is drawn in. The meaning is: by reflecting on these eight grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu)—birth, old age, sickness, death, suffering in the lower realms, suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the past, suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the future, and suffering rooted in the search for food in the present—one sees all existence, such as sensual existence, as a danger in the round of rebirth (saṃsāra). Then, seeing Nibbāna, the calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā) which are the means to it, and the monkhood which is the means to that [calm and insight]—these three kinds of renunciation (nekkhamma)—through the eye of wisdom established by hearing [the Dhamma] and so on, as the opposite of that [existence], one departs from the household life, which is cluttered with many faults, by entering the ascetic life.

"Dutiyikā" refers to one who was a former companion, who was a wife during the lay life. "Kanakasannibhā" means one whose skin is like the color of gold. "Vaṭṭe anapekkhā" means one who is without attachment to the round of rebirth. "Nekkhammaṃ abhinikkhami" means he left the house for the sake of renunciation and became a monk.

Beings are attached by this greed, thus it is called "ālaya" (attachment); it is indeed craving (taṇhā). Because of the absence of that craving, she is called "nirālayā" (without attachment). Because the bond of craving for relatives is severed for that very reason, she is called "chinnabandhu" (one whose bonds are severed). Having shown the absence of lay bonds, now to show that even the kind of bonds that occur to some who have become monks do not exist, it is said: "anapekkhā kule gaṇe" (without regard for families or groups). In that context, "kule" refers to the families of supporters. "Gaṇe" refers to the groups of ascetics. They are called "brahmacārino" (celibate practitioners). "Upāgamu" means "we both approached." In that context, "nipakā" means "those who are wise." "Nirākule" means "undisturbed because of the absence of people coming and going." "Appasadde" means "having little sound (or no sound) because of being away from the presence and sounds of animals and birds." "Rājuyyāne vasanto" means "two people living in the garden of the King of Bārāṇasī..."
132:
Having shown the absence of human bonds, to show the absence of bonds that can occur even among some ascetics and monks, it is said: "anapekkhā kule gaṇe". In that phrase, "kule" refers to the families of supporters. "Gaṇe" refers to the groups of hermits; the rest are called fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī). "Upāgamu" means "we both approached".

"Tattha" means in the vicinity of the city of Vārāṇasī. "Nipakā" means those who are wise. "Nirākule" means undisturbed by people due to the lack of human traffic. "Appasadde" means having little sound (or no sound) because of being free from the scaring of wild animals and birds, and even from their cries. "Rājuyyāne vasāmubho" means "at that time, we two were living in the garden of the King of Vārāṇasī".

The sequential story here is as follows: In the past, in this very Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), the Bodhisatta passed away from the Brahma realm and was reborn as the son of a wealthy Brahmin in an obscure village in the kingdom of Kāsi. At the time of his naming, they gave him the name "Bodhikumāra". When Bodhikumāra reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and upon his return, although he was unwilling, his parents brought him a young lady of the same caste. She too had passed away from the Brahma realm, possessed supreme beauty, and resembled a celestial nymph. Although both were unwilling, they performed the marriage ceremony for each other. In both of them, the practice of defilements had never occurred before; if there was not even a look at each other with lustful intent, what need is there to speak of other sexual relations? Thus, they were persons of pure virtue.

Later, when his parents passed away, the Great Being performed the funeral rites, called the young lady, and said, "Sister, take this wealth of eighty crores and live happily." When she asked, "My lord, what about you?", he replied, "I have no need for wealth; I shall become a monk." When she asked again, "Is becoming a monk not suitable for women?", he answered, "Sister, becoming a monk is also suitable for women." She then said, "If so, I too have no need for wealth; I shall also become a monk." Both of them renounced all their possessions, gave a great alms-offering, left the house, entered the forest, and became ascetics. Living on large and small fruits and subsisting on the bliss of renunciation for ten years, they traveled through the countryside to consume salt and vinegar. In due course, they reached the city of Vārāṇasī and stayed in the King's garden. Therefore, it is said: "Rājuyyāne vasāmubho" and so forth.

Then one day, the King of Vārāṇasī went to play in the garden. He went near those two ascetics who were spending their time in the bliss of renunciation at one side of the garden. Seeing the extremely graceful and beautiful female ascetic, he became possessed of a lustful mind through the power of defilements and asked the Bodhisatta, "How is this female ascetic related to you?" Then he said, "There is no sensual relationship between this female ascetic and me; we are only equal in our state as monastics. However, when we were laypeople, she was my attendant (wife)." Then the King thought, "This ascetic no longer has any concern for that female ascetic."
133:
Looking at the female wandering ascetic who possessed excellent beauty, the King, with a mind lustful through the power of defilements, asked the Bodhisatta, "Who is this female wandering ascetic to you?"

The Bodhisatta replied, "She is nothing to me; she has merely gone forth into the ascetic life as I have. However, when we were laypeople, she was my wife (attendant at my feet)." The King then thought, "This ascetic says she is nothing to him, yet she was his wife when they were laypeople. It would be good if I were to take this female ascetic into the palace; only by doing so will I know his reaction and conduct toward her." That extremely foolish King, unable to restrain his lustful mind toward the female ascetic, ordered a man, "Take this female wandering ascetic to the royal palace."

That man, obeying the King's command, took the female ascetic away even as she wept, saying, "Injustice is prevailing in the world," and so forth. Hearing her cries, the Bodhisatta looked once and did not look again. Reflecting, "If I were to forbid them, I would become angry with them, and there would be danger to my virtue," he sat there, focusing only on the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla Pāramī). Therefore, it was said in the verse beginning with: "Having gone to see the park, the King saw the Brahmin woman."

In that verse, "Tuyhe sā kā kassa bhariyā" means: Who is she to you? Is she your wife, or your sister, or the wife of another?

"Na mayhaṃ bhariyā esā" means: Although she was my wife when we were laypeople, she is no longer my wife from the time she went forth as an ascetic. I am also no longer her husband. In truth, she is a fellow practitioner of the Dhamma, a companion in the same teaching. I am a wandering ascetic and she is also a wandering ascetic; because we have the same practice and follow the same teaching of wandering ascetics, she is a fellow practitioner (sabrahmacārī).

"Tissā sāratta-gadhito" means being lustful and attached through sensual desire. "Gāhāpetvāna ceṭake" means having the female ascetic seized by ordering the servants or royal agents. "Nippīဠayanto balasā" means oppressing and harming her by force, such as by pulling and dragging her against her will. Thus, he had the royal agents forcibly seize the female ascetic, who did not want to go, and take her into his palace.

"Odapattakiyā" refers to a wife who is taken after touching a water bowl. This term is merely an indication of her status as a former wife.
134:
It should be understood thus: that wife was one who was given by her parents through the Brahmin marriage custom of bestowing wealth. The term "Odapattakiyā" is a locative case (bhāva-lakkhaṇa-sattami) used to mark one action by another. She is called "Sahajātā" because she is associated through the shared state of having gone forth. For this very reason, he said "Ekassāsanī" (one of the same teaching). This word "Ekassāsanī" is a nominative case used in the sense of the locative, meaning "Ekassāsaniyā." "Nayantiyā" means while she was being led away.

"Anger arose in me" means: This female ascetic was your virtuous Brahmin wife when you were a layman. Since becoming an ascetic, she is like a sister born together with you because she is a fellow practitioner. They are forcibly dragging and leading that female ascetic away in your very presence. When encouraged by manly pride, thinking, "O ascetic Bodhi, where is your manhood?", anger suddenly rose from within my mind, like a cobra that has slept for a long time in an anthill and, being struck by some man, makes the sound "su-su" and raises its hood.

34-35. "Along with the arising of anger" means at the same time that anger arose. "Reflected on the vow of virtue" means reflecting on his own Perfection of Virtue (Sīla Pāramī). "Subdued the anger right there" means restraining that anger while sitting in that very place. "Did not allow it to increase further" means not allowing that anger, which had arisen once, to grow any more.

This is what is meant: As soon as anger arose, he rebuked himself, thinking, "O wandering ascetic Bodhi, do you not wish to fulfill all the Perfections and realize Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)? For such a person as you, to slip even in a matter of virtue is like someone drowning in the water of a cow's footprint yet wishing to reach the far shore of the great ocean." Thus, subduing the anger in that very moment through the power of reflection, he prevented it from arising again. Therefore, he said the verse beginning with: "If that Brahmin woman..."

The meaning of that verse is: Whether it be that King or anyone else, even if they were to cut that female wandering ascetic into pieces with a sharp sword or spear, even if such a thing happened, I would not break my virtue, my Perfection of Virtue. Why? For the sake of Enlightenment (Bodhi) alone. Only through virtue that is unbroken in all respects can one reach Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), and not otherwise.
135: It is not that I do not love that brahmin woman, nor that I dislike her. In every way—by birth, by lineage, by family background, by perfection of conduct, by long association, and by the perfection of virtues such as renunciation—it is not that I do not love her, nor that she is unpleasant to me. There is not even a slight feeling of dislike toward her. It is also not that I lack strength; indeed, I possess it. I am one who has strength like that of a noble elephant and am endowed with power. If I so desired, I could immediately rise, strike down the men who are dragging her away, take her, and go wherever I wish. I love Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold more than that female wanderer. For that reason, I shall protect my virtue (sīla) alone. Then, the King did not stay long in the garden but went very quickly, summoned the female wanderer, and invited her with great honor. The female wanderer spoke of the faults of worldly honor, the virtues of renunciation, and how she and the Bodhisatta had renounced a vast amount of wealth and entered the monkhood through spiritual urgency (saṃvega). The King, unable to win her heart by any means, thought: "This female wanderer is virtuous and of good conduct. That wanderer also showed no sign of agitation even when she was being dragged away; he has a mind detached from all things. It is not proper for me to commit an offense against such virtuous persons. I should take this female wanderer back to the garden and apologize to both her and that wanderer." Having thought thus, he ordered his attendants, "Bring the female wanderer to the garden," and he himself went ahead to the Bodhisatta and asked, "O monk, did anger arise in your mind when I was taking that female wanderer away?" The Great Being said: "Anger arose in me but was not released; it was not released while I live. Like a heavy rain suppressing dust, I restrained it immediately." Hearing this, the King thought, "Is he speaking only regarding anger, or is he speaking of some other art or skill?" and asked again: "What arose in you and was not released? What did you not release while you live? Like a heavy rain suppressing dust, what was it that you restrained?"
136: In that verse, 'uppajji' means anger arose in me once, but did not arise again. 'Na muccittha' means I did not allow that anger to be released or let out through bodily or vocal intimation. 'Rajaṃva vipulā vuṭṭhī' means just as a heavy out-of-season rain instantly suppresses the dust that arises in the month of Nayon, the last month of summer, so too did I restrain that anger by calming it. Then, the Great Being, wishing to show the King of Bārāṇasī the dangers of anger in various ways, said: "When anger is born, one does not see the benefit; when it is not born, the virtuous person sees the benefit clearly. That anger arose in me but was not released; anger is the domain of the foolish. When anger is born, enemies who seek one's suffering rejoice. That anger arose in me but was not released; anger is the domain of the foolish. While anger is being born, one does not understand one's own benefit (how then could one understand another's?). That anger arose in me but was not released; anger is the domain of the foolish. One who is overcome by anger abandons merit and destroys even great wealth. O Great King, that anger—fearsome like a powerful army and crushing—was not released from me. Just as fire is born when wood is rubbed with a fire-stick, and that fire burns the very wood from which it was born; so too, in a dull, foolish, and ignorant person, anger is born from the desire to quarrel, and he is burned by that very anger. As fire blazes in grass and wood, so does anger increase in one; his fame and glory wane like the moon in the dark fortnight. As a smokeless fire is extinguished, so does anger subside in one; his fame and glory wax like the moon in the bright fortnight. Being beyond the reproach of others, he shines like a flame." Thus he preached the Dhamma with these verses. In those verses, 'na passati' means seeing neither one's own benefit nor the benefit of others. 'Sādhu passati' means the virtuous person sees both one's own benefit and the benefit of others well. 'Dummedhagocaro' means being the object of the foolish, or having the habit of foolishness, or having delusion as its root.
137:
In those verses, "na passati" means he does not see even his own benefit, let alone the benefit of others; he simply does not see. "Sādhu passati" means he clearly sees his own benefit, the benefit of others, and both. "Dummedhagocaro" means being the object of those without wisdom, or having the food or fuel of the foolish who lack wisdom. "Dukkhamesino" means desiring suffering. "Sadatthaṃ" means one's own benefit and prosperity. "Parakkare" means he should remove or destroy. "Sabhīmaseno" means that anger is endowed with a vast army of defilements that produce terrifying fear. "Pamaddī" means having the nature of crushing beings with great force. "Na me amuccathā" means "he did not obtain release from me, but was tamed within and made poisonless." Alternatively, it means that just as milk does not turn into curd in an instant, anger did not remain in the mind even for a moment.

"Manthamānasmiṃ" means while being rubbed with fire-sticks. There is also a variant reading "mathamānasmiṃ". "Yasmā" means because of which wood. "Ginī" means fire. "Bālassa avijānato" means for the ignorant fool. "Sārambhā ဇာယတေ" means that anger, like fire, arises from the excessive action of wishing to increase conflict, just as fire arises from rubbing fire-sticks. "Sapi tenevā" means that the fool is burnt by that very anger, just as wood is burnt by fire. "Anindho dhūmaketūva" means like a flame without fuel. "Tassa" means for that person endowed with the patience of endurance, fame and followers increase step by step, like the moon in the waxing fortnight.

The King of Bārāṇasī, after hearing the Dhamma discourse of the Bodhisatta, apologized to the Great Being and the female wanderer who had come from the palace, saying, "Venerable ones, please stay in this very park, enjoying the bliss of renunciation. I shall provide you with righteous protection and guardianship." Having said this and paid homage, he departed. Both of them lived in that very park. Later, the female wanderer passed away. The Bodhisatta entered the Himalayas, developed the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledges (abhiññā), and at the end of his life, was destined for the Brahma realm.

At that time, the female wanderer was the mother of Rāhula (Yasodharā). The King was the Elder Ānanda. Bodhi the wanderer was I, the Lord of the World.

In this Jātaka, the remaining perfections should also be extracted as appropriate. Likewise, the departure from home, similar to the Great Renunciation, by abandoning a great mass of wealth and a large circle of relatives; and after such renunciation, being respected by many people yet having supreme fewness of wishes, being unattached to families and groups, being disgusted with gains and honors, delighting in seclusion, and living a very austere life. When that virtuous and good female wanderer was being forcibly touched and harassed in front of him without her consent, he reflected on the Perfection of Virtue...
138:
...delighting greatly in seclusion due to disgust for gains and honors, having an extremely austere livelihood, and when such a virtuous and good female wanderer was being forcibly touched and harassed in front of him, he reflected on the Perfection of Virtue and remained without mental corruption. Furthermore, when that king who had committed the offense approached him, he established a mind of welfare and loving-kindness (mettā) and instructed him sequentially regarding the benefits of the present life and the future life. These and other qualities and powers of the Great Being should be understood in this Jātaka. Therefore, it is said: "Thus wonderful indeed... by the practice in accordance with the Dhamma."

## The Explanation of the Cūḷabodhi-cariyā is Finished.

## 5. Mahisā-rāja-cariyā-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth [story], the Mahisā-rāja-cariyā, "mahiṃso pavanacārako" means "the forest buffalo who used to roam in the great forest"; this is the connection of the meaning "at the time I was [such a buffalo]". "Pavaḍḍhakāyo" means having a very large body because the limbs and parts grew thick and full upon reaching maturity. "Balavā" means being endowed with great strength and power. "Mahanto" means having an extensive body. It is said that at that time, the Bodhisatta's body was about the size of a young elephant. "Bhīmadassano" means having a terrifying appearance because his large body and forest-buffalo nature caused fear in those who did not know his virtue.

"Pabbāre" means in a rocky overhang or a cave under a hanging rock. "Dakāsaye" means near a body of water. "Hotettha ṭhānaံ" means a certain place within this great forest that was a standing place for forest buffaloes. "Tahiံ tahiံ" means in various places.

"Vicaranto" means while wandering about to investigate a comfortable place to stay. "Ṭhānaံ addasa bhaddakaံ" means that while wandering thus, he saw a good place at the foot of a tree within that great forest which was comfortable for him. Having seen that place and approached it, he would stand and sleep there. It shows that after seeking food, he would go to that tree-foot during the day and spend the time standing and sleeping.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the species of buffalo in the Himalayan region. Upon reaching maturity, he was endowed with strength and had a large body about the size of a young elephant. While wandering through mountain bases, valleys, forests, and so on, he saw a large, comfortable tree-foot and lived there during the day after seeking food. At that time...
139:
While wandering at the foot of mountains, in mountain clefts, and through dense, difficult forests, he saw a pleasant spot at the root of a large tree. Having taken his food, he stayed there during the day. Then, a frivolous monkey descended from the tree, climbed onto the Great Being's back, and urinated and defecated. He also held the horns and hung from them, and held the tail and swung like a swing, playing in this manner. Because the Bodhisatta was endowed with the qualities of patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, he did not take the monkey's bad behavior to heart. The monkey did this repeatedly. Therefore, it was said: "Atha ettha kapi māgantvā," and so forth.

In that verse, "kapi māgantvā" means the monkey came; the letter "ma" is a sandhi consonant. "Pāpo" refers to one who has a wicked nature. "Anariyo" is called ignoble because he practices what should not be practiced, or because he does not practice what should be practiced; it means one with low conduct. "Lahū" refers to one who is frivolous. "Khandhe" refers to the region of the shoulder and back. "Mutteti" means he urinates. "Ohadeti" means he defecates. "Taṃ" refers to me, who was a buffalo at that time.

"Sakiṃ pi divasaṃ" means he ruins me even for one day, which implies he ruins me all the time. Therefore, it was said: "Dūseti maṃ sabbakālaṃ." It is not just for two, three, or four days, but he ruins me with urine and so forth at all times. It is intended to show that whenever he wishes to urinate and so forth, he does it only upon me. "Upadduto" means being oppressed. It means being one who is constantly oppressed because of that monkey hanging from the horns, smearing him with impurities such as urine, and because he had to wash those impurities away many times by sprinkling water mixed with mud using the tips of his horns and the tip of his tail.

"Yakkho" refers to the deity guarding that tree. That deity, standing on the tree trunk, wishing to clarify this meaning, asked: "King Buffalo, why do you endure the insults of this wicked monkey?" and spoke these words to me: "Nāsehetaṃ chavaṃ pāpaṃ, siṅgehi ca khurehi ca." The meaning of these words is: "King Buffalo, destroy this vile and wicked monkey with your horns and your hooves."

"Evaṃ vutte tadā yakkhe" means when the tree deity had spoken thus at that time. "Ahaṃ taṃ idamabraviṃ" means I spoke these words, which are about to be said, to that tree deity. "Kuṇapena" means by the stench of the defilements, which is called "kuṇapa" (corpse-like) because it is extremely loathsome to the pure and virtuous due to the oozing of the impurities of defilements, and because it smells very foul like a rotting corpse. "Pāpena" means by the wicked demerit of taking life. "Anariyena" means by the ignoble conduct, which is the practice of low men such as hunters and fishermen who are not Noble Ones (Ariyas) or virtuous people. "O tree deity, why do you smear me (with fault)? You have spoken improper words, urging me toward evil..."
140:
Because it is the habit of ignoble and non-virtuous people such as hunters and fishermen, it is an ignoble (anariya) practice. He showed this by saying, "O Goddess, for what reason do you smear me (with blame)? You, who incite me to evil, have spoken improper words."

Now, wishing to show the danger in that evil conduct, he spoke the verse beginning with "Yadihaṃ." The meaning of that verse is: O good Goddess, if I were to become angry at that monkey, I would become even more wicked than him. For that foolish monkey is called low because of his unrighteous conduct. If I were to practice an even stronger evil than him, would I not become more wicked than he because of that practice? It is an impossible thing (aṭṭhāna) that one like me, who stands knowing this world, the next world, and that which is beyond (lokuttara), and who is solely dedicated to the welfare of others, should practice such evil conduct. Furthermore, there is much more to be said: if I were to commit such evil, my virtue would be destroyed, and my perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī) would be breached. Wise deities and humans would also reproach me, saying, "Look, friends, this Bodhisatta, while seeking omniscience, has committed such evil."

In the phrase "hīḷitā jīvitā vāpi," the word "vā" is used for emphasis (avadhāraṇa). Death while possessing pure virtue is much better and more excellent than a life reproached by the wise in this way. "Knowing this, why should I harm another for the sake of my life?"—I, who know this, will no longer harm another being for the sake of my own life; the meaning is that there is no reason to harm this monkey.

However, this monkey will think other buffaloes are just like me and will perform such improper conduct toward them. Then, when he does this to fierce buffaloes, they will surely kill him. Through his being killed by others, I will be released from suffering and from the sin of taking life (pāṇātipāta). Therefore, he said:

"Thinking they are just like me, he will do the same to others;
They will kill him, and that will be my release (from the situation)."

In that verse, "mamevāyaṃ" means this monkey [thinking they are] just like me. "Aññepi" means to others as well. The rest is exactly as already explained.
141:
"Hīnamajjhima-ukkaṭṭhesu" means in the occurrence of low, middle, and superior objects. "Sahanto avamānitaṃ" means enduring the contempt and oppression committed by them without making any distinction. "Evaṃ labhati sappañño" means that one who is wise, without making distinctions between low and superior, establishing patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, and enduring their faults, develops perfections such as virtue and attains the desired and wished-for Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa); he penetrates it, and for him, that Omniscience is not far away.

In this way, the Great Being (Mahāsatta), the Bodhisatta, made his intention clear and preached the Dhamma to the deity. After two or three days, that Buffalo King went to another place. Another fierce buffalo, finding the place suitable for living, came and stood there. A wicked monkey, with the mistaken perception that "this is the same buffalo," climbed onto its back and behaved wickedly as before. Then, that fierce buffalo shook the monkey off, threw him to the ground, gored his chest with its horns, and trampled him with its feet, crushing him to pieces.

At that time, the virtuous Buffalo King was the Lord of the World, the Buddha.

The remaining perfections (pāramīs) of that Buffalo King should also be extracted from this Jātaka in the same manner as mentioned below. Likewise, the qualities and powers of the Great Being in this Mahiṃsa Jātaka should be understood just as in the Hatthināga, Bhūridatta, and Campeyya-nāgarāja Cariyās.

## The Explanation of the Mahiṃsa-rāja-cariyā ends.

## 6. Ruru-miga-rāja-cariyā-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth Jātaka, "Sutattakanakasannibho" means having an appearance like gold that has been well-smelted in fire so that it is free from all black spots. "Migarājā ruru nāma" means the King of Deer named Ruru by birth, a king of the deer who are Ruru by species. "Paramasīlasamāhito" means being endowed with supreme virtue, being both pure in virtue and concentrated in mind, or it should be understood in this context as having a mind well-established in pure virtue.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born in the species of Ruru deer. The skin of his body was like the color of a well-polished gold plate; his hands and feet were as if prepared with lac resin; his tail was like a yak's tail; his horns had the color of silver garlands; his eyes...
142:
...his eyes were like well-polished precious gems. His lips were like a piece of red blanket placed over the mouth. That Deer King, desiring to live in seclusion and abandoning association with the crowd, left his followers and lived alone in a delightful forest mixed with sāla trees and full of blooming flowers at a bend in the Ganges. Referring to that, it was said:

“In a delightful place, pleasant,
Secluded and uninhabited by humans,
There I went to dwell,
On the charming banks of the Ganges.”

In that verse, ‘ramme padese’ (in a delightful place) refers to a delightful forest region because it is endowed with ground areas spread with white sand like pearls, forest areas covered with smooth green grass, stone slabs as colorful as variegated rugs, and water bodies with water as clear as sapphire; and also because it is mostly covered with species of grass that are red like the color of velvet mites (indagopaka) and pleasant to the touch. ‘Ramaṇီye’ (pleasant) means pleasant in the sense of producing delight for a person who enters there, because it is beautified by forest thickets adorned with wide branches decorated with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, where various flocks of birds sing, which shine with various trees and creepers, and are mostly adorned with groves of mango and sāla trees. This was also said in the Ruru-miga-rāja Jātaka:

“In this forest grove, mango and sāla trees are in bloom;
In this place covered with grass the color of velvet mites,
This deer king remains.”

‘Vivitte’ (secluded) means empty due to the absence of human habitation. ‘Amanussake’ (uninhabited) means devoid of humans because even traveling humans are not there. ‘Manorame’ (charming) means charming because it delights the minds of those who especially desire seclusion due to being endowed with the aforementioned qualities.

## Atha uparigaṅgāya

In this context, the word ‘atha’ is a particle indicating the start of a new topic (adhikāra). By that word, it is shown that while I was living there in that manner, this new event occurred. ‘Uparigaṅgāya’ means in the upper current of the Ganges river. ‘Dhanikehi paripီḷito’ means a person who, having taken loans and being unable to repay them, is oppressed and harassed by creditors.

It is heard that—a wealthy merchant in the city of Bārāṇasī thought of his son, “If this son of mine learns a craft, he will be weary,” and thus did not have him learn any craft at all. Beyond singing, playing instruments, dancing, and eating, he knew nothing else. When he reached adulthood, his parents married him to a suitable wife, handed over the wealth, and then passed away. After his parents died, surrounded by womanizers, drunkards, and the like, he squandered all the wealth through various means of ruin. When he took loans in various places and was unable to repay them, being harassed by the creditors...
143:
After the death of his parents, that merchant's son, surrounded by womanizers, drunkards, and the like, squandered all his wealth through various means of ruin. Having taken loans from various places and being unable to repay those debts, when he was pressed by his creditors, he thought, "What is the use of living this life? In this state of existence, I have become like the son of another (an obscure person); death is better for me." He then said to the creditors, "Bring your debt records and come; I have ancestral wealth buried on the banks of the Gaṅgā River, and I will pay you with that wealth." They went along with him. The merchant's son, acting as if he were pointing out the places where the treasure was buried, saying, "The wealth is here, the wealth is there," thought, "In this way, I shall be free from debt," and he fled and jumped into the Gaṅgā River. While he was being carried away by the fierce current, he cried out piteously. Therefore, it was said, "Atha uparigaṅgāya," and so forth.

In that verse, "Jīvāmi vā marāmi vā" means: "Whether I, who have fallen into this current of the Gaṅgā, live or die, whether there be life or death for me here, in either case, I shall be free from the oppression of the creditors."

"Majjhe gaṅgāya gacchati" means that while the man was being carried away in the Gaṅgā day and night, because of his attachment to life, he had not yet reached death; fearing the danger of death and crying out piteously, he was carried away in the middle of the Gaṅgā where the water was deep.

At that time, the Great Being, the Deer King, hearing the sound of his piteous lamentation at midnight, thought, "The sound of a human is heard; let him not die while I am here; I will give him his life." He rose from his thicket-bed, went to the riverbank, and comforted him, saying, "O man, do not fear, I will give you your life." Then, cutting through the current, he went to him, took him upon his back, brought him to the shore, and led him to his own dwelling. He dispelled the man's exhaustion and fed him with various fruits. After two or three days had passed, he said to him, "O man, I will set you on the road leading to Bārāṇasī; do not tell anyone that a golden deer lives in such and such a place." The man agreed, saying, "Very well, lord." The Bodhisatta Deer King took him upon his back, set him down on the road to Bārāṇasī, and returned. Therefore, the verse beginning with "Tassāhaṃ saddaṃ sutvāna, karuṇaṃ paridevato" was spoken.

In that verse, "Ko si tvaṃ naro" means "Who are you, man? From where have you come floating thus?"
144:
## Attano karaṇanti attano kiriyaṃ. Dhanikehi bhītoti iṇāyikehi ubbiggo. Tasitoti utrasto.

"Attano karaṇaṃ" means one's own action (behavior). "Dhanikehi bhīto" means being afraid because of the creditors. "Tasito" means being terrified.

"Tassa katvāna kāruṇyaṃ, cajitvā mama jīvitaṃ" means having felt compassion for him and being urged by great compassion, sacrificing my own life for that man. "Pavisitvā nīhariṃ tassa" means entering the river, cutting through the current, going straight to him, taking him upon my back, and bringing him out (from the water). The word "tassa" is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative (the object). There is also a Pali reading "tattha," which means in that river. "Andhakāramhi rattiyā" means at the time of the darkness of the night, during the night of the dark fortnight.

"Assatthakālamaññāya" means having dispelled his exhaustion, fed him with various fruits, and knowing the time when his fatigue had vanished after two or three days. "Ekaṃ taṃ varaṃ yācāmi" means I ask one boon from you; give me one boon. If one asks, "What is that boon?" it is said: "Mā maṃ kassaci pāvada"—do not tell anyone, whether it be a king or a great minister, that "a golden deer lives in such and such a place."

Thereafter, on the very day that man entered the city of Bārāṇasī, the Chief Queen said to the King, "O Great King, I saw in a dream a golden-colored deer preaching the Dhamma to me. Since my dreams usually come true, such a deer must surely exist. Therefore, I wish to hear the Dhamma of the golden deer. If I hear it, I shall live; if not, I shall no longer live." The King comforted the Queen, saying, "If it exists in the world of men, you shall have it." He then summoned the Brahmins and asked, "Do golden deer exist?" Hearing their reply, "Yes, Great King, they do," he placed a thousand coins in a golden casket, set it upon the back of an elephant, and had a proclamation made by beat of drum throughout the city: "Whoever can point out the golden deer, I will give him this bag of coins together with the elephant." Desiring to give even more than that, he had this verse written on a golden plate and read throughout the whole city:

"To him who points out to me this deer,
The most excellent of deer among all deer,
I shall give an excellent village
And women adorned with ornaments."

Then, the merchant's son, hearing that verse, went to the king's men and said, "I will point out such a deer to the King."
145:
“I will tell you about the deer; show me to the King,” he said. The royal attendants took him to the King and reported the matter. The King asked, “Friend, is it true? Did you see it?” He replied, “It is true, Your Majesty. Please come with me; I will show you the deer.” The King made that very man his guide and went to that place with a large retinue. He surrounded the area pointed out by that treacherous man with armed men and ordered, “Make a loud shout!” while he himself stood in a suitable place with a few men. That man also stood not far away.

When the Bodhisatta heard the sound, he thought, “This is the sound of a large army. Surely, danger must have arisen because of that man I rescued,” and having risen, he looked at the whole assembly and thought, “I will be safe only where the King is standing,” and headed towards the King. When the King saw the approaching stag, he thought, “A deer with the strength of a noble elephant is coming to attack,” and prepared his arrow, thinking, “I will threaten this deer; if it flees, I will shoot it to weaken it and then capture it,” and stood facing the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta recited this verse:

“Wait a moment, Great King, chief of charioteers, do not shoot me.
Who told Your Majesty that this deer stays here?”

The King, captivated by the Bodhisatta's sweet speech, withdrew his arrow and stood respectfully. The Bodhisatta approached the King and spoke pleasant words of greeting. The people also laid down all their weapons and came to surround the King. Therefore, it was said:

“Desiring wealth, that man went to the city and, when asked, informed the King.
He took the King and came to my presence.”

The meaning of that verse is: That wicked man, a betrayer of friends, whom I saved from the peril of death when he was nearly losing his life, went to the city of Bārāṇasī and, hoping for the wealth he would receive, told the King about me. After telling him, he acted as a guide to have the King capture me and, bringing the King, arrived at my presence.

The Bodhisatta, with a voice as sweet as the tinkling of small golden bells, asked the King again, “Who told Your Majesty that this deer stays here?” At that moment, that wicked man stepped back a little and stood within earshot. The King pointed to that wicked man, saying, “This man pointed you out to me.” Then the Bodhisatta said:

“Truly, what some people say in this world is true:
It is better to salvage a log floating in the water than to rescue certain people.”

The meaning of that verse is: Great King, it is indeed true what some people have said in this world—that it is better to salvage a log floating in the water than to rescue certain people from the water. Hearing these words, the King was struck with emotion and said:

“Ruru King of Deer, why do you reproach the beasts, or the birds, or the humans?
Hearing you speak in a human tongue, a great fear has come upon me.”

The meaning of that verse is: Ruru King of Deer, why do you reproach any among the beasts, or any among the birds...”
146:
That wicked man stepped back a little and stood within earshot. The King pointed to that wicked man, saying, “This man pointed you out to me.” Then the Bodhisatta said: “Truly, what some people say in this world is true: ‘It is better to salvage a log floating in the water than to rescue certain people.’ That saying is indeed true.” Hearing those words, the King was struck with emotion and said: “O Ruru King of Deer, do you reproach the beasts, or the birds, or the humans? Hearing you speak in the language of humans, a great fear has come upon me.” Then the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), wishing to show, “Great King, I do not reproach the beasts or the birds; I only reproach the human,” said:

“I rescued that man who was being carried away by the swift current of the great waters of the Gaṅgā.
Because of him, this danger has come to me. Great King, association with the unrighteous is indeed painful.”

In that verse, ‘nipplavitaṃ’ means being salvaged onto dry land. ‘Ekacciyo’ means that even if a certain treacherous, wicked man falls into the water and is about to die, rescuing him is not noble. This is because a log can be of service for various types of construction, whereas a treacherous person only leads to destruction; therefore, a log is superior to such a person. ‘Migānaṃ’ is a question: “O Ruru King of Deer, do you reproach any of the beasts, or the birds, or the humans?” ‘Bhayañhi maṃ vindatinapparūpaṃ’ means a great fear has come upon me, as if it were my own possession. ‘Vāhane’ refers to the River Gaṅgā, which is capable of carrying away whatever falls into it. ‘Mahodake salile’ means in a great expanse of water. By these two terms, the abundance of water in the River Gaṅgā is shown. ‘Tatonidānaṃ’ means: “Great King, this man whom you pointed out, I rescued him at midnight while he was weeping piteously as he was being carried away by the River Gaṅgā. Because I saved him, this danger has come upon me. Association with the unrighteous is indeed painful.”
147:
Upon hearing those words, the King became angry with that man and thought, "This fool does not recognize the gratitude due to one who has been so helpful, but instead causes him distress. I shall pierce him with an arrow and bring his life to an end." Thus, he prepared his arrow. Therefore, it is said:

"Whatever service was done, I have informed the King;
Hearing my words, the King prepared his arrow;
'I shall slay this treacherous and ignoble person right here.'"

In that verse, "yāvatā karaṇaṃ" refers to all the helpful deeds I had performed for him. "Pakappayi" means he prepared or aimed the arrow. "Mittadubbhi" refers to one who has the habit of betraying his own helpful and good friends.

Then the Bodhisatta, the Deer King, thought, "Let not this fool perish because of me," and said, "Great King, killing—whether it be a fool or a wise man—is not praised by the virtuous; indeed, it is only blameworthy. Therefore, do not kill this man; let him go as he pleases. Furthermore, do not fail to give him the wealth you promised to bestow." He continued, "I will also perform whatever you desire; I surrender my body to you." Therefore, it is said:

"O Great King, seeking to protect him, I exchange myself for him;
Let him remain in safety; I shall be at your disposal."

In that verse, "nimminiṃ" means that out of a desire to protect that treacherous and evil person, I exchanged him with my own person; by surrendering myself to the King, I prevented his death which was imminent at the King's hands. "Tiṭṭhateso" and so forth show the manner of the exchange.

Now, to show for what purpose that self-exchange was made, the concluding verse is spoken. Its meaning is: At that time, although the King wished to deprive that treacherous man of life because of me, I surrendered myself to the King and protected only my virtue (sīla), but did not protect my life. It should be understood that the meaning of the final verse is that my practice of being endowed with virtue, without regard for my own life, was solely for the sake of Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi).

Then the King, seeing that the Bodhisatta Deer King had sacrificed his own life to prevent the death of that man, was filled with a joyful heart and said, "Go, man! By the grace of the Deer King, you are released from the danger of death at my hands," and he had the wealth given to him as promised. He granted the Bodhisatta his freedom as desired, and having invited him to the city, he had both the city and the Bodhisatta adorned, and requested him to preach the Dhamma to the Queen.
148:
"Though I surrendered myself to the King, I constantly protected only my virtue, and not my life. In every circumstance, I protected that virtue without regard for my own life. The perfection of virtue is solely for the sake of Supreme Enlightenment."

Then the King, seeing that the Bodhisatta Deer King had sacrificed his own life to prevent the death of that fool, was pleased in heart and said, "Go, man! By the grace of the Deer King, you are released from death at my hands," and he had that wealth given to him as promised. Granting the Great Being (Mahāsatta) as much freedom as he desired, he brought the Bodhisatta to the city, had both the city and the Bodhisatta adorned, and requested him to preach the Dhamma to the Queen. The Great Being, beginning with the Queen, preached the Dhamma in the sweet language of humans to the King and the royal assembly. He exhorted the King with the Ten Royal Virtues (Dasa-rājadhamma), instructed the multitude, and then entered the forest to live surrounded by a herd of deer. The King also, established in the Bodhisatta's exhortation, granted amnesty to all living beings, performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), and became one destined for a happy realm (sugati).

At that time, the merchant's son became Devadatta, the King became Ānanda, and the Ruru Deer King became the Lord of the World (the Buddha).

In this Jātaka as well, the remaining perfections should be extracted in the appropriate manner as previously mentioned. Likewise, in this Jātaka, one should understand the power of the Great Being's qualities, such as: his living alone, having abandoned the herd because of his delight in seclusion and lack of desire for association with others; his rising from his resting place upon hearing the distressed cry of a man drifting in the river at midnight and lamenting piteously; his going to the riverbank and, disregarding his own life, descending into the great flood of the Ganges to cut through the current; his carrying that man on his back to reach the shore and comforting him; his relieving the man's exhaustion by giving him various fruits; his again carrying him on his back to lead him out of the forest and setting him on the main road; his going fearlessly to face the King who stood ready to shoot with a prepared arrow and first greeting him in human tongue with sweet hospitality; his preaching the Dhamma to the King who wished to kill the treacherous and evil man, thereby again sacrificing his life to release him from death; his causing the King to give the wealth as promised; his causing the King to grant amnesty to all beings when offered boons by the King; his establishing the people in meritorious deeds like giving by preaching the Dhamma to the multitude with the King and Queen at the head; his giving exhortation to the deer who had received amnesty to refrain from eating the crops of humans; and his making that exhortation permanent until this day by the sign of the leaf (paṇṇasaññā).

## The Explanation of the Conduct of the Ruru Deer King is finished.
